Multi-patterning coloring conflicts that were not considered in global route

data.classic_trap: Assuming the global route was correct and treating the DRC as a routing bug, when it's actually a pin-access problem that requires cell flipping or layer assignment changes – global route ignores pin geometry.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, detailed-route hotspots are dominated by multi-patterning cut-layer coloring and via-resistance rules, requiring color-aware routing; at 28nm, it's usually simple spacing vs. enclosure.

data.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check the total cell area relative to the core area – if utilization >85%, it's likely a density limit
first_checks.why_first: Quick sanity check for fundamental capacity

first_checks.check: Check the overflow histogram for a specific macro or partition that has extremely high pin density
first_checks.why_first: Narrows to a specific block that is overpopulated

first_checks.check: Check if the overflow is on a single side of the chip (e.g., near the right edge) – could be a placement blockage from power grid or I/O
first_checks.why_first: Spatial bias indicates a fixed obstacle

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a placement with a 20% larger core area (virtual) by adding padding; if overflow drops to zero, the root is absolute density; if still high, it's a structural blockage (macros)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Drops with padding = density issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Remains high = macro/pin blockage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all hard macros from the design and run placement; if overflow disappears, the root is macro placement causing a ‘squeeze’ effect; if remains, it's cell-area overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Disappears = macro placement issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Remains = too many cells

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the unroutable area is exactly over an array of filler cells or tap cells – those can be placed elsewhere; if removing them frees enough tracks, the root is excessive filler density
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Filler removal helps = filler density
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No help = core logic overflow

common_root_causes.cause: Overall core utilization exceeding the practical routable limit (typically ~70-75% for high performance, 85% for low performance)
Hard macro placement creating narrow corridors that break global routing
High pin density on macros (e.g., memory) that consume all routing tracks near the macro boundary
Placement guidelines that forced cells to specific layers, causing local track overflow

data.classic_trap: Blowing up the core area or reducing cell count, when the real problem is a single macro placed badly, creating a choke point – check macro-to-macro spacing first.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, unroutable placement is often due to finFET width quantization and pin accessibility constraints that are stricter than density; at 28nm, it's usually just density and macro spacing.

data.pattern_name: Block-boundary input delay budget (input-to-register)
data.situation: When assigning a maximum input delay (setup) from a chip pin to the first register inside the block, given an external launch clock and a board/interconnect delay.
data.derivation: Assume external clock period T = 10ns. External launch path delay from chip pin to external register clock is Lc = 0.5ns (assumed, conf 0.7). Board trace delay from external register to our pin is Bd = 0.8ns (assumed, conf 0.6). Our internal clock skew (clock uncertainty) is U = 0.2ns. We reserve a derate/margin of 15% of T for process variation on the external side: M = 1.5ns (assumed, conf 0.5). The input delay (max) = T - (Lc + Bd + U + M)? Actually, standard equation: external clock path to launch register + board delay + our internal clock path skew. The official SDC set_input_delay -max = (external launch clock path delay + board trace delay) - (external capture clock path delay). We usually simplify: set_input_delay -max = (1 - alpha) * T, where alpha is the fraction of cycle available for internal logic. We choose alpha = 0.6, so input delay = 0.4 * T = 4.0ns. Then internal logic has 6.0ns to meet. Derivation: we measure external board timing and clock jitter, then back-calculate: input_delay = T - (internal_path_required_time). We compute required internal path = T - board_delay - clock_uncertainty - margin. So input_delay = board_delay + clock_uncertainty + margin. Here we set input_delay = 4.0ns (board+margin+uncertainty).
data.wrong_way: Using the chip pin's own output driver delay as the input delay, or setting it to zero because 'the board is short' – this silently forces the internal logic to run at full cycle minus zero, leaving no time for the external launch path, causing hidden timing violations at the top level that require massive respin.
data.defense: Present the external timing budget document from system engineering: measured or simulated board trace delays, clock source jitter, and the allowed internal logic time. Show that the internal logic has at least 60% of the cycle, which is validated by a timing-closure histogram of the first registers.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (input delay too large): internal logic is over-constrained, causing over-optimization, area/power blowup, and possible routing congestion; too loose (input delay too small): top-level integration fails with setup violations at the pins that cannot be fixed without board re-spin.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, board-level interconnect OCV is smaller but on-chip variation (OCV) is larger, so we add a separate on-chip derate to the internal path; at 28nm, board delay dominates.

data.pattern_name: Block-boundary output delay budget (register-to-output)
data.situation: When assigning a maximum output delay (setup) from the last register inside the block to an external chip pin, given a capture clock at an external register.
data.derivation: Given period T = 10ns. External capture clock path to the external register is Ccapture = 0.6ns (assumed, conf 0.6). Board trace from our pin to the external register is B = 1.2ns (assumed, conf 0.7). Our internal clock skew to the launching register is U = 0.15ns. We reserve a margin of 10% of T for external variation M = 1.0ns (assumed, conf 0.5). The output delay (max) = T - (Ccapture + B + U + M) ? Actually, the standard is: set_output_delay -max = (external capture clock path + board delay) - (external launch clock path) but we typically set it as the time allowed from our launch clock to the pin, so we compute: output_delay = T - (time available for external logic). We set output_delay = T - (Ccapture + B + margin) = 10 - (0.6+1.2+1.0) = 7.2ns? That would mean our internal path gets only 2.8ns, which is too tight. Actually, we set output_delay so that our internal logic can take a fraction of T. We choose output_delay = 0.35*T = 3.5ns, leaving internal logic 6.5ns. The arithmetic: we measure board + external capture = 1.8ns, plus margin = 1.0ns, so total external overhead = 2.8ns. Then output_delay = external overhead + some guard = 3.5ns, meaning we allocate 3.5ns for the external path, leaving 6.5ns for internal path. Derivation step: output_delay = (board_delay + capture_clock_delay + margin) * 1.1 (safety factor).
data.wrong_way: Setting output delay to zero or to the Tclk-to-Q of the last flop, because you think the external capture is instantaneous – this silently hides that the board and external clock path consume almost half the cycle, causing top-level hold violations that are impossible to fix because the internal data arrives too early.
data.defense: Provide the system-level interface spec showing the external capture clock phase and board propagation. Show that the combined external path (board + capture skew) is under 3.5ns, which is the budget we allocated.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (output delay too high): internal logic is over-tightened, may fail to close within block; too loose (output delay too low): external setup violations at top level, requiring board delay reduction or higher drive strength.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, the output delay is often limited by package parasitics and the external capture clock is more predictable due to improved PLL jitter; at 28nm, board traces dominate.

data.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path on non-critical combinatorial logic
data.situation: A data path between two flops has a large logic depth that cannot meet the clock period, but the signal is not timing-critical (e.g., a status register updated infrequently).
data.derivation: Check the functional specification: the path is enabled by a write enable that asserts only once every N cycles. We set a multicycle path with N=2 (or 3). Derivation: we compute the worst-case delay of the combinational cloud, say 12ns, while period is 5ns. We set multicycle setup = 3 (i.e., 3 cycles) so the capture flop uses launch edge 3 cycles earlier. We do not set multicycle hold, or we set hold=2 to avoid hold violation on the launch edge. We derive the number M = ceil(delay / period) + 1 margin. For delay=12ns, period=5ns, M=ceil(12/5)+1 = 3+1? Actually, we use M=3 (capture on the 3rd edge). We verify that the path is not a feedback path that would affect next state incorrectly.
data.wrong_way: Setting a false path instead of multicycle because it's 'not used often' – this can break the path if the enable is ever asserted on consecutive cycles (e.g., due to a burst), leading to functional corruption that is extremely difficult to debug.
data.defense: Show the RTL that the enable signal is a one-hot pulse that repeats every 4 cycles minimum. Also show the timing report that the path has 12ns delay, and we have 3 cycles = 15ns budget, so it's safe. The design review signs off on the functional correctness of the delayed capture.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (using false path or 1-cycle): the path will not close, causing massive logic restructuring. Too loose (using too many cycles): area blow-up due to extra pipeline stages if we relax, but if using multicycle constraint without changing RTL, it's a functional risk – if the enable frequency increases, data is read too late, causing data corruption.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, multicycle paths are more common due to higher wire delays; we often use multicycle setup = 2 and hold = 1 as a default for cross-hierarchy routes.

data.pattern_name: CDC constraint for asynchronous dual-flop synchronizer (setup/hold exemptions)
data.situation: A signal crosses a clock-domain boundary where the two clocks are asynchronous (no known phase relationship).
data.derivation: We identify the synchronizer: two flops back-to-back in the destination domain, with no combinatorial logic between them. We set `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` between the two clocks, which removes all timing paths between them. However, we must explicitly set a false path from the source flop to the first synchronizer flop (since it's timing-critical only for metastability, not setup/hold). We derive that we need to add a `set_max_delay -from src_clk -to dst_clk`? No, we set `set_false_path -from [get_clocks src] -to [get_clocks dst]`. Then we add a `set_clock_uncertainty` on the synchronizer’s first flop to ensure metastability margin (sometimes not needed if the library provides metastability-robust flops). We also set a `set_multicycle_path -setup 2 -hold 1` from the first synchronizer flop to the second to allow an extra cycle for settling (if the clocks are slow). Derivation: we look at the synchronizer's required MTBF; we ensure the data toggle is slow enough (e.g., < 1/10 of the dst clock) by constraining the source logic to produce stable data for at least two dst cycles.
data.wrong_way: Simply applying `set_false_path` on all cross-domain paths without the explicit multicycle for the synchronizer stages, leading to the timing analyzer ignoring the settling time, which may allow the second flop to capture metastable data, causing functional failures.
data.defense: Show the CDC document that lists all synchronizers. Show that the source flop to first dst flop has a false path, and the first-to-second flop has a multicycle setup=2 to guarantee metastability settling. Also show that the source data is stable for at least 2 cycles of the destination clock (by constraining the source toggling rate).
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (no false path, or single-cycle path): massive timing violations at CDC crossing, impossible to close, may force adding more pipeline stages. Too loose (false path without any timing constraint): the synchronizer may not have enough time to settle if the source data changes too fast, causing intermittent failures that are impossible to reproduce.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, we often use a third flop (three-stage synchronizer) for high-speed interfaces, and we set multicycle setup=3, hold=2; at 28nm, two flops suffice.

data.pattern_name: Budgeting between two unbuilt blocks (top-down split)
data.situation: At the early chip planning stage, the top-level period T is known, but two blocks (Block A and Block B) are not yet implemented. The interconnect between them is fixed, and we need to split the available time between internal logic of A, the interconnect, and internal logic of B.
data.derivation: Total period T = 10ns. Fixed interconnect delay between blocks (estimated from floorplan) = 2.0ns (assumed, conf 0.6). We reserve 10% of T for clock skew and margin = 1.0ns (assumed, conf 0.5). Remaining time for logic = T - interconnect - skew = 10 - 2 - 1 = 7ns. We split this 7ns between A and B based on their estimated logic depth: if A has roughly twice the logic of B, we give A 4.7ns and B 2.3ns. Derivation: we compute gate counts or estimated stage delays from previous designs. We set `set_input_delay` and `set_output_delay` for each block accordingly. For example, for Block A output to Block B input: we set output delay of A = interconnect + time_allocated_for_B? Actually, if we are constraining A's output to the top-level pin, we include the interconnect plus B's input budget. So we set set_output_delay -max = (interconnect + B_internal_budget) = 2.0 + 2.3 = 4.3ns from A's clock. For B, set_input_delay -max = interconnect + A_internal_budget = 2.0 + 4.7 = 6.7ns? That would exceed 10? Wait, we need consistency: A_launch + A_internal + interconnect + B_internal + B_capture_skew = T. We define A_internal = 4.7, B_internal = 2.3, interconnect = 2.0, skew=1.0. Then 4.7+2.3+2.0+1.0=10.0. So for A's output delay (time from A clock to A pin), we set it to A_internal + interconnect? Actually, set_output_delay from A is the time from A clock to the input of B's flop, but it's relative to B's clock. The typical derivation: set_output_delay -max (from A) = (interconnect + B_internal_budget + B_clock_uncertainty) - (A_clock_uncertainty) ... we simplify by distributing the skew. We just allocate explicit numbers and back-annotate.
data.wrong_way: Splitting the period equally (50/50) without considering the actual logic depth, or ignoring the interconnect and assuming it can be pipelined later, causing both blocks to over-optimize one and under-optimize the other, resulting in a late respin to repartition.
data.defense: Show a spreadsheet of estimated gate-level delays per block, derived from RTL synthesis on a reference technology. Show floorplan wire lengths and resistance-capacitance extraction for the interconnect. The split is reviewed by the block owners and adjusted based on their confidence.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight on one block: that block fails to close, requiring interface repartition; too loose on the other: the top-level period is still met but the tight block may have to use higher Vt or larger buffers, increasing power.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, interconnect delay is much more variable, so we allocate a larger uncertainty margin (up to 20%) and use statistical budgeting; at 28nm, we use fixed RC estimates.

data.pattern_name: Over-constraining strategy (aggressive early target) and relaxation phase
data.situation: During early RTL synthesis and placement, the clock period is not yet tight; we set a more aggressive (shorter) period to push the tools to optimize, with a plan to relax later.
data.derivation: Given final target T_final = 10ns. We set an over-constrained period T_early = 0.85 * T_final = 8.5ns (assumed, conf 0.7). We also tighten all input/output delays proportionally. The derivation is based on historical data that the tools lose 10-20% performance after clock tree insertion and routing. We set a linear scaling factor = 0.85. We also set a more aggressive clock uncertainty (e.g., 0.2ns vs 0.5ns) to force better placement. We plan to relax to 10ns at the post-CTS stage by adjusting the SDC to T_final and increasing uncertainty to actual values.
data.wrong_way: Keeping the over-constrained target throughout the flow, because you think it will 'ensure margins,' which causes excessive area, power, and route congestion, and often makes the design unroutable because the tool tries too hard to optimize impossible paths.
data.defense: Show a graph of slack degradation over the flow from previous projects, proving that 85% is a safe overdrive that does not blow up area. Also show that the design meets 8.5ns in synthesis with reasonable area, so we have margin.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (e.g., 70%): tools may fail to converge, causing endless loops; too loose (e.g., 95%): when the real degradation hits, the design fails at signoff, forcing a last-minute constraint relaxation that may not be enough.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, the degradation from synthesis to route is larger (up to 25%), so we use 0.75 factor; at 28nm, 0.85 is typical.

data.pattern_name: Virtual clock for board-level input/output (IO) timing
data.situation: The chip interfaces with an external device that has its own clock, which is not the same as the chip's internal PLL clock. We need to model that external clock as a virtual clock for IO constraints.
data.derivation: We define a virtual clock `virt_clk` with the same period as the external device's clock (e.g., 20ns) and a defined waveform (e.g., rising at 0ns). We then set `set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -max` and `set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -max` for all IO ports. The derivation: we measure the external clock skew between the external device and our chip – say the external clock arrives at our chip pin with a delay of 1.5ns relative to the virtual clock (assumed, conf 0.6). For input, we set input_delay = external_clock_to_pin + board_trace_to_pin + external_device_clock_to_data. We sum them: e.g., 2.0ns external device launch, 0.8ns board trace, so input_delay = 2.8ns. For output, we set output_delay = board_trace + external_device_setup_time. We assume external device setup = 1.0ns, board=0.8ns, so output_delay = 1.8ns.
data.wrong_way: Using the chip's internal clock for IO constraints without a virtual clock, assuming the external clock is the same as internal, which ignores the phase and frequency difference, causing unrealistic timing that fails when the external clock is out of phase.
data.defense: Provide the external device datasheet and the board delay analysis. Show that the virtual clock waveform matches the external device's clock signal as measured on the PCB. Show that we have a board-level timing simulation that validates these values.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (input/output delays too large): internal logic is over-constrained, may fail; too loose: external device sees setup/hold violations, causing system failure.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, virtual clocks are often used with double-data-rate constraints and require exact duty-cycle modeling; at 28nm, single-edge is common.

data.pattern_name: Generated clock (divide-by-2 with phase shift) constraint
data.situation: A clock divider flop produces a divided clock (e.g., half frequency) that is used as a clock for a large portion of the design, often with a known phase relationship.
data.derivation: Assume master clock `clk` period = 5ns. The divider flop toggles on the rising edge of `clk`. The divided output `div_clk` has period 10ns, rising at 5ns and falling at 10ns? Actually, if toggles at 0,5,10, the rising edge of div_clk is at 0ns, then falling at 5ns, rising again at 10ns – so it's a 50% duty cycle with period 10ns. We use `create_generated_clock -name div_clk -source [get_pins clk] -divide_by 2 -master_clock clk`. The tool automatically derives the waveform. If we need a specific phase (e.g., rising edge at 2.5ns), we use `-edges {1 3 5}`. Derivation: we set the divide-by factor, and the tool computes the edges. We also need to set `set_clock_groups -physically_exclusive` if the master and divided clocks never interact, but often they do (data crosses from fast to slow), so we set a multicycle path.
data.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as a separate unrelated clock with its own period, ignoring the phase relationship, which breaks the timing analysis at the cross-over because the tool will not know they are synchronous, leading to unsafe false paths or missing timing checks.
data.defense: Show the RTL divider circuit and the timing diagram. The generated clock declaration is consistent with the edge flop's toggle. The tool's derived latency is verified by checking the arrival time at the clock pins of the flops in the divided domain.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (if defined as unrelated): cross-domain paths may be incorrectly timed or false, causing either missing violations or false violations. Too loose (if defined correctly but with incorrect phase): the crossover paths have wrong slack, causing signoff failure when the phase is mis-specified.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, generated clocks are often used for multiple frequency domains and require careful duty-cycle variation due to on-chip variation; at 28nm, divide-by-2 is straightforward.

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous interface handshake (req/ack) with no clock relation
data.situation: An interface uses a request-acknowledge handshake where the request is sent from one clock domain and the acknowledge comes back, without a fixed clock ratio. The path between the two is purely combinatorial, and we need to ignore timing.
data.derivation: We identify that the handshake signals are synchronized via dual-flop synchronizers in both directions. However, there is also a combinatorial path from the source flop of the req to the destination flop of the ack? Actually, the req path is synchronized, the ack path is synchronized. The timing between the source req flop (in src domain) and the dest ack flop (in src domain) might have a combinatorial path? Often, the source sends req, waits for ack, which goes through synchronizers. The path from req to ack is usually asynchronous and we set `set_false_path -from [get_clocks src] -to [get_clocks src]` for the combinational logic that combines ack? Actually, we set false path on the asynchronous handshake logic because it is not cycle-accurate – it is sampled only when stable. Derivation: we set `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` between the two clocks, and then set `set_false_path` on all paths that are purely combinatorial between the synchronizer outputs and the state machine logic that interprets the ack, because the state machine is designed to wait for a stable ack.
data.wrong_way: Trying to constrain the handshake with a multicycle path based on the ratio of clocks, which breaks if the clocks are not frequency-locked, causing functional failures when the ack arrives at an unpredictable time.
data.defense: Show the RTL state machine that does not sample the ack until it is stable for at least two cycles of the source clock. The false path is justified because the timing of the ack arrival does not affect the next state transition – it only enables the transition after a period of waiting.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (no false path, trying to time it): the path will have huge violations because the crossing is truly asynchronous. Too loose (false path everywhere, but missing the metastability constraints): could miss a setup violation on the synchronizer flops, which are actually critical for metastability.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, we often use a four-phase handshake with additional timing constraints on the synchronizer delays; at 28nm, simple false path suffices.

data.pattern_name: Clock-gating check (enable path) timing constraint
data.situation: An integrated clock-gating cell (ICG) uses an enable signal that must be stable around the clock edge to avoid glitches. We need to constrain the enable path relative to the clock.
data.derivation: ICG has a setup and hold requirement on the enable pin relative to the clock. We derive the `set_clock_gating_check -setup 0.5ns -hold 0.3ns` (values from library, assumed, conf 0.9). We also need to ensure that the enable arrives in time. We derive the maximum delay from the source flop to the enable pin: it must be less than (T - ICG_setup - skew - margin). We set a multicycle path on the enable? Actually, we use `set_clock_gating_check -setup` and let the tool time it. We derive the allowable enable delay by subtracting the ICG setup from the half-cycle or full-cycle depending on latch type. For a latch-based ICG, the enable must be stable before the falling edge of the clock for a negative latch. We set `set_clock_gating_check -setup [expr 0.4*T]` if the enable is generated from the same clock.
data.wrong_way: Assuming the enable is always stable and not timing it, which can lead to glitches on the clock, causing functional errors and timing violations that are hard to debug.
data.defense: Show the library timing arc for the ICG and demonstrate that the enable path slack is positive at all corners. Also show that the enable is registered and goes through a simple path.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (aggressive gating check): the enable path may be over-constrained, causing large buffers; too loose (relaxed check): glitches can occur, causing race conditions.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, ICG setup/hold are more sensitive due to lower voltage; we use tighter values and also check across all timing corners; at 28nm, default library values suffice.

data.title: Adoption of a full-system design approach over a chip-only focus
data.decision: Designed the entire system—processor, memory, and I/O bridge chips—together from the outset, rather than designing a chip in isolation.
data.rationale: To optimize the system, the team started with the full design in mind up front, marrying process technology, packaging, and microarchitecture to allow software to exploit them; a new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to effectively feed it.
data.outcome: The processor core was designed to fit effectively in this environment, and the system was built as a cohesive whole.
data.quote_as_recalled: To optimize the system, we started with the full design in mind up front.
data.weakest_point: The exact page number is a guess; the quote may be slightly paraphrased.

data.title: Prioritization of very high frequency design with system balance
data.decision: Committed from the outset to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies, revamping chip design with new transistor-level tools and transforming complex control logic into regular data-flow constructs.
data.rationale: To maintain a leadership position in operating frequency, and to permit system balance to be preserved as technology improvements allow even higher frequencies.
data.outcome: The system was designed so that bus frequencies scale proportionately with processor frequency, maintaining system balance as frequencies increase.
data.quote_as_recalled: To maintain a leadership position, we planned, from the outset, to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies.
data.weakest_point: The exact page number is a guess; the quote may be slightly paraphrased.

data.title: RAS philosophy: proactive error elimination and redundancy over mere error correction
data.decision: Adopted a RAS approach that eliminates outages and provides redundancy where errors cannot be eliminated, transforming hard machine stops into synchronous machine interrupts where possible.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: The paper explicitly rejects the approach of achieving reliability by only choosing reliable parts and building ECC into major arrays.
data.rationale: Servers require continuous operation; outages are not tolerated. High reliability requires an approach that goes beyond error correction to proactively eliminate failures.
data.outcome: RAS attributes previously seen only in mainframe systems were designed into POWER4 systems pervasively.
data.quote_as_recalled: With POWER4, we accepted the principle that one does not achieve high levels of reliability by only choosing reliable parts and building error correction codes (ECC) into major arrays.
data.weakest_point: The exact page number is a guess; the quote may be slightly paraphrased.

data.title: Single-chip design to serve both pSeries and iSeries workloads
data.decision: Created a single design to address both commercial (iSeries) and technical (pSeries) application requirements, rather than separate chips for each.
data.rationale: The need to satisfy high-performance computing requirements (high bandwidth) and commercial requirements (data sharing and SMP scaling) dictated a single design to address both environments.
data.outcome: A single POWER4 design met the needs of both IBM @server pSeries and iSeries systems.
data.quote_as_recalled: The need to satisfy high performance computing requirements with its historical high bandwidth demands and commercial requirements with its data sharing and SMP scaling requirements dictated a single design to address both environments.
data.weakest_point: The exact page number is a guess; the quote may be slightly paraphrased.

data.title: Maintenance of binary compatibility with prior PowerPC/PowerPC-AS systems
data.decision: Accepted the absolute requirement of maintaining binary compatibility for both 32-bit and 64-bit applications with prior PowerPC and PowerPC-AS systems.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: The paper implies an alternative of breaking compatibility for architectural change, but this was rejected.
data.rationale: Internal IBM task forces found no technical impediment to scaling PowerPC to higher frequencies, and to protect customers' software investment, compatibility was deemed absolute.
data.outcome: Binary compatibility was maintained from a hardware perspective.
data.quote_as_recalled: With no technical reason to change, in order to keep our customers software investment in tact, we accepted the absolute requirement of maintaining binary compatibility.
data.weakest_point: The exact page number is a guess; the quote may be slightly paraphrased.

data.reasoning: The operative trigger language 'exceed … more than 2 percent' uses a strict inequality (> 2.00%), so a penalty of exactly 2.00% does not breach the threshold.
The phrase 'more than 36 months' establishes a strict greater-than threshold (> 36), meaning a 36-month duration does not trigger the restriction.
The statutory test 'by 1.5 or more percentage points' includes the boundary value (>= 1.50), causing the HPCT classification to trigger at exactly 1.50.
The pass condition 'does not exceed … by 2.25 or more' negates an inclusive trigger (<= 2.25), meaning a spread of exactly 2.25 percentage points passes.
Both underlying tests use strict less-than conditions ('less than 10M' and 'less than 1M'), requiring revenue < 10.0M and income < 1.0M simultaneously.
The safe harbour rule explicit phrase 'equal to or greater than' makes the 16.00% threshold inclusive (>= 16.00%).
The eligibility floor phrase 'at least equal to' creates an inclusive boundary (>= 50.00%), satisfying the requirement at exactly 50.00%.
The framing 'equal to or greater than' sets an inclusive lower bound (>= threshold), triggering the incident reporting obligation at exactly the threshold value.

data.weakest_point: Rule 8 (NIS2 significant incident - users leg): The exact wording in NIS2 primary text (Article 23) uses broad qualitative criteria, whereas specific numerical thresholds are defined in the EU Implementing Regulation (2024/2690) across varying digital service sub-sectors rather than a single universal constant.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Check local pin density map and pin access orientation (layer distribution of macro/stdcell pins in the hotspot).
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest spatial check that rules out local pin-starvation before blaming routing strategy.

first_checks.check: Check cell area vs pin count (e.g., high-density muxes, AOI/OAI, or multi-bit flip-flops concentrated in one spot).
first_checks.why_first: Fastest way to distinguish high net-density from high cell-area density.

first_checks.check: Check layer utilization and routing blockages / direction constraints across M1-M4 in the hotspot.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out artificial capacity bottlenecks caused by improper floorplan constraints or blockage settings.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Apply a local placement halo / partial keepout margin (e.g. 20-30% density cap) over the hotspot box and re-run global/detail route.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Pin density / local pin-access bottleneck (DRCs clear when cells are physically spread despite low global cell area density).
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Macro placement blockage or global signal feedthrough congestion crossing the region.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily disable M1/M2 routing for signal nets or force higher min routing layer for local nets in that region.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Track exhaustion / pin-access blockage on lower metal layers.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: High global net-degree/topology interconnect density passing through from adjacent blocks.

common_root_causes.cause: High pin-density logic clusters (e.g., dense multiplexers or wide AOI/OAI trees) causing pin-access track starvation.
Over-constrained routing track availability due to aggressive PG grid, signal blockages, or macro halo overlap.
Global feedthrough routing tracks passing through a local region due to floorplan macro placement bottlenecks.

data.classic_trap: Assuming low global cell-density means plenty of routing supply, ignoring that pin count per unit area (pin density) can saturate M1/M2 tracks completely.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, unidirectional routing rules and extreme pin-access track offset constraints make local pin-density failures exponentially more frequent than at 28nm.

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS vs post-CTS timing reports for the failing paths, specifically checking clock insertion delay and clock skew.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest delta analysis to isolate whether path logic degraded or clock tree inserted latency/skew.

first_checks.check: Check actual extracted RC corner and wire-length model vs estimated virtual-route RC pre-CTS.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out routing layer shift or RC estimation mismatch on long data paths.

first_checks.check: Check for holding buffer / delay buffer insertion placed in the data path during early CTS/hold fixing.
first_checks.why_first: Identifies if hold-fixing aggressively added data-path delay to a setup-critical path.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare launch vs capture clock tree latency for failing paths: if capture clock latency shrank significantly relative to launch.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Unbalanced clock tree insertion delay / negative clock skew created by CTS.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data-path net wire-length expansion or crosstalk/RC extraction discrepancy.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing setup paths share clock gating cells (ICGs) with heavy fanout or excessive clock tree depth.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock gating enable path setup failure due to clock-tree delay added upstream of the ICG.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Standard register-to-register data-path timing degradation.

common_root_causes.cause: Clock latency/skew degradation (capture clock delayed less than launch clock or unexpected negative skew across hierarchies).
Excessive hold-buffer insertion along setup-critical paths during aggressive post-CTS hold fixing.
Congestion causing indirect routing detour on long data-path nets during initial trial-routing after CTS.

data.classic_trap: Sizing up data-path gates repeatedly without checking if CTS inserted unexpected clock skew or delay buffers on the same path.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, waveform slews and On-Chip Variation (OCV/POCV) derates on deep clock trees degrade setup far more aggressively than uniform derates at 28nm.

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check clock tree skew between launch and capture registers (specifically large positive skew: capture clock arriving much later than launch).
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest check that isolates the vast majority of post-CTS hold failures.

first_checks.check: Check path topology: fast back-to-back reg-to-reg paths (0-1 logic levels) or cross-corner/cross-domain clock crossings.
first_checks.why_first: Identifies structural paths naturally prone to hold violations once real clock edges propagate.

first_checks.check: Check OCV / POCV derate settings and extraction corner used for min-delay analysis.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out over-pessimistic timing constraints or incorrect fast-fast/slow-slow corner combinations.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Filter failing hold paths into short physical distance vs long physical distance paths: if failing paths are physically adjacent with zero logic.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock skew / clock insertion latency mismatch between neighboring registers.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data-path wire delay variation or interconnect RC extraction discrepancy.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trace failing hold paths across hierarchy boundaries or power domains: if failures disproportionately cluster at voltage/domain interfaces.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Level shifter / isolation cell delay model mismatch or clock tree domain imbalance.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Intra-block standard register-to-register hold timing.

common_root_causes.cause: Large positive clock skew between communicating flop pairs (capture clock arriving later than launch clock).
Short physical distance / zero-logic data paths (e.g. shift registers) with insufficient intrinsic wire delay.
Aggressive POCV derating or fast-corner delay over-estimation on short data paths.

data.classic_trap: Adding hold buffers manually without realizing the clock tree has a severe skew bug, leading to buffer bloat and subsequent setup failures.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, low-voltage operation and severe local variation make hold timing highly sensitive to local layout variation, requiring far more hold buffers than at 28nm.

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay dynamic and static IR-drop heatmaps with the failing timing paths in the layout viewer.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest spatial correlation check that confirms if failing cells reside in high-drop regions.

first_checks.check: Check cell density, switching activity / clock-gating vector assumptions, and decap cell placement in the failing region.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out missing decap or localized simultaneous switching noise (SSN).

first_checks.check: Check PG grid continuity, strap width, and via density on upper metal layers near the failure region.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out structural power grid open or high resistance bottlenecks.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run vector-based dynamic IR analysis vs vectorless dynamic IR analysis on the failing timing window.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Simultaneous switching activity / peak clock-edge dynamic power draw (if failure appears only in vector-based run).
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Static PG grid resistance / DC current delivery bottleneck.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add localized decap cells around the failing timing path in trial layout and re-simulate dynamic IR drop.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Local transient dynamic IR drop (decap alleviates voltage dip and recovers gate delay).
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Global power grid strap starvation requiring top-level metal grid reinforcement.

common_root_causes.cause: Localized dynamic IR drop caused by dense simultaneous switching of clock-gated registers or bus drivers.
Insufficient decap cell allocation in high-density or high-frequency clock regions.
PG grid structural necking or missing vias between upper global metal straps and lower local rails.

data.classic_trap: Trying to fix the timing failure by sizing up logic gates, which increases dynamic current demand and worsens the localized IR drop.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, lower supply voltages (~0.7V) and higher wire/via resistance make circuit delay non-linearly sensitive to minor millivolt IR drops compared to 28nm.

data.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Check CTS log for clock tree exceptions, balance groups, or conflicting min/max delay constraints.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest check to see if tool constraints forced contradictory tree building targets.

first_checks.check: Check physical placement distribution of sink pins across the floorplan (macro blocks, far corners, IO regions).
first_checks.why_first: Identifies isolated or distant sinks driving extreme insertion latency.

first_checks.check: Check clock cell NDR (Non-Default Routing) rules, shielding settings, and layer allocation.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out track availability issues or high RC routing layers used for clock trees.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate failing sinks: test if outlier sinks are located inside hard macros, behind narrow routing channels, or in separate power/voltage domains.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Physical barrier / blockage or macro internal pin-delay bottleneck.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Global clock tree buffer balancing / CTS engine tuning issue.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove target latency/skew constraints and run unconstrained CTS.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Over-constrained CTS target specs forcing tool into suboptimal buffer topology.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Physical routing track exhaustion or clock pin access failure.

common_root_causes.cause: Outlier / geometrically isolated clock sinks (e.g. corner macros or IO interface logic) dragging down overall tree latency.
Conflicting CTS constraints, improper balance groups, or explicit ignore/don't-touch attributes on clock pins.
Routing blockage or layer restriction preventing clock tree from using fast top metal layers.

data.classic_trap: Increasing CTS target max latency to force convergence, which inflates total clock tree power and sensitivity to OCV variation.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, CTS relies heavily on multi-corner multi-mode (MCMM) clock tree synthesis and mesh/H-tree topologies rather than traditional flexible trees at 28nm.

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Check LVS detailed text report for text label alignment, net name mapping errors, and short circuit location coordinates.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest method to locate the exact physical location of open/short markers.

first_checks.check: Inspect power/ground net connectivity and global net connect rules (PG text labels / global PG connectivity script).
first_checks.why_first: Rules out top-level PG naming mismatch causing thousands of false open/short errors.

first_checks.check: Check for dangling vias, boundary floating metals, or unrouted net stubs in the detailed router report.
first_checks.why_first: Isolates signal net routing incompleteness from schematic structure differences.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with power/ground structures ideal or bypassed: if signal net errors clean up completely.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: PG network shorting or improper PG pin labeling / global connect statements.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Signal net routing shorts / opens or schematic netlist mismatch.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Highlight shorted nets in the layout viewer across all metal layers.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Physical metal overlap, macro pin overhang, or filler-cell boundary boundary DRC/LVS rule violation.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Abstract-versus-full-custom GDS boundary text / net name mismatch.

common_root_causes.cause: Unrouted or partially routed signal nets due to detail routing DRC abort or pin access failure.
Inconsistent PG net naming or missing global connect rules in layout verification scripts.
Macro cell abstract (LEF) boundary pin physical overlap or incorrect macro LEF vs GDS layout alignment.

data.classic_trap: Debugging thousands of signal net shorts individually when a single top-level power net label is misnamed or shorted to ground.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, complex color-aware routing (colored metals / multi-patterning) and complex VIA rules significantly increase detail-router induced short/open LVS errors compared to 28nm.

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Check LVS netlist extraction log for parameter scaling units (e.g. micron vs meter, grid scale factors).
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest check that instantly resolves global systematic device size discrepancies across the entire chip.

first_checks.check: Check standard cell / macro cell GDS vs spice netlist version consistency.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out mismatch between physical layout library (GDS) and logical simulation models (CDL/Spice).

first_checks.check: Identify physical location of extra devices in layout viewer (e.g. inside fill cells, tap cells, or guard rings).
first_checks.why_first: Isolates dummy/utility structures from actual functional schematic mismatch.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if extra devices belong to decap, filler, or well-tap cells: filter out non-functional cells in LVS run setup.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: LVS rule deck missing rule to reduce/ignore dummy filler or decap transistor structures.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Real schematic vs layout gate instantiation or size discrepancy.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare single failing instance across layout vs CDL netlist: check parameter width W and length L multiplier (M/N factors).
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: ECO/synthesis netlist parameter mismatch or cell swap error during optimization.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Global extraction deck scaling factor misconfiguration.

common_root_causes.cause: CDL/Spice netlist library version mismatch against physical GDS macro/stdcell library.
LVS rule deck configuration failing to filter/combine dummy decap or well-tap transistor structures.
ECO netlist update swapped gate variant (e.g. LVT/HVT or size) without updating physical footprint correctly.

data.classic_trap: Manually editing layout geometries when the issue is a mismatched CDL netlist file or missing device-filter rule in the LVS deck.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, FinFET device width is quantized by fin count (nf) rather than continuous W, making parameter mismatches manifest as fin-count discretizations.

data.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Check antenna report for ratio details (metal area to gate oxide area ratio vs foundry limit) and layer where violation occurs.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest check to determine if failure is a long upper-metal trace or long lower-metal pin feedthrough.

first_checks.check: Check if failing net is connected to an input pin without a protective diode or receiver diffusion tie.
first_checks.why_first: Identifies missing hardware protection on long routing tracks.

first_checks.check: Check router auto-antenna fixing log to confirm if layer hopping or diode insertion was executed.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out tool configuration flag or library diode unavailability during detail routing.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check metal layer distribution of the failing net: if long track segments exist entirely on long lower metal layers without stepping to top metal.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Detail router layer-hopping strategy failure (failed to bridge to higher metal near receiver).
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Inadequate antenna diode availability in the local placement area.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Manually place a local antenna diode cell near receiver input and re-route local net segment.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Missing antenna diode protection (diode provides required discharge path to ground).
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Incorrect antenna rule definitions or cumulative multi-layer antenna calculation bug in DRC deck.

common_root_causes.cause: Long continuous routing tracks on lower metal layers directly connected to high-impedance gate inputs.
Detail router auto-antenna insertion disabled or antenna diode library cell not specified / constrained properly.
High local cell density preventing router from dropping antenna diodes near failing receiver pins.

data.classic_trap: Trying to fix antenna violations exclusively by manually placing diodes, when simple routing layer-hopping (jumping to upper metal) fixes the ratio automatically.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, ultra-thin gate oxides and FinFET structures have tighter cumulative antenna ratio limits, requiring aggressive diode insertion and early layer-hopping.

data.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Overlay DRC hotspot location with local track density, cell pin density, and routing blockage maps.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest spatial correlation to see if global router underestimated local track utilization.

first_checks.check: Check DRC error types in the hotspot (e.g., end-of-line enclosure, minimum area, parallel run length, cut spacing).
first_checks.why_first: Distinguishes generic track congestion from complex node-specific design rule violations.

first_checks.check: Check if DRCs cluster around specific macro boundaries, standard cell pin columns, or power grid straps.
first_checks.why_first: Isolates pin-access/via-ladder conflicts from free-track routing congestion.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run local detail routing with reduced cell density (apply a small keepout or 15% density drop over hotspot).
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Global router abstraction underestimating local pin access / via-ladder conflicts.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Flawed tech LEF / DRC rule deck definitions or bad standard cell footprint design.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Inspect via choices in hotspot: check if detail router is forced to use non-preferred single-cut vias instead of multi-cut vias due to track spacing.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Via spacing / via enclosure rule constraints swamping track availability.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Macro boundary track alignment / pin blockage issue.

common_root_causes.cause: Global router wire-capacity estimation failing to account for complex 2D/3D detail routing constraints (e.g. via rules, EOL spacing).
Pin access congestion in high-density stdcell regions where adjacent cell pins align on the same track grid.
Power grid straps or macro blockages creating local track pitch offset mismatches.

data.classic_trap: Trusting a 100% clean global routing report and blaming the detail router, rather than tightening global router congestion loss factors.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, complex multi-patterning, VIA ladders, and line-end spacing rules make global routing estimates much less predictive of detail routing cleanability than at 28nm.

data.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check design total utilization vs available core area, including macro placement footprint and hard blockages.
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest sanity check to prove basic physical capacity exists.

first_checks.check: Check placer log for net weight extremes, invalid physical constraints, or unplaced/fixed cell conflicts.
first_checks.why_first: Identifies erroneous user constraints forcing placer engine divergence.

first_checks.check: Inspect macro floorplan layout: check for narrow channels, dead ends, or isolated core regions.
first_checks.why_first: Rules out floorplan geometry bottlenecks that prevent legal standard cell distribution.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reset all timing net weights and high-fanout net constraints to default (1.0) and rerun global placement.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extreme net weighting / aggressive timing constraints tearing placement apart.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Physical capacity overflow or bad floorplan geometry.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove all hard/soft placement blockages and macro halos, then run global placement.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Over-constrained placement blockages or excessive macro halo sizes packing cells unroutably.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Real netlist net-degree / hypergraph connectivity explosion (e.g. un-synthesized bus interconnect).

common_root_causes.cause: Bad floorplan layout with narrow macro channels or fragmented core area preventing legal placement.
Over-aggressive timing net weighting or physical region constraints forcing tool divergence.
RTL/synthesis structure issue creating massive hypergraph connectivity (e.g. uncollapsed wide crossbars or registers).

data.classic_trap: Tuning global placer solver settings for hours when the true cause is an illegal floorplan channel width or runaway net weights from timing constraints.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, placement requires strict cell-alignment rules, edge-type compatibility, and power-rail alignment, causing placement solvers to diverge much faster under tight congestion.

data.pattern_name: Symmetric 50/50 Block Boundary IO Budgeting
data.situation: Budgeting input and output delay constraints (`set_input_delay` / `set_output_delay`) for two top-level blocks being designed concurrently before either layout or routing exists.
data.derivation: Given clock period T_clk: deduct clock uncertainty T_unc and target setup timing margin M (e.g. 10%, confidence 0.8) to get net usable period T_net = T_clk - T_unc - M. Divide T_net evenly: 50% allocated to internal block logic/reg-to-out, 50% allocated to external block in-to-reg plus top-level wire RC flight time. Thus, set_input_delay -max = T_clk - (0.5 * T_net) and set_output_delay -max = T_clk - (0.5 * T_net). For hold, budget external minimum delay as 0ns initially with explicit top-level trace delay checks deferred to post-route.
data.wrong_way: Constraining IOs with 0ns or arbitrary 80% T_clk input delays without coordinating with the partner block owner. Downstream, one block optimizer bloats logic to meet impossible 20% residual margins while the partner block wastes area by under-optimizing.
data.defense: Budget spreadsheet signed off by both block leads showing explicit T_net breakdown, clock uncertainty allocation, and assumed top-level routing layer / length limits.
data.signoff_risk: If too tight: synthetic timing violations force unnecessary logic restructuring, area bloat, or gate sizing that exacerbates local congestion. If too loose: top-level integration timing fails after full chip routing, requiring expensive late-stage ECOs.
data.node_era_note: At 28nm, a simple 50/50 period split was sufficient; at 7nm and below, top-level wire RC delay dominates, requiring reserving up to 30% of T_clk purely for top-level interconnect (confidence 0.85) before splitting the rest.

data.pattern_name: Virtual Clock Framing for System-Synchronous IO
data.situation: Constraining external off-chip input/output interfaces where the clock originates off-chip or board trace delays create a phase offset relative to the internal core clock.
data.derivation: Create an unattached virtual clock (`create_clock -name v_clk -period T_clk`). For input constraints: set_input_delay -clock v_clk -max (T_ext_launch_max + T_board_trace_max) -min (T_ext_launch_min + T_board_trace_min). For output constraints: set_output_delay -clock v_clk -max (T_ext_setup + T_board_trace_max) -min (-T_ext_hold + T_board_trace_min). This decouples internal clock tree synthesis (CTS) insertion delay adjustments from board-level absolute timing reference requirements.
data.wrong_way: Referencing the internal clock directly (`set_input_delay -clock clk_core`). When CTS builds the internal clock tree and adds 1.5ns insertion delay, the tool shifts the input setup target by 1.5ns, causing false timing violations or invalid optimizations.
data.defense: Board-level PCB layout trace length report and external device AC timing datasheet parameters explicitly mapped to `v_clk` parameters.
data.signoff_risk: If too tight: forces extreme I/O delay cell insertion or local pad logic sizing. If too loose: silicon fails AC timing specifications at the PCB boundary despite clean internal timing reports.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Validating and Defending Multicycle Paths for Handshake Protocols
data.situation: Constraining multi-cycle data paths controlled by a validated enable signal or state machine handshake (e.g., data bus stable for N clock cycles).
data.derivation: Identify data path driven by enable pulse active every N cycles (e.g. N=2). Derive setup multicycle: `set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_cells src_reg] -to [get_cells dst_reg]`. Derive hold multicycle: because setup shift implicitly moves hold capture edge forward by N-1 cycles, explicitly reset hold capture edge to launch edge via `set_multicycle_path 1 -hold -from [get_cells src_reg] -to [get_cells dst_reg]` (N-1 cycles relative to setup).
data.wrong_way: Applying `set_multicycle_path 2 -setup` without the corresponding `-hold 1` exception. Synthesis/STA engines will evaluate hold timing against cycle N-1 instead of cycle 0, causing the tool to insert massive streams of unnecessary hold buffers.
data.defense: Formal verification proof or RTL assertion proving the enable generator guarantees data stability for N cycles before capture edge, attached directly to the constraint review record.
data.signoff_risk: If too tight (or left unconstrained as 1-cycle): tool over-optimizes combinatorial logic at expense of area/power. If too loose (e.g., N set to 3 when enable allows 2): functional hold or setup race occurs in silicon, causing data corruption.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Gray-Code Bus Asynchronous Clock Domain Crossing Exception
data.situation: Constraining an asynchronous FIFO pointer or Gray-coded multi-bit bus crossing between completely asynchronous clock domains.
data.derivation: Because clocks are asynchronous, standard period-based setup/hold checks are invalid. Apply false path: `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` or `set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]`. To prevent the router from placing bits of the Gray-code bus arbitrarily far apart (which invalidates single-bit transition assumptions), add a maximum delay constraint: `set_max_delay -from [get_cells ptr_reg[*]] -to [get_cells synchronizer_reg[*]] T_dest_period` with `-ignore_clock_latency` to bound skew across bus bits (e.g., max skew <= 0.5 * T_dest_period, confidence 0.85).
data.wrong_way: Applying `set_false_path` without a corresponding `set_max_delay` or `set_bus_skew` constraint. The router treats the net as unconstrained and may route one bit across the chip, causing multi-bit transitions at the synchronizer and FIFO pointer corruption.
data.defense: CDC structural check report (e.g., SpyGlass CDC) confirming synchronizer cell presence plus STA report verifying max-delay and bus-skew constraints on CDC bits.
data.signoff_risk: If too tight: routing engine chokes trying to achieve tight absolute latency across asynchronous domains. If too loose (or false path only): pointer skew causes multi-bit transitions at receiver synchronizers, causing FIFO data corruption or system deadlock.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, explicit `set_bus_skew` constraints are mandatory alongside `set_max_delay` due to large local wire variation across parallel bit tracks.

data.pattern_name: Phased Over-Constraining Derate Strategy during Synthesis/Placement
data.situation: Preventing downstream timing degradation during physical design by applying deliberate margin during early synthesis and placement steps.
data.derivation: In early synthesis/place, actual clock tree latency, wire RC, and OCV variations are unknown. Add deliberate setup clock uncertainty or clock period derate: `set_clock_uncertainty -setup U_synth clk` where U_synth = T_clk * 0.15 (15% of period, confidence 0.8). During post-CTS / detailed routing, remove the synthetic over-constraint and apply real signoff OCV/POCV derates + actual clock tree jitter/skew numbers: `set_clock_uncertainty -setup U_signoff clk` (e.g., 3-5% of period, confidence 0.85).
data.wrong_way: Applying full signoff POCV derates and final low clock uncertainty during early RTL synthesis. Synthesis produces undersized gates and tight logic depth; once routing capacitance and CTS skew appear post-layout, the design fails timing catastrophically.
data.defense: Historical floorplan correlation data showing typical timing degradation from synthesis to post-route for the given node and implementation flow.
data.signoff_risk: If too tight at signoff: design bloats in power and area trying to meet artificial margin. If too loose during synthesis: physical design cannot converge post-route without major logic restructuring.
data.node_era_note: At 28nm, a uniform 10% clock uncertainty over-constraint worked well; at 7nm and below, over-constraining must be done via tight path-based margin / distance-based wire models rather than pure global clock uncertainty to avoid tool divergence.

data.pattern_name: Synchronous Divide-by-N Generated Clock Derivation
data.situation: Constraining an internal clock generated by a flip-flop divider circuit driven by a master clock.
data.derivation: Define the generated clock on the output pin of the divider register: `create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [get_pins div_reg/CP] -divide_by 2 [get_pins div_reg/Q]`. STA automatically derives phase relationship, frequency, and edge alignments relative to the master clock source pin. For setup/hold between master and generated clock, STA checks the most restrictive edge combination (e.g., launch on master at t=0ns, capture on div2 at t=T_master).
data.wrong_way: Defining the output clock using `create_clock -period (2*T_master)` instead of `create_generated_clock`. STA treats the two clocks as completely independent with unmanaged phase relationships, masking real clock-path latency and skew correlations.
data.defense: Schematic/RTL inspection showing register-based clock divider topology and STA clock-network report confirming traced source pin connection.
data.signoff_risk: If misconfigured as primary clock: STA misses phase correlation and clock tree latency sharing between master and child clocks, causing severe false setup/hold violations or masking real timing errors.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.title: Dual-Core Multi-Chip Module (MCM) Integration vs. Single-Core Die
data.where_in_paper: Processor Chip and MCM Architecture / Executive Summary
data.decision: Integrate two full 64-bit symmetric processing cores onto a single silicon die and package four such dies on a multi-chip module (MCM) to form an 8-way SMP building block.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Building traditional single-core processor dies interconnected at the board level.
data.rationale: Placing two cores on the same die drastically reduces inter-processor communication latency, enables extremely high-bandwidth L2/L3 cache sharing, and reduces package footprint while providing high instruction throughput per package.
data.outcome: Achieved a dense 8-way SMP MCM module with high-bandwidth chip-to-chip and module-to-module interconnects, forming the core building block for large SMP systems.
data.weakest_point: Exact page number for the MCM layout section

data.title: Instruction Grouping and Execution (I-Group / Slice Architecture)
data.where_in_paper: Instruction Execution Pipeline / Dispatch and Completion
data.decision: Form fixed groups of up to five instructions (I-groups) at dispatch that travel together through the pipeline and complete atomically in program order.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Fully independent, instruction-by-instruction out-of-order dispatch and completion tracking.
data.rationale: Group-based tracking significantly reduces the hardware complexity and queue tracking overhead of tracking dozens of individual out-of-order instructions through completion.
data.outcome: Simplified completion logic and tracking queues while sustaining up to 5-instruction dispatch/completion width per cycle.
data.weakest_point: Exact max count of instructions in an I-group across all execution paths

data.title: On-Chip Shared L2 Cache Design
data.decision: Implement a large, unified L2 cache shared directly by both processor cores on the same chip, organized into multiple autonomous modules/slices.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Dedicated private L2 caches for each core on the die.
data.rationale: A shared L2 dynamically adapts to asymmetric workloads between the two cores, reduces overall L2 cache miss rates, and eliminates duplicate cache entries for shared data/instructions.
data.outcome: Provided high-bandwidth, low-latency cache access for both cores with efficient hardware cache coherence mechanisms.
data.weakest_point: Specific latency numbers or cycle count figures given for L2 cache access

data.title: Distributed Point-to-Point Interconnect and Coherence Protocol
data.decision: Use point-to-point buses with distributed snoop logic across MCM packages rather than a single global shared command bus.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Centralized global bus interconnect architecture for multi-module SMP scaling.
data.rationale: Centralized buses create severe pin count, bandwidth, and electrical physical scaling bottlenecks at gigahertz clock speeds.
data.outcome: Allowed scalable high-bandwidth interconnect across 32-core (4 MCM) SMP configurations.
data.weakest_point: Specific terminology used for the snoop bus protocol layers

data.title: Hardware Instruction Prefetching and Dynamic Data Prefetch Engines
data.decision: Implement aggressive hardware-based stream prefetch engines to fetch data and instructions into L2/L3 caches ahead of execution.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Relying purely on software/compiler-directed prefetch instructions.
data.rationale: Hardware stream detection captures dynamic memory access patterns and stride changes in real-time without increasing instruction stream bandwidth overhead.
data.outcome: Significantly mitigated long memory latency stalls for scientific and commercial database workloads.
data.weakest_point: Number of concurrent stream prefetch engines supported per core

assumptions_invoked: Start date = first drawdown, t=0; intervals in years with month = 1/12 year (Annex I/III remark (c): year = 12 equal months, so integer months are exactly k/12)
The EUR 100 arrangement fee is a charge payable at conclusion: it enters the payments side D at s=0 with discount factor (1+X)^0 = 1 (basic equation: D_l covers repayments AND payments of charges)
Agreement runs full agreed term; both parties perform as scheduled (Art. 19(3) / Art. 30(3)-type assumption)
Result expressed to at least 1 decimal place, round half-up (remark (d))
Annex I/III Part II(d): overdraft facility -> total amount deemed drawn in full at t=0 and for the whole duration of the agreement
Duration not determinable -> assumed to be 3 months (Part II(d), second sentence)
12% nominal p.a. charged monthly -> 1% per month on 3000 = EUR 30 interest at t=1/12, 2/12, 3/12; principal 3000 repaid at t=3/12 (agreement runs full assumed term, both parties perform)

EUR 25 monthly account fee treated as a charge at t=1/12, 2/12, 3/12 (remark (a): amounts/intervals need not be equal; here regular monthly as stated; obligatory account fees are in the total cost of credit)
Intervals = k/12 years; start = first drawdown; result 1 decimal place (remarks (b), (c), (d))

Annex I/III Part II(e): open-end credit (not an overdraft) -> credit deemed provided for 1 year from the initial drawdown; capital repaid in equal monthly payments starting 1 month after drawdown; final payment clears capital, interest and charges

Instalment sized as an annuity at the contractual monthly rate i_m = 0.18/12 = 0.015: A = 1500*0.015/(1-1.015^(-12)) = 137.5196 (an equal-capital-plus-interest-on-balance schedule is flow-equivalent at 1.5%/month and yields the same APRC)
No other fees -> APRC is purely the annualisation of the monthly internal rate
Intervals = k/12 years; start = first drawdown; result 1 decimal place (remarks (b), (c), (d))
Unascertainable drawdown -> the full limit is deemed drawn at the earliest date, t=0 (Part II(a)/(f)(i) logic: freedom or uncertainty of drawdown => immediate drawdown in full)

Financed broker fee: the total sums made available = 5000 + 200 = 5200 at t=0 (the creditor disburses EUR 200 to the broker on the consumer's behalf), so the fee enters the DRAWDOWN side as part of C_1 = 5200
8% nominal applied as a flat 8% over the single 12-month term on the financed balance: interest = 5200*0.08 = 416; single repayment 5616 at t=1 (annual accrual assumed for a single-payment term)
Start = first drawdown; single interval of exactly 1 year; result 1 decimal place (remarks (b), (c), (d))

data.weakest_point: Case 4's rate convention: '8% nominal' is applied as a flat 8% over the single 12-month term (interest 416 on the financed balance 5200, repayment 5616, APRC 8.0%); if the nominal rate is instead compounded monthly - the convention used in cases 2-3 and the usual meaning of 'nominal' - the repayment is 5200*(1+0.08/12)^12 = 5631.60 and the APRC becomes 8.3%. Secondary divergence risk: case 2 assumes the EUR 25 fee is collected monthly in arrears alongside interest; collecting all fees upfront (75 at t=0) shifts cash flows earlier and raises the APRC to roughly 24.8%. Case 1's fee placement is safe (fee at s=0 vs net-of-fee drawdown are algebraically identical), and case 3's result is invariant to the equal-instalment vs equal-capital reading of Part II(e).

data.reasoning: The operative phrase 'can exceed, in total, more than 2 percent of the amount prepaid' uses strict 'more than,' so exactly 2.00% sits outside the trigger and only 2.01% fires.
'More than 36 months after consummation' is strict, so 36 months exactly is outside the trigger and only 37 months fires.
'Exceeds the average prime offer rate ... by 1.5 or more percentage points' is inclusive via 'or more,' so a spread of exactly 1.50 itself fires.
The fail-side comparator '2.25 or more percentage points' is inclusive, so the pass condition holds strictly below 2.25 and a spread of exactly 2.25 fails to pass.

verdicts.at: (10.0M, 0.9M): NO FIRE on the revenue leg; (9.9M, 1.0M): NO FIRE on the income leg
verdicts.above: n/a — no listed pair exceeds a cap, and any pair with a leg at or above its cap yields NO FIRE

data.reasoning: Both legs use strict 'less than,' so a pair qualifies only when strictly below both caps — 10.0M revenue is not less than 10M and 1.0M income is not less than 1M, so both boundary pairs fail while (9.9M, 0.9M) fires.
'Equal to or greater than' the transition rate is inclusive, so a simplified ETR of exactly 16.00% clears the test.
'At least equal to' 50% of SCR is inclusive, so a ratio of exactly 50.00% satisfies the Tier 1 floor.
The 'equal to or greater than' framing of the affected-users minimum is inclusive, so the threshold value itself fires.

data.weakest_point: Rule 8: the final NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 defines 'significant incident' qualitatively (severe operational disruption, financial loss, or considerable material/non-material damage to other persons) with no numeric affected-users minimum in the operative text, so the 'equal to or greater than the minimum' users phrasing likely derives from the Commission proposal, impact-assessment thresholds, or a national transposition rather than text I can quote verbatim; a secondary caveat is rule 6, where the 16% rate depends on the transitional safe harbour's fiscal-year banding (15/16/17%) and the mapping of '2026 fiscal year' to 16% is taken as stipulated rather than verified.

data.symptom: Congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Overlay the post-route violation map on the global-route overflow/congestion heatmap, split by direction (horizontal vs vertical) and by layer
first_checks.why_first: cheapest check and it immediately splits 'real overflow the router reported' from 'violations with no overflow anywhere near them'

first_checks.check: Check whether the violating region is dominated by non-cell objects: PG straps, clock trunks, macro pin channels, pre-routes, or leftover obstructions
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common 'density looks clean but routing resources were eaten' case before any re-run is spent

first_checks.check: List the NDR (non-default rule) nets passing through the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: a single wide/double-spacing NDR net can fabricate a whole hotspot of neighbor violations

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run global route with the hotspot's obstruction class temporarily removed or thinned (e.g., one strap lane or one IP's channel) while everything else stays fixed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if overflow and DRCs in that region collapse, the specific obstruction class is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists at the same coordinates with unchanged cell density, cell/pin-driven congestion is excluded and the structural resource conflict is confirmed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trial route with the NDRs stripped from only the nets crossing the hotspot
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations disappear with NDRs off means the hotspot is self-induced by the rule, not by congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persist without NDRs means rule-driven shorts are excluded

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Macro/hierarchical-block pin-escape analysis on the hotspot boundary
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: all violations ringing one macro or block pin array confirms pin-escape/channel planning as the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations distributed mid-row away from any pin array excludes pin-access and points back at wire resources

common_root_causes.cause: Macro pin channels / pin escapes not planned wide enough
PG straps or clock trunks consuming specific layers through the region
NDR overuse on many nets through one corridor
Local hierarchy-boundary placement imbalance invisible in the global utilization number
Forgotten padding/inflation or keepout settings from an earlier congestion fix

data.classic_trap: globally lowering utilization targets and re-placing the whole block when the real problem is one macro pin channel or one strap lane; engineers blame the router first and burn a full rerun before measuring where the wire resources actually went
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, pin access, self-aligned via restrictions, and coloring/multi-patterning rules can masquerade as congestion shorts where 28nm violations were plain spacing

data.symptom: Setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Bucket the failing paths by clock domain and path group, and by launch/capture clock-gating cell
first_checks.why_first: cheapest report, and it immediately splits 'one clock tree is late' from 'everything degraded uniformly'

first_checks.check: Compare actual clock insertion delay per sink against what the pre-CTS scenario assumed
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common cause — latency that the pre-CTS budget never modeled — in one report

first_checks.check: Check clock-net transition/slew at endpoints against the CTS spec targets
first_checks.why_first: a degraded slew on one trunk explains a whole subtree of failures in a single glance

first_checks.check: Diff the analysis setup against the last clean run: uncertainty, derate/OCV mode, corner assignment
first_checks.why_first: if the analysis changed, the physical timing may not have — this rules out a whole class of phantom regressions cheaply

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-time with the real propagated clock but the pre-CTS latency assumptions (or subtract the measured mean insertion delay from the failing slack)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if slack recovers by roughly the added latency, the failure is unbudgeted insertion delay, not path degradation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if slack does not recover, pure latency is excluded and real data/clock-path delay degradation is confirmed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Trace each failing capture clock back to the root and compare tree depth against its launch counterpart
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: failing paths sharing one deep CTS subtree or one late CG cell while launch trees are shallow confirms a gating/branch latency imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: launch and capture trees of similar depth exclude tree-imbalance and point at data-path or model changes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Toggle the derate/OCV mode off in an analysis-only run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations vanishing means the post-CTS derating/OCV change is the cause, not physical delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations persisting excludes analysis-mode change as the explanation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Measure routed/estimated detour ratio on the failing nets against the congestion map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: failing nets detouring in congested regions confirms congestion-induced delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: straight, uncongested failing nets exclude congestion and leave cell delay or clock structure

common_root_causes.cause: Clock insertion latency never budgeted pre-CTS
Latency imbalance across clock-gating cells or branches
Analysis setting drift (uncertainty, derate, corner) between scenarios
Congestion detours inflating data-path delay
CTS run on a stale sink list or with wrong excluded pins
