data.pattern_name: block-boundary I/O delay budget split
data.situation: Deriving set_input_delay / set_output_delay for a hierarchical block whose neighbors are not yet implemented or whose internal timing is still fluid
data.derivation: Start from the common period T of the interface clock. Reserve a fixed chip-level margin M (typically 10-20% of T). Split the remainder (T-M) into three parts: launch-block internal path budget L, interconnect/board/wire budget I, capture-block internal path budget C, with L+I+C = T-M. For an input delay the constraint becomes set_input_delay = L+I (or a chosen fraction); for output delay set_output_delay = C+I. Arithmetic shape: input_delay = (T-M)*f_launch_interconnect where f is usually 0.4-0.6 depending on which side owns more logic. Numbers assumed: M=15% of T (confidence 0.55), L:I:C split ≈ 40:20:40 (confidence 0.5)
data.wrong_way: Copying a flat full-chip I/O delay or using the entire period minus only clock uncertainty; this either starves the neighbor blocks of budget or leaves the current block with an unrealistically easy constraint that hides internal problems until integration
data.defense: Show the arithmetic split against the interface clock period, the reserved margin, and the relative logic depth expected on each side of the boundary; cite any existing similar interfaces already closed at those fractions
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: block fails timing even though the real system path would close, causing unnecessary ECOs or frequency reduction. Too loose: block closes easily but the integrated system fails at the boundary, forcing late redesign of both sides
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher relative variation and OCV usually force a larger reserved margin M than typical 28nm budgets

data.pattern_name: false-path versus multicycle-path decision
data.situation: A path exists in the netlist between two flops but is either functionally unreachable or is allowed more than one cycle by protocol
data.derivation: First prove functional unreachability (case analysis, formal, or exhaustive simulation of the enabling conditions). If unreachable under all legal modes → set_false_path. If reachable but the protocol guarantees N cycles of separation (e.g., a handshake that asserts only every Nth cycle) → set_multicycle_path -setup N -hold N-1 (or the appropriate hold adjustment). The multicycle value N is taken directly from the protocol specification or from the minimum observed separation in directed tests, never from a timing report
data.wrong_way: Declaring a false path simply because the path is not critical or because it is long; or setting multicycle without adjusting hold, which creates optimistic hold analysis and real silicon races
data.defense: Present the functional proof (waveform, state-machine excerpt, or formal property) that shows either unreachability or the guaranteed N-cycle separation; never defend solely with 'it timed'
data.signoff_risk: False path that is actually reachable: real timing violation in silicon, often intermittent. Multicycle too aggressive (N too large): same silicon failure. Multicycle too conservative or missing hold adjustment: either unnecessary timing pressure or hold violations that appear only after CTS
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: synchronous clock-domain-crossing constraint
data.situation: Two clocks are known to be synchronous (same source, defined phase relationship) and data crosses between them
data.derivation: Use create_generated_clock or set_clock_groups -asynchronous only if truly async. For synchronous crossings, leave the path timed but budget the available window as the phase difference minus setup/hold requirements of the capture flop minus any known skew bound. If the phase relationship is fixed by a PLL or divider, the constraint is simply the normal setup/hold check under the defined clocks; no extra exception is added unless an explicit multicycle or false-path justification exists
data.wrong_way: Blindly applying set_clock_groups -asynchronous to any crossing, which disables all timing checks and hides real violations when the clocks are actually synchronous
data.defense: Show the common root clock, the generation relationship (divider/PLL), and the static phase offset; demonstrate that the timed window is still positive after OCV
data.signoff_risk: Treating a synchronous crossing as async: silent functional failure when the phase relationship is violated by jitter or mis-lock. Over-constraining a true sync crossing: unnecessary timing ECOs on a path that already has adequate phase margin
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below larger on-chip variation makes the residual phase margin after OCV smaller, so engineers more often add explicit skew bounds

data.pattern_name: early over-constraint with planned relaxation
data.situation: During floorplan / placement / early CTS the design is intentionally given tighter constraints than the final target so that implementation produces extra margin
data.derivation: Choose a final target period T_final. For early stages use T_early = T_final * (1-k) where k is typically 0.05-0.15. Keep the same exceptions (false paths, multicycle) but scale only the clock period or the I/O delays. After CTS and before final routing, restore T_final and re-optimize. The value of k is chosen so that the extra margin roughly equals the expected degradation from CTS latency, routing detour and OCV increase
data.wrong_way: Leaving the over-constraint in place through signoff, or relaxing too early (before CTS) so that the recovered margin is immediately consumed by later stages
data.defense: Show the planned schedule of constraint tightening/relaxation points and the measured margin recovery at each stage; cite historical degradation numbers from similar blocks
data.signoff_risk: Never relaxing: final timing is artificially tight, causing needless area/power or frequency loss. Relaxing too early or too much: late-stage violations appear that could have been avoided by keeping pressure on the tools longer
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher late-stage degradation from routing and variation usually forces a larger early k than was common at 28nm

data.pattern_name: virtual clock for external I/O modeling
data.situation: Chip-level or block-level I/O must be timed against an external device whose clock is not present inside the design
data.derivation: create_clock -name VIRTUAL_IF -period T on a virtual object (or on a port that is later declared virtual). Then set_input_delay / set_output_delay relative to VIRTUAL_IF, using the external device's output-valid / input-setup numbers plus board uncertainty. The virtual clock is never used as a source for any on-chip generated clock; it exists only to anchor the external delays
data.wrong_way: Attaching the external delay numbers to an internal clock, which incorrectly applies on-chip OCV and latency to an off-chip path and can create optimistic or pessimistic checks depending on the latency values
data.defense: Show the external device datasheet timing, the board-trace uncertainty, and that the virtual clock has no network latency inside the design
data.signoff_risk: Too-tight external numbers: chip fails timing against a board that would actually work. Too-loose numbers: chip passes STA but fails in the real system when the external device is slower or the board is longer than assumed
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: generated / divided clock constraint
data.situation: A clock is produced by a divider, clock gate with enable, or PLL feedback inside the design
data.derivation: create_generated_clock -source <master> -divide_by N (or -edges / -edge_shift for non-integer or phase-shifted cases) on the divider output pin. The tool then automatically derives the period and waveform. For a clock gate used only as an enable, prefer set_clock_gating_check or a generated clock with -combinational if the intent is to model the gated clock as a real clock network. Always verify that the generated clock is not also constrained by a conflicting create_clock on the same pin
data.wrong_way: Creating a primary create_clock on the divider output with a manually computed period; this severs the phase relationship to the master and disables correct inter-clock timing and latency propagation
data.defense: Show the divider RTL or schematic, the exact edge relationship, and that report_clocks shows the generated clock correctly parented to the master
data.signoff_risk: Missing or wrong generated-clock definition: inter-clock paths are timed with incorrect period or phase, producing both false violations and missed real violations. Over-constraining with an extra create_clock: double-counting of latency and skew
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: asynchronous interface quasi-static constraint
data.situation: Data crosses between two truly asynchronous clocks (no known phase relationship) and the design uses synchronizers
data.derivation: set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clkA} -group {clkB} (or the equivalent set_false_path between the two clock domains). Then separately constrain the synchronizer chain: the first synchronizer flop is allowed to go metastable; the path from the first to the second synchronizer flop is timed for the full destination period (or a multicycle if the synchronizer is multi-stage and the protocol allows). No setup/hold check is required on the async arrival itself; the constraint only ensures the synchronizer resolves before the data is consumed
data.wrong_way: Leaving the async paths timed as ordinary synchronous paths (produces meaningless violations) or forgetting to time the synchronizer-to-logic paths, allowing the metastable value to be sampled by downstream logic
data.defense: Show the synchronizer structure, the MTBF calculation or stage count, and that set_clock_groups covers exactly the async domains without accidentally cutting synchronous paths
data.signoff_risk: Missing async exception: flood of false violations that hide real problems. Overly broad async exception that also cuts a synchronous path: real timing bug reaches silicon. Under-constraining the synchronizer output path: functional failure under rare phase alignments
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher metastability susceptibility sometimes forces an extra synchronizer stage compared with 28nm practice

data.pattern_name: pre-implementation inter-block budget handshake
data.situation: Two blocks that will later be integrated must each be given I/O constraints now, before either is fully implemented
data.derivation: Agree on a common interface clock period T. Allocate a shared interconnect budget I (wire, muxing, or feed-through). Remaining budget B = T - M - I is split by negotiation according to relative expected logic depth or by equal share if unknown. Block A receives output_delay = its share of B plus half of I; Block B receives the complementary input_delay. Both sides document the assumed numbers so that later integration can re-balance if one side closes with excess margin
data.wrong_way: Each block independently assumes it can consume most of the period, producing a pair of constraints that cannot be satisfied simultaneously when the blocks are stitched
data.defense: Present the written budget table signed by both owners, the reserved margin, and the plan for re-budgeting after first integration timing
data.signoff_risk: Budgets that sum to more than available period: integration fails and both blocks must be reopened. Budgets that are collectively too pessimistic: both blocks over-design, wasting area and power
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.title: Embrace high clock frequency alongside traditional high-IPC approach
data.decision: Adopt a high-frequency (speed-demon) design philosophy in addition to the traditional high-IPC (brainiac) approach for IBM UNIX systems
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Pure brainiac (complex design prioritizing higher instructions-per-cycle at lower frequency), which IBM UNIX systems had traditionally followed
data.rationale: To maintain a leadership position and deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies while still pursuing complex superscalar out-of-order design; system designed so bus frequencies scale with processor frequency to preserve balance as technology improves
data.outcome: POWER4 introduced at 1.1 GHz and 1.3 GHz, surpassing other 64-bit microprocessors in key benchmarks; long pipeline mitigated by heavy investment in multilevel branch prediction
data.quote_as_recalled: In the ongoing debate between the “speed demons” (high clock rate) and the “braniacs” ... IBM opted to also embrace the speed-demon approach.
data.weakest_point: Exact wording of the full quote fragment may have minor punctuation variation

data.title: RAS philosophy: eliminate outages and convert checkstops to recoverable interrupts
data.where_in_paper: Guiding principles (Leadership in reliability, availability, and serviceability)
data.decision: Require an approach that eliminates outages, provides redundancy where errors cannot be eliminated, and transforms hard machine stops (checkstops) into synchronous machine interrupts to software whenever possible
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Achieving high reliability merely by choosing reliable parts and incorporating ECC into major arrays
data.rationale: Servers have evolved toward continuous operation; high levels of reliability cannot be achieved only by reliable parts and ECC; system must circumvent problems if possible
data.outcome: RAS attributes previously seen only in mainframes designed into POWER4 systems (detailed further in companion paper by Bossen et al.)
data.quote_as_recalled: we accepted the principle that one does not achieve high levels of reliability only by choosing reliable parts and incorporating error-correction-code (ECC) logic into major arrays.
data.weakest_point: Precise length of the quoted fragment

data.title: Full-system design and distributed-switch interconnect for scalable SMP
data.where_in_paper: Introduction and Guiding principles (Full-system design approach); later interconnect discussion
data.decision: Design the entire system together (processor, packaging, memory, I/O) from the outset and use a new distributed-switch interconnect topology to form SMPs up to 32-way
data.rationale: A new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to feed it effectively; marriage of process technology, packaging and microarchitecture allows software to exploit them; interconnect appears bus-like to a chip but switch-like to a module and is new to the industry
data.outcome: Four chips form an 8-way MCM; four MCMs form a 32-way SMP; buses scale with processor frequency so system balance is maintained as frequency rises
data.quote_as_recalled: The interconnect topology, referred to as a distributed switch, is new to the industry.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly contrasts against a pure bus or pure crossbar alternative

data.title: Dual cores sharing on-chip unified L2 via CIU crossbar
data.decision: Place two identical processor cores on one chip sharing a unified second-level cache through a core interface unit (CIU) implemented as a crossbar among three autonomous L2 controllers
data.rationale: SMP optimization principle: large number of transistors used to improve total system performance in multitasking server environments; provides two-way SMP model to software on a single chip
data.outcome: Each L2 controller can feed 32 bytes per cycle concurrently; chip contains 174 million transistors; four chips packaged on one module yield an 8-way SMP
data.quote_as_recalled: The design features two processors on one chip; ... The two processors share a unified second-level cache ... through a core interface unit (CIU)
data.weakest_point: Exact page of the logical-view figure description

data.title: Binary compatibility and single design for both commercial and technical workloads
data.where_in_paper: Guiding principles (Binary compatibility; Balanced technical and commercial performance)
data.decision: Maintain absolute binary compatibility for 32-bit and 64-bit applications with prior PowerPC and PowerPC AS systems, and use a single design addressing both technical (high-bandwidth) and commercial (data-sharing/SMP) requirements
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Changing the architecture (rejected because internal task forces found no technical impediment to scaling PowerPC to higher frequencies)
data.rationale: Keep customers’ software investment intact; satisfy high-performance computing bandwidth demands together with commercial data-sharing and SMP scaling needs so that one design serves both pSeries and iSeries
data.outcome: POWER4 implements and extends the 64-bit PowerPC Architecture in a compatible manner; first used in pSeries, later staged into iSeries
data.quote_as_recalled: With no technical reason to change, in order to keep our customers software investment intact, we accepted the absolute requirement of maintaining binary compatibility
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper lists any specific rejected architectural change beyond the general statement

data.iterations: Closed-form: X = 5616/5000 − 1 = 0.1232; bisection verify on [0.10, 0.15]: iter 1 c=0.125000 f(c)=+8.00; iter 2 c=0.112500 f(c)=−48.09; iter 3 c=0.118750 f(c)=−19.89; converged to X=0.1232000000. Financed fee enters by enlarging the balance that bears interest (5200 vs 5000), whereas a cash fee at t=0 would appear as an immediate charge reducing net credit: 5000 = 200 + 5400/(1+X) → X=12.5%.

data.weakest_point: Case 2 (overdraft) — the treatment of monthly interest and fee timing is the most assumption-sensitive step. National implementations diverge on whether assumption (d)'s 'amount remains drawn for the duration' permits interest capitalization into a single end-of-term repayment, or requires monthly interest payments in arrears as done here. The fee timing (in arrears vs in advance) and whether the final month double-counts interest+fee also vary across software, making this the highest-divergence case.

data.reasoning: The operative phrase 'more than 2 percent' imposes a strict floor, so a penalty capped at exactly 2.00 percent cannot trigger the HOEPA prepayment-penalty threshold.
The phrase 'more than 36 months' requires strict inequality, meaning the 36th month itself is inside the safe zone and only month 37 triggers coverage.
The phrase '1.5 or more' treats the boundary inclusively, so a spread of exactly 1.50 percentage points is sufficient to classify the loan as higher-priced.
Because the pass condition is 'does not exceed ... by 2.25 or more,' a spread of exactly 2.25 falls into the prohibited zone and the test fails.
Both 'less than' conditions are strict, so touching either threshold—revenue at EUR 10 million or income at EUR 1 million—causes the de-minimis exception to fail.
The phrase 'equal to or greater than' is inclusive, so a simplified ETR of exactly 16.00 percent satisfies the transitional CbCR safe-harbour test.
The phrase 'at least equal to' is inclusive, so Tier 1 capital of exactly 50.00 percent of the SCR meets the Solvency II floor.
The phrase 'equal to or greater than' is inclusive, so an affected-user count exactly at the minimum threshold triggers the NIS2 significant-incident reporting obligation.

data.weakest_point: Rule 4 (General QM price limit): the actual regulatory text may use 'more than 2.25 percentage points' rather than '2.25 or more,' which would flip the boundary from strict to inclusive and change the at-boundary verdict from FAIL to PASS.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Inspect macro pin access patterns and orientations for track blockage
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common cause with visual inspection

first_checks.check: Review routing layer utilization map for resource starvation
first_checks.why_first: cheapest report to confirm if raw tracks are exhausted

first_checks.check: Check for multi-patterning coloring conflicts in DRC hotspot
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes advanced-node-specific issue from generic congestion

first_checks.check: Verify cell spacing constraints in dense standard-cell rows
first_checks.why_first: eliminates simple density-rule violation before deep debugging

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove macro pin-access blockages from routing constraints and re-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs shift to macro edges or reduce significantly → macro pin access is the root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs remain in std-cell regions unchanged → not macro pin access, investigate std-cell density or track starvation

discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRC count decreases significantly → routing resource shortage
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRC count unchanged → pin access or coloring issue, not raw resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force single-cut vias throughout the design and re-run detailed route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: DRCs reduce → via-array spacing or multi-cut enclosure issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: DRCs unchanged → not via-related, investigate metal track or pin access

common_root_causes.cause: Macro pin access conflicts blocking adjacent tracks
Macro placement orientation creating channel blockage
Routing layer utilization imbalance starving specific layers
Cell spacing violations in dense standard-cell rows

data.classic_trap: Blaming placement density when the issue is actually macro pin access or orientation
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, FinFET complex pin shapes and multi-patterning coloring constraints dominate, whereas at 28nm macro blockage and track availability were primary

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Report clock skew on all failing timing paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common post-CTS setup failure mode

first_checks.check: Identify common clock gating cells shared across failing paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to find localized insertion-delay imbalance

first_checks.check: Verify OCV and derate settings applied to analysis
first_checks.why_first: eliminates systematic margin pessimism before physical debugging

first_checks.check: Run timing with ideal clocks zeroing insertion delay and skew
first_checks.why_first: definitively separates clock problem from data path in minutes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run static timing analysis with ideal clocks removing all insertion delay and skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: All violations disappear → clock skew or insertion delay is the root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations remain with similar magnitude → data path problem, not clock

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if every failing path passes through a specific clock gating cell
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Yes → clock gating insertion delay imbalance is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No, spread across unrelated hierarchies → broader skew or data path issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Measure actual skew on each failing path relative to clock period
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Skew exceeds order of 15-20% of clock period → skew-dominated failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Skew is small relative to period → data path delay dominates

common_root_causes.cause: Excessive clock skew between launch and capture
Optimistic OCV margins or derate settings
Clock gating causing late launch or early capture
Data path congested causing detour routing

data.classic_trap: Throwing buffer insertion and cell upsizing at data paths when the real problem is clock skew
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, AOCV and POCV variation models plus clock mesh complexity matter more, whereas at 28nm basic skew optimization and useful skew were standard practice

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Determine if violations are on scan paths versus functional paths
first_checks.why_first: rules out broad category with netlist inspection

first_checks.check: Check clock skew direction on failing min-delay paths
first_checks.why_first: identifies skew-induced hold versus simple short-path hold

first_checks.check: Check setup slack margin on the same failing paths
first_checks.why_first: prevents hold fix from breaking setup

first_checks.check: Test if violations exist only at fast process corner
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes structural issue from corner-analysis problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add small delay buffer to a representative failing path and re-check both hold and setup
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Hold fixes but setup now fails → tight margin coupling requiring co-optimization
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Both hold and setup pass → simple short path, delay can be safely added

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hold violations are exclusive to fast process corner
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Yes → min-delay corner specific, investigate library characterization or derates
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Present at all corners → structural short path or clock skew issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if all violations occur on scan chain paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Yes → scan-specific hold issue, likely scan ordering or scan clock distribution
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No → functional path issue, investigate data path or system clock

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew with fast data paths causing early capture
Missing delay cells on short paths
Clock gating causing early capture relative to launch
Scan chain ordering creating short paths

data.classic_trap: Adding hold buffers blindly without checking whether setup margin exists on the same paths
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, process variation and advanced on-chip variation models make hold fixing more unpredictable, whereas at 28nm hold was more deterministic

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Correlate timing failure locations with power density map
first_checks.why_first: rules out or confirms IR drop in minutes

first_checks.check: Run timing analysis with ideal power supply removing voltage drop
first_checks.why_first: definitively isolates voltage-drop effect from other causes

first_checks.check: Inspect power grid strap density and integrity in hotspot
first_checks.why_first: identifies infrastructure weakness before detailed analysis

first_checks.check: Compare vector-based versus vectorless IR drop results
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes activity-dependent drop from grid-resistance issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run static timing analysis with ideal power supply zeroing IR drop
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Timing passes → IR drop is the confirmed root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Timing still fails → not IR drop, investigate other timing causes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add decoupling capacitors in the hotspot region and re-run IR and timing analysis
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR drop reduces and timing improves → localized switching hotspot
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Minimal or no improvement → power grid resistance or package inductance issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce switching activity factor by half in dynamic power analysis
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR drop reduces proportionally → activity-dependent, check stimulus patterns
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Minimal change → grid resistance dominated, not activity dependent

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient power grid straps in high-switching regions
Inadequate decoupling capacitor placement
Simultaneous switching of wide buses
Package or bump inductance limiting current delivery

data.pattern_name: Block boundary I/O delay budget for unimplemented blocks
data.situation: Two blocks are being implemented in parallel and their top-level routing is not yet complete; input and output delays must be negotiated before physical integration.
data.derivation: 1. Start with clock period P. 2. Subtract clock uncertainty U (assumes 50 ps at 28nm, confidence 0.6) and setup margin M (assumes 10% of P, confidence 0.7) to get available budget B = P - U - M. 3. Estimate interconnect delay I from floorplan distance d and average intermediate-metal delay (assumes 120 ps/mm, confidence 0.6). 4. Negotiate split between launch and capture blocks based on RTL complexity; if complexity is equal, each gets (B - I)/2. 5. set_input_delay on the capture block = launch_budget + I = (B + I)/2. 6. set_output_delay on the launch block = capture_budget + I = (B + I)/2. 7. Document assumptions in the constraint header.
data.wrong_way: Split the period 50/50 without accounting for interconnect distance or relative logic depth. One block receives an impossible budget while the other has unusable slack, and top-level integration fails because the slack-rich block was optimized for area rather than speed.
data.defense: Show the floorplan distance, RTL complexity comparison such as pipeline depth or gate count, and reference actual achieved delays from a previous project on the same node.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight -> block fails timing and requires a late ECO or respin. Too loose -> block passes standalone but top-level integration fails because the external delay was underestimated, requiring late-stage top-level buffer insertion.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, wire delay is less dominant but RC variation is higher, so margin increases and wire delay estimates are more uncertain

data.pattern_name: False path versus multicycle path from control-signal analysis
data.situation: A path in the netlist is not intended to be a single-cycle path, such as a register loaded by a decimated clock enable or a logically impossible combination.
data.derivation: 1. Trace the capturing flop's enable signal back to its source, which may be a counter, pulse generator, or gating logic equation. 2. Determine the minimum stable interval N in clock cycles from RTL inspection or simulation. 3. If the data source is guaranteed stable for N cycles and the capture only occurs on the Nth cycle, apply set_multicycle_path -setup N and set_multicycle_path -hold N-1. 4. If the path is logically never exercised for functional data transfer, such as a constant tie-off or scan-only path, apply set_false_path. 5. Verify with a waveform or formal property check before review.
data.wrong_way: Declare a false path when the path is actually a multicycle functional path. The tool ignores the path entirely, so if the enable logic has a bug and the path is exercised in a single cycle, silicon fails silently because no timing check ever existed.
data.defense: Show the RTL enable equation or a simulation waveform proving the N-cycle interval. For a false path, show the constant tie-off or mutually exclusive select logic that makes the path logically unreachable.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose (false path when multicycle needed) -> functional failure if the path is accidentally exercised single-cycle. Too tight (multicycle when false path sufficient) -> wasted optimization effort and possible congestion from unnecessary buffering.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, complex clock gating and enable logic make multicycle derivation harder; at 28nm, simple counter-based enables were more common

data.pattern_name: Gray-code FIFO pointer CDC max_delay constraint
data.situation: A clock-domain crossing carries gray-coded FIFO pointers from one domain to another.
data.derivation: 1. Identify source and destination clocks and determine the faster period P_fast = min(P_src, P_dest). 2. Gray-code encoding guarantees only one bit changes per increment, but the entire bus must propagate within one receiving clock period to avoid sampling a multi-bit transition. 3. Apply set_max_delay -datapath_only from source to destination equal to P_fast (confidence 0.8), or 0.8 times P_fast for margin (confidence 0.6). 4. Do not apply set_false_path, because that would remove all timing checks and allow arbitrary delay. 5. Optionally add set_bus_skew if the tool supports it.
data.wrong_way: Set false path on the gray-code pointer bus. The tool ignores timing, so if a logic error causes two bits to toggle or if routing delay exceeds one clock period, the destination samples an invalid code and the FIFO corrupts data silently.
data.defense: Show the gray-code encoding table and explain that max_delay ensures the single-bit transition is captured within one cycle. Reference the CDC verification report or protocol specification.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose (false path) -> FIFO pointer mismatch, data loss, or system lock-up. Too tight (max_delay significantly less than P_fast) -> impossible routing, forced buffer chains, and power or area bloat.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, on-chip variation makes max_delay harder to meet, so some teams use quasi-synchronous schemes or hard FIFO macros instead

data.pattern_name: Early-implementation over-constraining budget
data.situation: Pre-CTS synthesis and placement need margin for unknown clock skew, variation, and late ECOs.
data.derivation: 1. Estimate expected post-CTS skew S from a previous project on the same node (assumes 80 ps at 28nm, confidence 0.6). 2. Estimate OCV impact D as a percentage of nominal period (assumes 15%, confidence 0.6). 3. Reserve ECO margin E (assumes 5% of P_nominal, confidence 0.5). 4. Compute effective period P_eff = P_nominal - S - (D * P_nominal) - (E * P_nominal). 5. Apply P_eff during synthesis and initial placement. 6. After CTS, measure actual skew S_actual and relax toward P_nominal if the actual skew is smaller than estimated.
data.wrong_way: Over-constrain by a fixed large percentage such as 30% without a basis in estimated skew or variation. The tool inserts excessive buffers, causing congestion and power issues that are difficult to undo when relaxing later.
data.defense: Present a spreadsheet with the skew estimate, OCV table from library characterization, and historical ECO count from a previous project on the same node.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight -> excessive buffering, congestion, and power or area bloat that may not fully recover on relaxation. Too loose -> no headroom for CTS skew or late ECOs, causing a signoff crunch and potential silicon failure.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, AOCV and POCV replace flat OCV derates, so over-constraining uses statistical margins rather than flat period subtraction

data.pattern_name: Virtual-clock-based IO delay from board and package parameters
data.situation: The chip interfaces with external devices and the board-level clock arrives at the pad, requiring constraints that account for off-chip delays.
data.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock V with the same period and waveform as the board clock. 2. Estimate package trace delay T_pkg (assumes 100 ps for wirebond, confidence 0.6). 3. Estimate PCB trace delay T_pcb from trace length and dielectric constant (assumes 6-7 ps/mm, confidence 0.7). 4. For inputs, set_input_delay = T_ext_tco + T_pcb + T_pkg. 5. For outputs, set_output_delay = T_pcb + T_pkg + T_ext_setup. 6. Reference virtual clock V on all IO constraints so that internal clock insertion delay is not incorrectly applied.
data.wrong_way: Use the internal clock directly as the reference for set_input_delay without a virtual clock. The tool incorrectly accounts for internal clock latency, causing IO timing to be off by the insertion delay, which is on the order of 200-500 ps.
data.defense: Show the board stackup, package length extraction or IBIS model, and the external device datasheet specifying Tco and setup values.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight -> IO passes in block-level signoff but fails in system test. Too loose -> internal paths are over-optimized to compensate for the IO budget, wasting power and area.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, high-speed SerDes and source-synchronous interfaces dominate, making virtual-clock-based SDC less common than protocol-specific timing models

data.pattern_name: RTL-complexity-based timing budget for unimplemented blocks
data.situation: Two blocks have not yet been synthesized and there is no gate-level netlist to measure actual path delays, but a boundary budget must be established.
data.derivation: 1. Estimate combinational depth for each block from RTL by counting logic levels between flops, for example Block A at 8 levels and Block B at 4 levels. 2. Apply historical delay per level L from the same node library (assumes 35 ps per level at 28nm typical VT, confidence 0.6). 3. Compute raw estimates D_A = levels_A * L and D_B = levels_B * L. 4. Add margin M for unknown optimization (assumes 25%, confidence 0.5). 5. Allocate budget proportionally: Block_A_budget = P * D_A / (D_A + D_B + I), where I is estimated interconnect delay. 6. Set input and output delays to match the negotiated budgets.
data.wrong_way: Split the clock period 50/50 regardless of logic depth or complexity. The deep block receives an impossible budget and requires late restructuring, while the shallow block finishes quickly with slack that cannot be transferred across the boundary.
data.defense: Show the RTL levelization report and reference previous block actuals demonstrating the correlation between level count and achieved delay on the same node.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight -> deep block fails timing and requires pipeline insertion or architecture change. Too loose -> shallow block is optimized for area rather than speed, and top-level integration fails because its output delay was underestimated.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, delay per level varies widely with VT and track type, making raw level count less predictive

data.pattern_name: Clock gating setup and hold check derivation
data.situation: An integrated clock gating cell must be constrained so that the enable signal does not change near the active clock edge and create a glitch.
data.derivation: 1. Extract the ICG library setup T_setup_lib and hold T_hold_lib from the timing library, for example 40 ps setup and 30 ps hold (confidence 0.8). 2. Estimate clock skew U between the enable launch flop and the ICG cell based on the clock tree plan (assumes 50 ps, confidence 0.6). 3. Derive effective setup = T_setup_lib + U and effective hold = T_hold_lib + U, conservatively adding the skew magnitude regardless of direction. 4. Apply set_clock_gating_check -setup [effective_setup] -hold [effective_hold]. 5. Verify against the post-CTS skew report in the gating region.
data.wrong_way: Use the raw library setup and hold values without adding skew uncertainty. If the enable launch flop and the ICG are physically separated, clock skew can cause the enable to arrive after the clock edge, producing a glitch on the gated clock.
data.defense: Show the CTS skew estimate for the gating region and the library characterization values for the specific ICG cell.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose -> clock glitches, functional failure, and sporadic silicon bugs. Too tight -> impossible to meet with realistic skew, causing the tool to insert unnecessary buffers on the enable path.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, clock mesh and multi-source CTS reduce ICG skew sensitivity, but glitch windows are narrower due to higher frequency

data.pattern_name: Combinational feedthrough max_delay budgeting
data.situation: A hard macro or block contains a pure combinational path from an input pad to an output pad that must meet a system-level delay requirement.
data.derivation: 1. Determine the system-level requirement T_system from the top-level timing budget, for example 2 ns. 2. Subtract input pad delay T_inpad and output pad delay T_outpad from the library (assumes 100 ps each, confidence 0.7). 3. Compute remaining budget B = T_system - T_inpad - T_outpad. 4. Apply set_max_delay -datapath_only -from [input] -to [output] B. 5. Do not use set_false_path because the path must meet board-level timing.
data.wrong_way: Leave the path unconstrained or apply set_false_path. If no clock is present the path is unchecked; if a virtual clock is present the tool may apply an arbitrary period. The path fails at board-level timing test.
data.defense: Show the board-level timing budget and the pad delay extraction from the library, demonstrating that the macro budget is a derived subset of the system requirement.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose -> system-level setup failure at board test. Too tight -> impossible macro timing that requires pipeline insertion or a specification change.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, pure combinational feedthroughs are rare due to high integration; at 28nm they were common in IO macros

data.pattern_name: Post-CTS clock uncertainty update from actual skew
data.situation: After clock tree synthesis, the pre-CTS pessimistic uncertainty must be replaced with realistic numbers for signoff.
data.derivation: 1. Run CTS and extract actual global skew S_global and local skew S_local from the CTS report. 2. Add PLL jitter J from the device datasheet. 3. Add margin M for residual on-chip variation (assumes 5% of period for setup, confidence 0.6). 4. Compute setup uncertainty = S_global + J + M. 5. Compute hold uncertainty = S_local + J + M_hold. 6. Replace the pre-CTS pessimistic uncertainty with these computed values. 7. Re-run static timing analysis.
data.wrong_way: Keep the pre-CTS uncertainty, which was intentionally pessimistic to account for unknown skew. After CTS this double-counts the actual skew and causes over-design in the final stages.
data.defense: Show the CTS skew report and the PLL jitter specification, and explain that the margin is a percentage of period based on historical variation from the same node.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight -> area and power bloat from over-pessimism that cannot be recovered late in the flow. Too loose -> setup or hold failures at signoff if actual variation exceeds the reduced budget.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, POCV and statistical timing reduce the need for flat uncertainty margins, though skew and jitter remain

data.pattern_name: Mode-based case analysis for multiplexed clocks
data.situation: A block has multiple clocks selected by a multiplexer, such as a functional clock and a slower test clock.
data.derivation: 1. Identify the select signal for the clock mux, for example TEST_EN. 2. Apply set_case_analysis 0 or 1 to the select pin to disable the inactive clock tree during each mode. 3. Derive constraints for functional mode with the functional clock period P_func. 4. Derive constraints for test mode with the test clock period P_test, which is often slower, for example by a factor of 10. 5. Run separate timing sessions or use multi-mode analysis. 6. Verify that no paths are timed between mutually exclusive clocks.
data.wrong_way: Constrain both clocks simultaneously without case analysis. The tool analyzes cross-domain paths between functional and test flops, reporting massive false violations and causing over-design or impossible closure.
data.defense: Show the mux RTL and the test protocol document specifying the clock frequencies and mode selection per test phase.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose (no case analysis and modes switch dynamically) -> missing real paths in untested mode combinations. Too tight (both modes active) -> false violations, wasted engineering time, and over-optimization.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, UPF-based power intent and multi-mode multi-corner analysis formalize mode handling; at 28nm, manual set_case_analysis was more common

data.title: Clock-frequency philosophy
data.decision: Target clock frequency chosen as a balanced trade-off against power and die area rather than maximized
data.rationale: Optimize overall processor efficiency and performance through a balanced design point among frequency, power, and area
data.outcome: Competitive frequency achieved within the intended power and thermal envelope
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly frames higher frequency as a rejected alternative or only states the balanced objective

data.title: Comprehensive RAS hardware checking
data.decision: Extensive parity and ECC protection on arrays and data paths, plus hardware instruction retry
data.rationale: Enable transparent hardware recovery from transient errors without requiring software intervention
data.outcome: High system availability with automatic detection and correction of errors
data.weakest_point: Exact scope of protection claimed and whether instruction retry is detailed in this paper versus follow-on literature

data.title: Shared L2 cache between dual cores
data.decision: Two processor cores on the die share a single unified L2 cache
data.rationale: Conserve die area and efficiently maintain cache coherence between the two cores
data.outcome: Reduced total cache area with high-bandwidth sharing between the paired cores
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly lists coherence simplification as a stated rationale or only describes the shared structure

data.title: Off-chip L3 cache in MCM
data.decision: L3 cache implemented on separate dedicated chips within the multi-chip module rather than on the processor die
data.rationale: Provide large cache capacity without consuming excessive processor die area, enabled by MCM technology
data.outcome: Large L3 accessible via high-bandwidth MCM interconnect without growing the processor die
data.weakest_point: Exact page and whether MCM bandwidth is explicitly cited as part of the rationale

data.title: SMP packet-switched interconnect
data.decision: Distributed packet-switched interconnect for multi-processor scaling instead of a shared bus
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Shared bus architecture used in prior POWER systems
data.rationale: Eliminate bus bandwidth bottleneck and enable scalable multi-processor systems
data.outcome: SMP configurations scalable to 32 processors
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly contrasts the switch with a rejected bus alternative or merely describes the chosen architecture

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Run global routing congestion map with actual layer assignment, compare against placement density heatmap
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest: rules out placement vs routing layer mismatch in minutes

first_checks.check: Check macro pin accessibility and channel utilization between macros
first_checks.why_first: Rules out most common structural cause (macro feedthrough congestion)

first_checks.check: Verify NDR (non-default routing rule) usage on high-fanout nets
first_checks.why_first: Rules out spacing rule violations from wide-clock-tree-like nets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run global routing with congestion-driven mode disabled (pure timing-driven), compare hotspot locations
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Congestion is routing-algorithm artifact, not placement problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Placement density is root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Generate per-layer congestion histogram: if hotspots cluster on lower metal layers (M1-M3), it's pin-access; if on upper layers (M4+), it's global wiring demand
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Pin-access congestion vs global wiring overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Opposite layer distribution

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check cell density in 50um grid bins overlapping hotspots: if <70% utilization, it's not density-driven
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Non-density congestion (e.g., logic cloud with high connectivity)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Placement density as cause

common_root_causes.cause: Macro feedthrough ports with insufficient channel width
High-fanout nets (reset, scan enable) without NDR causing local pin starvation
Placement blockage overlap creating artificial bottlenecks
Inaccurate global routing track allocation vs actual layer stack

data.classic_trap: Assuming placement density is the cause and spreading cells, when the real issue is macro channel width or missing NDR on high-fanout nets
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, pin-access congestion dominates due to smaller M1/M2 pins; at 28nm, global wiring overflow is more common

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check if clock tree is propagated (not ideal) and uncertainty values are post-CTS correct
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest: rules out constraint/setup errors in minutes

first_checks.check: Report worst negative slack (WNS) paths: check if they share a common clock domain or hierarchy
first_checks.why_first: Rules out single-clock vs multi-clock issue quickly

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS vs post-CTS setup slack: identify paths that degraded after CTS
first_checks.why_first: Rules out CTS-introduced vs pre-existing problems

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run report_timing on failing paths with -clock_tree_pessimism_removed: if slack improves >10% of WNS, it's CRPR (clock reconvergence pessimism removal) issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Excessive OCV pessimism, not real timing violation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Genuine data-path delay problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if all failing paths end at the same clock-gating cell: if yes, it's clock-gating insertion delay; if spread, it's data-path
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock-gating leaf latency issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data-path logic delay

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run useful-skew optimization: if WNS improves significantly, it's recoverable via clock timing; if not, it's data-path
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Timing recoverable via clock adjustment
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Hard data-path limit

common_root_causes.cause: Incorrect post-CTS clock uncertainty (still includes skew margin)
CRPR pessimism not removed, over-budgeting common clock path delay
High-fanout clock-gating cells with large insertion delay
CTS used wrong reference cells (e.g., HVT instead of LVT) for data-path optimization

data.classic_trap: Blaming data-path logic and optimizing gates, when the real issue is incorrect clock uncertainty or missing CRPR removal
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, CRPR is critical due to high OCV impact; at 28nm, setup is more often data-path limited

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check if hold violations are on scan-chain paths (false paths not set)
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest: rules out constraint errors in minutes

first_checks.check: Report hold slack distribution: check if violations cluster in one clock domain
first_checks.why_first: Rules out single-domain vs cross-domain issue

first_checks.check: Verify min-delay cells (hold buffers) are in the target library and not marked dont-use
first_checks.why_first: Rules out library/setup issue quickly

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run report_clock_tree -local_skew_skip_icg: if large skew exists between launch/capture ICG leaves, it's clock-gating skew issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock-gating leaf skew dominating hold violation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data-path too fast

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing paths have data delay < 20% of clock period: if yes, it's min-delay violation; if no, it's clock skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Genuine data-path too fast
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Clock distribution issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run hold fixing with -effort high: if TNS improves >50%, it's fixable with buffers; if not, it's structural
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Hold fixable via delay insertion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Structural clock skew problem

common_root_causes.cause: Scan-chain paths not set as false paths, causing thousands of fake violations
Clock-gating leaf skew unbalanced (ICG output to different register clusters)
OCV derating too aggressive on min-delay paths
Hold buffers excluded from library or marked dont-use

data.classic_trap: Spending days inserting hold buffers when the real issue is missing false-path constraints on scan chains
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, OCV derating dominates hold fixing; at 28nm, clock skew is the primary cause

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Run static IR drop analysis: check if failing instances are in high-drop regions (>10% VDD)
first_checks.why_first: Cheapest: rules out IR drop as cause in minutes

first_checks.check: Check if timing failure correlates with high-activity switching vectors (e.g., reset sequence)
first_checks.why_first: Rules out dynamic vs static IR drop issue

first_checks.check: Verify power grid connectivity to failing instances (no missing vias, PG open)
first_checks.why_first: Rules out PG design error quickly

discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR drop is root cause of timing failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Timing failure independent of voltage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing paths are in clock tree (clock latency increases with voltage drop) or data path
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock-path IR drop (clock buffer delay increases)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Data-path IR drop

discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Dynamic IR drop (simultaneous switching)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Static IR drop (power grid resistance)

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or insufficient decoupling capacitance in high-switching regions
Power grid mesh too sparse (strap width/via count insufficient)
High-fanout nets (reset, scan) switching simultaneously causing local dynamic drop
Incorrect IR drop derating margins in STA (too optimistic)

data.classic_trap: Optimizing data-path logic to fix timing, when the real issue is local IR drop increasing cell delay
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, dynamic IR drop dominates due to lower voltage and higher di/dt; at 28nm, static IR drop is primary

data.title: Dual-core single-die design for server workloads
data.decision: Integrate two full 64-bit PowerPC processor cores on a single POWER4 die (first commercial single-chip dual-core server processor).
data.rationale: To enable a single-chip symmetric multiprocessor (SMP) and to unify the i-series and p-series server platforms on one hardware design, improving performance and time-to-market.
data.outcome: POWER4 became the first production single-chip dual-core server CPU, supporting up to 32-way SMP via multi-chip modules and enabling the eServer p690 (Regatta) and i-series systems.
data.weakest_point: Exact wording of the SMP-on-a-chip rationale and page number are not directly confirmed from the paper text.

data.title: Clock-frequency philosophy: frequency vs. microarchitectural balance
data.decision: Prioritize a balanced microarchitecture with moderate frequency (1 GHz+) and wide execution (up to 200 in-flight instructions) rather than chasing the highest possible clock rate.
data.rationale: To avoid the power, thermal, and microarchitectural imbalance that would come with a narrower, frequency-focused design; the goal was to sustain high throughput across both commercial and technical workloads.
data.outcome: POWER4 achieved 1.1–1.3 GHz initial frequencies with a wide, deeply pipelined superscalar core and delivered leading server performance without extreme clock rates.
data.weakest_point: The precise section name and the exact quote are not verified against the original paper.

data.title: RAS approach: convert hard machine-check interrupts to synchronous software-handled events
data.decision: Design the error-handling architecture so that, where possible, hardware-detected errors are converted from asynchronous machine-check aborts into synchronous, software-recoverable interrupts, with redundancy for uncorrectable cases.
data.rationale: To eliminate unnecessary system downtime from transient hardware errors and to allow the operating system to recover gracefully, improving overall system availability.
data.outcome: POWER4 could transparently handle many error conditions without crashing, supporting the high-availability requirements of enterprise server partitions.
data.weakest_point: The exact phrasing of the synchronous-interrupt conversion and the page number are not confirmed from the paper.

data.title: Interconnect and SMP fabric: on-chip fabric controller with distributed L2/L3
data.decision: Use an on-chip fabric controller to manage inter-processor and L2/L3 cache coherency traffic, enabling scalable multi-chip SMP configurations.
data.rationale: To support glueless multi-chip SMP scaling (up to 32-way) and to control data flow between on-chip L2 and off-chip L3 caches without a centralized bottleneck.
data.outcome: POWER4 multi-chip modules (up to 8 dies) and the fabric controller allowed efficient, scalable SMP systems such as the 32-way p690.
data.weakest_point: The term 'fabric controller' and its exact description are recalled from secondary summaries, not directly verified in the paper.

data.title: Branch prediction: hybrid local/global with selector table
data.decision: Implement a hybrid dynamic branch predictor combining a local history table, a global history table (16k-entry), and a selector table that chooses the better predictor per branch.
data.rationale: To achieve high prediction accuracy across diverse workload types by leveraging both per-branch local patterns and global correlation history.
data.outcome: The hybrid predictor delivered very high accuracy, supporting the wide superscalar pipeline and two-branch-per-cycle prediction capability.
data.weakest_point: The exact predictor sizes and the selector-table mechanism are recalled from a secondary source and not directly confirmed from the paper.

receipt_kinds.when_produced: Default output of risc0 prover when guest execution spans multiple segments due to cycle limit / continuations. Each segment is a STARK. Composite aggregates segments via host-side recursion metadata but is not yet a single succinct proof.
receipt_kinds.verifier_note: Verified by STARK recursion verification, not directly Groth16. Must be compressed before on-chain use.

receipt_kinds.when_produced: Produced by compressing a Composite receipt using the recursion circuit (lift -> join -> resolve). Result of `receipt.compress()` / `default_prover.prove()` with succinct mode or `ProverOpts::succinct()`. Single proof for whole execution.
receipt_kinds.verifier_note: Still STARK, not BN254 Groth16. Needs Groth16 wrapping for Ethereum.

receipt_kinds.type_shape: Groth16 proof over BN254 + claimDigest + journal
receipt_kinds.when_produced: Produced from Succinct receipt via Groth16 prover (`groth16` feature, `risc0-groth16` crate). Seal = Groth16 proof (a,b,c). Used for on-chain verification. Encoded as 4-byte selector + abi-encoded Seal (256 bytes raw: pi_a 64, pi_b 128, pi_c 64).
receipt_kinds.verifier_note: What Ethereum contracts verify. Public inputs are control_root (2x128-bit), claimDigest (2x128-bit), BN254_CONTROL_ID (1x).

receipt_kinds.when_produced: When RISC0_DEV_MODE=1 or `FakeProver`. No cryptographic security.
receipt_kinds.verifier_note: Must be rejected in production verifiers.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: bytes, decoded as Seal { a: uint256 (G1), b: uint256 (G2), c: uint256 (G1) } total 256 bytes raw; wire format = 4-byte selector + abi.encode(Seal)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: BN254 Groth16 proof that the recursion circuit verified the inner STARK succinct receipt and that claimDigest is correctly bound to control_root
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Split claimDigest into 2x128-bit chunks with byte-reverse per chunk, combine with control_root chunks and BN254_CONTROL_ID as 5 public inputs, then call Groth16 pairing verifier with the version-pinned verifying key (VK). Check pairing equation e(a,b)*e(...) ==...
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Trivial forgery: any random 256 bytes accepted as proof; attacker can claim arbitrary imageId/journal without proving execution.

groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Truncated hash of verifier parameters: sha256(tag='risc0.Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters', control_root, reverse(BN254_CONTROL_ID), vk_digest). Routes receipt to correct verifier version.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compute expected selector from local verifier's control_root, BN254_CONTROL_ID, VK digest and require bytes4(seal[:4]) == expected. Revert with SelectorMismatch otherwise.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Version confusion forgery: attacker reuses Groth16 proof generated under old/vulnerable recursion circuits or different VK (e.g., dev control_root) that shares same on-chain verifier interface but has different trusted setup; verifier would accept proof that does not correspond to its pinned circuits.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: bytes32 digest of ReceiptClaim struct; ReceiptClaim = { preStateDigest: bytes32, postStateDigest: bytes32, exitCode: {system: u8 (Halted=0,Paused=1,SystemSplit=2), user: u8}, input: bytes32, output: bytes32 } - field names may vary: preStateDigest sometimes holds imageId in Solidity ok() constructor
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Commitment to all public claims about execution. In Solidity helper ok(imageId, journalDigest), preStateDigest = imageId, postStateDigest = SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST (0x...), input = 0, output = digest(Output{journalDigest, assumptionsDigest=0}).
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute claimDigest via tagged struct hashing (SHA256-based, not Keccak) from expected imageId, journalDigest, zero pre/post for ok() case, Halted(0) exit, input=0, output=Output digest. Compare recomputed digest to public inputs derived from seal verification. For generic receipts, ensure pre/post are expected values.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Claim substitution: attacker keeps valid Groth16 seal for claim A but presents different claim B (different imageId or exit code) that verifier does not bind to seal, bypassing program identity.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: journal: bytes (Vec<u8>), journalDigest: bytes32 = SHA256(journal bytes)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Public output committed by guest via env::commit / env::journal. JournalDigest lives inside Output struct, inside claim.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compute journalDigest = sha256(journal bytes) using SHA256 (risc0 Digest is SHA256, byte order is raw, not reversed). Require journalDigest == Output.journalDigest extracted from claim. For ok() helper, also require Output digest = tagged hash of (journalDigest, assumptionsDigest).
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Journal substitution forgery: valid proof for program that committed journal 'balance=0' reused to claim journal 'balance=1000000' because verifier never hashes journal bytes; same claimDigest not checked or different journal allowed.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: bytes32, digest of list of assumed ReceiptClaims
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: If guest called env::verify / zkvm::Verify to compose proofs, those assumed claims are accumulated into assumptionsDigest. Zero means unconditional receipt with no assumptions.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: For unconditional receipts expected by most dApps, require assumptionsDigest == bytes32(0). If composition allowed, require caller provides list of assumed claims and that digest matches.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Assumption forgery: attacker creates receipt that is valid only if another receipt (e.g., 'I am admin') is valid, but never provides that assumption proof; verifier treating assumptionsDigest as irrelevant accepts conditional proof as unconditional.

groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: preStateDigest = digest of SystemState before execution (pc + merkle_root). For standard start, SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST or imageId depending on version. postStateDigest = digest after execution. input = reserved, must be zero digest currently. These bind initial memory image and final state.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: For ok() unconditional case, require preStateDigest == imageId (or imageId supplied maps to expected pre), postStateDigest == SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST, input == 0, exitCode.system == Halted, exitCode.user == 0. Reject Paused or SystemSplit unless resumption logic intended.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Program substitution / incomplete execution forgery: attacker proves execution of different ELF (different imageId) or proves execution that paused early or halted with user error code 1, but verifier still treats as success for expected program; or uses non-zero input to smuggle hidden pre-image.

groth16_receipt_fields.field: control_root and BN254_CONTROL_ID (verifier parameters, not in receipt but in public inputs)
groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: bytes32 each, split into 2x bytes16 for control_root in circuit
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: control_root = Merkle root / hash committing to set of allowed recursion circuits (lift, join, resolve, etc.) for this zkVM version. BN254_CONTROL_ID = field element identifier for BN254 recursion circuit.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Pin these constants per zkVM version (e.g., v1.x, v2.x, v3.0.5 values differ). Include them as public inputs to Groth16 verification and in selector calculation. Ensure they match expected release.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Control root substitution: attacker generates Groth16 proof with custom control_root that includes malicious recursion circuit that always accepts; if verifier does not pin control_root, proof verifies against attacker's VK and is accepted as valid execution of any program.

components.preStateDigest: Digest of SystemState before execution: SystemState = {pc: u32, merkle_root: bytes32}. For ReceiptClaim::ok(), this field holds imageId in some Solidity versions (e.g., RiscZeroGroth16Verifier ok() does ReceiptClaim(imageId, SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST,...)), in Rust native struct it is preStateDigest = zero and imageId is separate field historically - field name changed across versions. Must check version.
components.postStateDigest: Digest of SystemState after execution. For halted execution, SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST (all zeros hash of zero state) per ok() helper.
components.exitCode: Struct {system: SystemExitCode enum (Halted=0, Paused=1, SystemSplit=2), user: u8}. For successful execution, Halted, user=0. Non-zero user indicates guest called env::exit with code.
components.input: bytes32, currently must be zero digest. Reserved for future committed input (currently unused).
components.output: bytes32 = digest(Output). Output = {journalDigest: bytes32, assumptionsDigest: bytes32}. journalDigest = SHA256(journal bytes). assumptionsDigest = digest of list of assumed claims, or zero.
components.imageId: In newer Rust API, imageId not inside ReceiptClaim but supplied separately to verify(imageId). In older Solidity libs and Go verifier, imageId is encoded as first field of ReceiptClaim (preStateDigest). CalculateClaimDigest(imageId, journalDigest) helper hides this.

claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: ReceiptClaim is Merkle-ized / tagged struct using SHA256 (not Keccak, not EIP-712 keccak but similar idea with sha256 tags). Steps per risc0-zkvm 1.x-3.x: (1) digest Output: tag = sha256('risc0.Output'), outputDigest = sha256(tag || sha256(journalDigest) || sha256(assumptionsDigest) || little-endian length encoding). Actually implementation uses StructHash::tagged_struct with tagged list. (2) digest ReceiptClaim: tag = sha256('risc0.ReceiptClaim'), digest = sha256(tag || digest(preState) || digest(postState) || digest(exitCode) || digest(input) || digest(output) || u16(5)<<8 ). In Solidity ReceiptClaimLib.ok(), this is done via StructHash. (3) final claimDigest is what becomes Groth16 public input (split). Exact byte order uses reverseByteOrderUint256 for BN254 field conversion.
claim_structure.journal_binding: journal bytes themselves not inside claim, only journalDigest. Verifier must recompute sha256(journal) and ensure equals Output.journalDigest.

binding_chain: 1. Guest writes journal bytes via env::commit / env::commit_slice.
2. Host computes journalDigest = SHA256(journal bytes) (risc0 Digest uses SHA256, raw bytes, no extra length prefix in digest input besides tag).

3. Host collects assumptions list from env::verify calls: each assumed ReceiptClaim digest collected, tagged list hashed into assumptionsDigest = tagged_list_hash('risc0.Output.assumptions', claimDigests) or zero if empty.
4. Host builds Output struct {journalDigest, assumptionsDigest} and computes outputDigest = tagged_struct_hash('risc0.Output', journalDigest, assumptionsDigest).
5. Host builds ReceiptClaim {preStateDigest=imageId or zero depending on version, postStateDigest=SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST, exitCode=Halted(0), input=zero, output=outputDigest}.
6. Host computes claimDigest = tagged_struct_hash('risc0.ReceiptClaim', pre, post, exitCode, input, output). This is the digest exposed as receipt.claimDigest.

7. For Groth16 wrapping: claimDigest bytes are reversed byte order (reverseByteOrderUint256) then split into two 128-bit halves: claim0 = low 128 bits reversed, claim1 = high 128 bits reversed. Same split for control_root.
8. Public inputs for Groth16 circuit = [control_root_0, control_root_1, claim0, claim1, BN254_CONTROL_ID] each as BN254 Fr element (uint256 < field modulus).

9. Succinct STARK proof is verified inside Groth16 circuit: circuit checks FRI verification against control_root and that inner claimDigest equals public input claim. BN254_CONTROL_ID binds which recursion circuit variant.

10. Groth16 prover produces proof Seal {a,b,c} for those public inputs using Groth16 proving key. Encoded seal = selector (first 4 bytes of sha256('risc0.Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters' || control_root || reverse(BN254_CONTROL_ID) || vk_digest)) + abi.encode(a,b,c).
11. On-chain verifier: checks selector matches its pinned parameters, splits digests same way, calls Groth16 pairing check with pinned VK (IC points). If passes, claimDigest is considered proven.
12. Application verifier then checks journalDigest binding (sha256(journal) == expected) and imageId binding (preStateDigest == expected imageId or imageId param equals expected).

circuit_version_dependent_parts: CONTROL_ROOT - hash of recursion circuit set, changes every zkVM release (e.g., 1.0, 1.1, 2.0, 3.0.5 have different control roots)
BN254_CONTROL_ID - identifier for BN254 Groth16 recursion verifier circuit, changes with recursion circuit update
Groth16 verifying key (VK) - alpha, beta, gamma, delta, IC[0..5] points - tied to control_root and BN254_CONTROL_ID, changes with each release
SELECTOR - derived from control_root + BN254_CONTROL_ID + vk_digest, so version-dependent
SYSTEM_STATE_ZERO_DIGEST - constant zero state hash, stable but may be redefined
ReceiptClaim field layout - preStateDigest vs imageId field name changed between risc0-ethereum-contracts versions (some versions have imageId field, some have preStateDigest holding imageId)
what_breaks_if_wrong_version: SelectorMismatch revert if verifier checks selector - receipt rejected even if proof is valid for other version; dApp appears broken

If selector check skipped and VK mismatched, Groth16 pairing check fails - proof rejected with VerificationFailed, but attacker could supply proof from old version with known vulnerability if verifier still pins old VK

If verifier uses wrong control_root as public input, honest proofs from new prover will have public inputs that don't match verifier's expected control_root, causing verification failure even though claimDigest correct

If verifier pins old control_root that included buggy recursion circuit, attacker could generate fake succinct receipt that old circuit accepted (e.g., accepting invalid FRI), then wrap to Groth16 and it would verify against old VK - upgrade required
Byte order change: older versions used different reverseByteOrder convention; using wrong splitDigest leads to claim0/claim1 mismatch, valid proof fails

Field name change: if verifier expects ReceiptClaim.preStateDigest to be imageId but new version expects separate imageId param, claimDigest reconstruction yields different hash, causing journal binding bypass or false rejection

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Journal hash not checked - using journal bytes directly without comparing sha256(journal) to Output.journalDigest in claim
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: Recompute journalDigest = sha256(journal bytes) and require equality with claim's Output.journalDigest; also require Output digest matches claim's output field
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Journal substitution: attacker takes valid receipt for program that committed '0' and presents journal '1000000' with same seal; verifier accepts inflated balance because proof still valid but journal not bound.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: ImageId / preStateDigest not checked against expected program
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: Require receipt claim's preStateDigest (or separate imageId param) equals expected ImageID for the application logic; for ok() case, require preStateDigest == expected imageId
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Program substitution: attacker proves execution of attacker-controlled ELF that commits same journal (e.g., program that just commits attacker-supplied data) and passes it as proof of honest program; verifier accepts because it never checks which program was executed.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: ExitCode not validated - accepting Paused or Halted with non-zero user code as success
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: Require exitCode.system == Halted (0) and exitCode.user == 0 for successful unconditional execution; explicitly reject SystemSplit and Paused unless resumption flow is intended
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Failure acceptance: attacker submits receipt where guest called env::fail or exited with user code 1 indicating business logic failure (e.g., insufficient funds check failed), but verifier treats as success because it only checks Groth16 proof, not exit code.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: AssumptionsDigest not required to be zero for unconditional receipts
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: For unconditional verification, require Output.assumptionsDigest == bytes32(0). If composition allowed, require explicit list of assumed claims and verify each recursively
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Assumption smuggling: attacker creates receipt that says 'this is valid if assumption X is valid' where X is 'admin approved', but never proves X; verifier ignoring assumptionsDigest accepts conditional proof as unconditional, granting admin rights.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Selector / ControlRoot / BN254_CONTROL_ID not pinned or not checked
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: Pin expected CONTROL_ROOT and BN254_CONTROL_ID per zkVM version; compute expected selector = first 4 bytes of sha256(tag || control_root || reverse(bn254_control_id) || vk_digest) and require seal[:4] == expected; also use pinned control_root as Groth16 public input
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Version downgrade / custom circuit forgery: attacker builds custom recursion circuit that accepts any claim, generates its own control_root and VK, produces Groth16 proof for arbitrary claim, and submits to verifier that does not check selector/control_root; proof verifies against attacker's VK if verifier uses attacker-supplied VK, or against old vulnerable VK if verifier still accepts old version.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Byte order / splitDigest mishandled - using keccak256 instead of sha256 or forgetting reverseByteOrderUint256
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches: Use SHA256 for all digests (not Keccak256), and splitDigest = reverseByteOrderUint256(digest) split into low/high 128-bit halves as uint128. Recompute public inputs exactly as in RiscZeroGroth16Verifier.splitDigest
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_if_missed: Public input malleability: if verifier uses wrong hash or wrong byte order, honest proofs fail, and attacker can craft two different claimDigests that map to same public inputs under buggy split, causing collision and acceptance of wrong claim; or more commonly, verifier never accepts any honest proof leading to DoS and fallback to unchecked path.

When each is produced (prover default -> composite, compress() -> succinct, groth16 -> wrapped) confirmed from risc0 examples and cartesi-risc0-cli docs. Medium certainty on exact enum names (InnerReceipt vs ReceiptKind) may have changed between v1.x and v3.x.

High certainty for selector as first 4 bytes of encoded seal from RiscZeroGroth16Verifier.sol source lines 274-300 and encode_seal docs. High certainty for public inputs = control_root (2), claim (2), bn254_control_id (1) from RiscZeroGroth16Verifier _verifyIntegrity lines 354-376. Field names may have changed across versions.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: High certainty for ReceiptClaim fields preStateDigest, postStateDigest, exitCode, input, output from docs.rs risc0_ethereum_contracts ReceiptClaim struct and Go verifier struct (PreStateDigest, PostStateDigest, ExitCode, Input, Output). High certainty for Output containing journalDigest and assumptionsDigest from Go Output struct and Solidity OutputLib. Medium certainty for imageId location: in Go GetOKReceiptClaim, imageId is passed separately; in Solidity ok() helper, first field of ReceiptClaim is imageId (preStateDigest = imageId). This discrepancy is version-dependent - noted as such. High certainty for exitCode structure (SystemExitCode enum Halted/Paused/SystemSplit + user u8) from Go ExitCode struct. Claim digest computation as tagged struct SHA256 is high certainty from StructHash library usage and risc0 source references to tagged_struct, but exact tag strings 'risc0.ReceiptClaim' and 'risc0.Output' are inferred from verifier_key_digest tag 'risc0_groth16.VerifyingKey' and need confirmation - medium certainty on exact tag spelling.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High certainty for steps 1-6 from Solidity RiscZeroGroth16Verifier verify() calling ReceiptClaimLib.ok(imageId, journalDigest).digest() and from Go docs journal hash -> Output -> ReceiptClaim -> claim digest -> sys_verify_integrity. High certainty for splitDigest reverseByteOrder and 5 public inputs from Solidity splitDigest function and verifyIntegrity public inputs array. Medium certainty for intermediate recursion steps (lift, join, resolve) names - general recursion knowledge, not verified against specific risc0 monorepo bootstrap output. High certainty for selector derivation from verifier parameters including vk_digest from Solidity verifier_key_digest() function lines 222-265.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: High certainty that control_root, BN254_CONTROL_ID, VK, selector are version-dependent from RiscZeroGroth16Verifier contract comments lines 168-204 stating control root controls what set of recursion programs will be accepted and new releases require updating values via cargo xtask bootstrap.
