data.reasoning: Operative phrase 'more than 2 percent' means >2%, so equality does not satisfy the trigger.
Operative phrase 'more than 36 months' means >36, so 36 is not included.
Operative phrase 'by 1.5 or more' means >=1.5, so equality triggers.
Pass requires NOT (>=2.25), i.e. <2.25, so '2.25 or more' inclusive threshold causes fail at and above.

verdicts.at: FAIL at (10.0M, 0.9M) and FAIL at (9.9M, 1.0M) - strict < fails on equality
verdicts.above: FAIL - any dimension >= threshold fails due to strict < and AND

data.reasoning: Both legs use strict 'less than' (<), so equality on either leg fails the AND test.
Phrase 'equal to or greater than' means >=16%, so equality passes.
Phrase 'at least equal to' means >=50%, so equality satisfies the floor.
Phrase 'equal to or greater than' means >= threshold, so equality triggers significant incident.

data.weakest_point: Rule 8 NIS2 significant incident users leg - least certain verbatim EU text and national transposition vary between 'exceeds', 'more than', and 'equal to or greater than', and Rule 5 GloBE de-minimis revenue/income phrasing is also secondary source; 8 is weakest due to NIS2 implementing act vs directive wording.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Overlay global-route congestion map with pin-density map and cell density map in same window
first_checks.why_first: cheapest visual check that rules out hidden pin bottleneck vs cell overcrowding

first_checks.check: Report routing resource blockage: PG mesh track usage, routing guides, and macro halo blockages per layer
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most common invisible blockage that placement density does not see

first_checks.check: List top 20 nets by pin count and bounding box that cross the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: cheap netlist topology check before rerunning router

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Color DRC markers by net class: if >80% of shorts/spacing markers touch PG via pillars or are within 2 tracks of wide PG straps, vs markers concentrated at macro pin channels
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: PG mesh / strap blockage and via pillar blocking is cause if PG-adjacent
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Pin access at IP boundary is cause if concentrated at macro channels, ruling out PG mesh

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Bump available routing layers by one or flip preferred direction on congested layer and rerun global route only: if overflow drops >50%, vs adding 2um channel spacing does nothing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: insufficient layer resource / wrong layer assignment if layer bump helps
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pin access / cell architecture issue if layer bump does not help but cell-swapping or access-optimized cells does

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement-aware pin-access checker / report pin access DRCs: if fails cluster exactly where routing DRCs are
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: cell pin access / low-track cell architecture issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: netlist high-fanout topology if pin checker is clean

common_root_causes.cause: Pin density / pin access at hard macro, IP boundary, or dense low-track stdcell region
Over-constrained PG mesh, wide straps, or routing blockages / guides stealing tracks
Insufficient routing layers allocated, wrong preferred direction, or layer-specific NDRs
Netlist with unbuffered high-fanout, high pin-count nets (clocks, resets, tie nets) not declared as such
Cell architecture with weak M0/M1 access window (e.g., 7.5T cell at low utilization)

data.classic_trap: Spreading placement to lower density, which increases wirelength and makes congestion and routing DRCs worse instead of fixing pin/blockage root
data.node_era_note: At 28nm congestion correlated with cell density; at 7nm-and-below congestion occurs at 50-60% density driven by M0/M1 pin access and PG via pillars even when placement looks clean

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Compare same paths pre-CTS (ideal clocks) vs post-CTS timing

first_checks.check: Check SDC constraints: false paths, multicycle paths, case analysis still valid after CTS
first_checks.why_first: avoids optimizing intentionally false paths

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all failing paths share a single common clock gating cell, common point, or long common clock trunk with large detour, vs failures spread across unrelated clock domains and hierarchies
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock gating / common clock trunk / CTS detour around blockage if shared
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: floorplan / macro placement causing long data wires if spread unrelated

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with useful-skew disabled / zero skew and with OCV derates set to 0: if violations shrink dramatically with zero skew, skew balancing is culprit

discriminating_experiments.rules_out: high logic depth / high fanout data path if violations remain with ideal clocks

discriminating_experiments.rules_out: placement / floorplan wirelength if shallow but long wire

common_root_causes.cause: High logic depth / high fanout data paths that were marginal pre-CTS
CTS detours around placement blockages / macros adding insertion delay and skew
Floorplan with long macro-to-macro or macro-to-IO distances forcing long wires
Incorrect or missing false path / multicycle exceptions causing over-constraining
Unrealistic OCV / pessimism or latency-budget mismatch between synthesis and CTS

data.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budgeting between unimplemented blocks
data.situation: Top-level integration where Block A launches to Block B and neither block is implemented yet, need to assign set_input_delay to B and set_output_delay from A to close top level early
data.derivation: Step1: Get top-level period T (e.g., T=1000ps confidence 1.0 if given). Step2: Estimate top-level interconnect between blocks: assumes 15% of T for 28nm (confidence 0.6) and 25% of T for 7nm-and-below (confidence 0.55) due to via resistance. So T_interconnect = T * 0.15 (confidence 0.6). Step3: Estimate uncertainty/jitter: assumes 10% of T (confidence 0.65) for setup. Step4: Remaining budget T_remain = T - T_interconnect - T_uncert = T * 0.75 (confidence 0.6). Step5: Split between launch and capture based on logic depth from RTL: if balanced, 50%/50% of T_remain (confidence 0.6); if one block is known control-heavy, 40%/60% (confidence 0.5). Step6: For Block B input: set_input_delay -max = T_launch + T_interconnect (e.g., 0.375*T + 0.15*T = 0.525*T). For Block B input -min for hold: assumes 10% of T (confidence 0.5) to ensure short path not over-optimistic. For Block A output: set_output_delay -max = T_capture + T_interconnect.
data.wrong_way: Assign 50% period to each block and 0% to interconnect, or assign set_input_delay = 0.5*T and set_output_delay = 0.5*T independently, double-counting period and leaving no room for top-level wire; downstream fails with uncloseable top-level paths after both blocks harden, requiring ECO re-budget
data.defense: Show RTL stage count estimate per block, historical wire delay from previous similar floorplan with similar bump pitch, and top-level floorplan distance estimate; keep budget spreadsheet with T_launch/T_interconnect/T_capture columns and review with both block owners; validate with zero-interconnect top-level trial route
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (over-budgeting interconnect/launch): block becomes bloated, inserts excess buffers, area/power spiral, may still pass signoff but fails PPA; Too loose (under-budgeting interconnect): block passes alone but top-level fails setup with real wires, requires late re-budget and full block re-implementation
data.node_era_note: At 28nm interconnect estimate 10-15% of period was safe; at 7nm-and-below need 20-30% plus via ladder and BEOL variation margin due to thin wires

data.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision and defense
data.situation: Long timing path that looks like setup failure but is functionally not exercised every cycle, e.g., config register to datapath, mode mux, one-hot FSM branch, or debug path
data.derivation: Step1: Trace enable condition: does path go through a MUX select that is static for N cycles? Check RTL: if select comes from config reg that only writes on boot, N >= 10 cycles (confidence 0.7). Step2: Check temporal exclusivity: can launch and capture happen in same cycle per spec? Run formal reachability or check simulation that config write and datapath active are mutually exclusive. Step3: If mutually exclusive never in same cycle for functional operation, candidate for set_false_path. If mutually exclusive for K cycles but re-converges, candidate for set_multicycle_path K. Example: N=2 cycles for double-flop mode change (confidence 0.6), so set_multicycle_path -setup 2 -hold 1. Step4: Validate that all side-paths covered: ensure no other timing arc uses same net without the static condition. Step5: Require waiver: list startpoint-endpoint pair plus RTL condition signal name.
data.wrong_way: Mark any failing long path as false path to close timing quickly without proving static condition, or mark a true multicycle as false, or mark as multicycle 2 when hold needs explicit -hold 1 handling; silently breaks because synthesis/place no longer fixes path, but in rare functional mode path is active and silicon fails at speed or hold fails in silicon due to missing hold multicycle
data.defense: Provide waveform showing config stable for >N cycles, formal proof of mutual exclusivity, or static signal tied in this mode (case analysis); show CDC or mode constraint file that forces MUX select; get architect sign-off on mode table; keep false path list in version-controlled exceptions file with comment referencing spec section
data.signoff_risk: Too loose (false when should be multicycle or timed): path unbounded, late transition causes functional failure at speed, not caught at signoff STA because exception hides it; Too tight (timed when should be false): over-constrains implementation, creates congestion and setup/hold ping-pong, may still signoff but with PPA penalty and possible hold fixes that hurt setup
data.node_era_note: At 28nm false paths often tolerated; at 7nm-and-below false paths hide OCV and aging effects, reviewers require formal proof plus set_clock_groups handling

data.pattern_name: Clock-domain crossing max-delay budgeting for 2-flop sync and async FIFO
data.situation: Signal crossing from clkA to clkB asynchronous, protected by 2-flop synchronizer or async FIFO pointers, need SDC to prevent STA from timing it as synchronous
data.derivation: Step1: Identify sync chain: first flop after crossing is synchronizer, mark set_false_path or set_asynchronous_group between clocks, or set_max_delay -datapath_only. Step2: For data with valid handshake, constrain data delay to be less than destination period to ensure it is stable when sampled: assumes max allowed = 80% of min(dest period, source period) (confidence 0.6) minus 15% margin for jitter (confidence 0.55). Example: if dest period = 1000ps (confidence 1.0), set_max_delay = 800ps (confidence 0.6) -datapath_only from launch to first sync flop. Step3: For FIFO pointers gray-coded, set_max_delay = 1 * dest period (confidence 0.65) and set_min_delay = 0 for hold. Step4: Do NOT cut control path with same max: sync chain itself gets set_false_path -from launch -to sync0 to allow unlimited metastability resolution time, but keep set_max_delay on data bus.
data.wrong_way: Apply set_clock_groups -asynchronous to both data and control without max-delay, which allows data to have infinite delay and FIFO pointer to drift multiple cycles, causing functional CDC bug that STA hides; or apply set_false_path to data bus instead of control, silently allowing 10ns route on 1GHz interface
data.defense: Show synchronizer schematic, point to 2-flop chain in RTL, provide CDC tool report (e.g., Questa CDC) that data is qualified by synchronized valid, and show max-delay report that data arrives within one dest clock; retain pointer gray-coding proof
data.signoff_risk: Too loose (pure false path on data): CDC passes STA but fails in silicon due to data changing during sync window, metastability + data incoherence, signoff CDC checker will flag unbounded delay; Too tight (max-delay too small, e.g., 20% of period): implementation over-constrains, fails to route, forces unnecessary pipelining
data.node_era_note: At 28nm set_clock_groups -asynchronous often sufficient; at 7nm-and-below need set_max_delay -datapath_only plus OCV-aware margin due to larger variation on short cross-domain nets

data.pattern_name: Early over-constraining and staged relaxation
data.situation: Early floorplan/placement stage where wire estimates are optimistic and late degradation from CTS, routing, and OCV is expected
data.derivation: Step1: Start with target period T. Step2: Apply over-constraint factor: assumes 15% over-constraint (confidence 0.6) at synthesis, so T_synth = T * 0.85 (confidence 0.6). Step3: Add clock uncertainty: assumes 10% of T for early stage (confidence 0.65) vs 5% at signoff (confidence 0.7). Step4: Keep input/output delays at nominal, do NOT over-constrain both period and IO simultaneously; only over-constrain core. Step5: Staged relaxation: after CTS, relax to 7% over-constraint (confidence 0.55) (T * 0.93), after route to 3% (confidence 0.5) (T * 0.97), before signoff to 0%. Step6: Track slack histogram: if worst slack >20% of T (confidence 0.6) early, indicates too much margin still available.
data.wrong_way: Over-constrain period by 30% (confidence misapplied) AND set_input_delay to 60% of period AND set_output_delay to 60% of period simultaneously, creating impossible 120% budget that forces tool to bloat logic and insert buffers everywhere, leading to power/area blowup and later unfixable congestion
data.defense: Show historical degradation curve from previous similar design: synthesis to place ~5% loss (confidence 0.55), place to CTS ~5% (confidence 0.55), CTS to route ~5-8% (confidence 0.5); justify over-constraint factor as sum of expected degradation; track QOR trend weekly and relax only when slack stable for 2 runs
data.signoff_risk: Too tight early: implementation becomes unnecessarily large, high power, congestion prevents closure, may still signoff but with 20-30% area penalty; Too loose early: early optimism hides real failures, late surprise with -200ps slack at route requiring full re-synthesis
data.node_era_note: At 28nm 10% over-constraint often enough; at 7nm-and-below need 15-20% due to via resistance and low-Vdd variation, but must relax earlier to avoid excessive low-Vt usage

data.pattern_name: Virtual clock for IO budgeting
data.situation: Chip-level IO interface where external device clock does not exist inside chip, need to model external launch/capture for set_input_delay and set_output_delay
data.derivation: Step1: create_clock -name VCLK -period T_ext equal to external device period (e.g., T_ext=1000ps confidence 1.0). Step2: Set virtual clock latency = 0 (confidence 1.0) because no internal network, but set uncertainty = board jitter + chip jitter: assumes 10% of T_ext (confidence 0.6). Step3: For input: set_input_delay -clock VCLK -max = T_board_max + T_ext_Tco_max + margin. Example: board delay max 300ps (confidence 0.6), Tco max 400ps (confidence 0.6), margin 50ps (confidence 0.5), so input max = 750ps. Set -min = board min + Tco min - margin (e.g., 100ps + 100ps -50ps =150ps). Step4: For output: set_output_delay -clock VCLK -max = T_board_max + T_setup_external (e.g., 300ps+200ps=500ps confidence 0.6), -min = T_board_min - T_hold_external.
data.wrong_way: Constrain IO using internal generated clock that includes internal insertion delay, causing double-counting of clock latency: input delay appears to have extra 500ps insertion, tool over-constrains data path and fails IO timing that is actually external-only; or using same clock for both input and output with zero virtual latency causing hold miscalculation
data.defense: Provide external device datasheet Tco/Tsu/Th numbers, board trace length to delay conversion (approx 6ps per mm (confidence 0.5)), and show virtual clock has no source latency; cross-check with IBIS or board simulation; keep VCLK separate per IO bank
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (large input/output delay): chip fails to close IO timing, adds unnecessary pipeline, may still signoff but with reduced Fmax; Too loose (small delay): chip passes internal STA but fails at system level on board, setup/hold failure at external device not caught until lab
data.node_era_note: At 28nm virtual clock latency 0 was sufficient; at 7nm-and-below need to model board and package via separate clock latency and include package trace variation

data.pattern_name: Generated and divided clock constraint derivation
data.situation: Internal clock divider, muxed clock, or PLL output that is not master clock, need correct timing relationship for STA
data.derivation: Step1: Master clock period T_master (e.g., 1000ps confidence 1.0). Step2: create_generated_clock -source [get_pin divider/Q] -divide_by N (e.g., N=2 confidence 1.0) so T_gen = T_master * N = 2000ps. Step3: If divided by 2 with 50% duty, set edges -edges {1 3 5} or -divide_by 2. Step4: Clock latency: generated clock latency = master insertion + divider cell delay: assumes divider delay 30ps (confidence 0.5) + wire 20ps (confidence 0.5). Step5: Uncertainty: master uncertainty 50ps (confidence 0.6) + divider jitter 20ps (confidence 0.5) = 70ps total (confidence 0.55). Step6: Set clock groups: if muxed clocks are mutually exclusive, set_clock_groups -physically_exclusive, else -logically_exclusive; do NOT use -asynchronous unless truly asynchronous.
data.wrong_way: Create generated clock with -combinational instead of -divide_by, losing edge relationship and causing STA to analyze 1-cycle path as 2-cycle or vice versa; or forget to set generated clock source latency, leading to 0 skew assumption and hold failures in silicon; or use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for muxed synchronous clocks, hiding synchronous transfer
data.defense: Show clock divider schematic, simulation showing divided edge aligns to master, and report_clocks showing master is source; verify with report_clock -skew that generated relationship matches RTL expectation; check that generated clock period matches measured division in gate sim
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (wrong divide factor, e.g., divide_by 4 instead of 2): half the paths appear as multicycle incorrectly, tool under-fixes, silicon fails at double frequency; Too loose (false -asynchronous between related generated clocks): cross-clock paths not timed, potential setup/hold failure between divide domains that are actually synchronous
data.node_era_note: At 28nm generated clock auto-derived often worked; at 7nm-and-below need explicit -master_clock and latency adjustment due to large divider variation and duty-cycle distortion

data.pattern_name: System-synchronous and source-synchronous output budgeting with board trace
data.situation: Chip drives data and clock/strobe to external device, need to split timing budget between chip, board, and external setup/hold
data.derivation: Step1: External device requires T_setup_ext = 200ps (confidence 0.6) and T_hold_ext = 100ps (confidence 0.6) at its pins. Step2: Board trace mismatch between clock and data: assumes max skew 50ps (confidence 0.55) due to 8mm mismatch (6ps/mm confidence 0.5). Step3: For source-synchronous (clock and data both from chip, edge-aligned): set_output_delay -max = T_board_max + T_setup_ext + board_skew_max = 300ps+200ps+50ps=550ps (confidence 0.6), set_output_delay -min = T_board_min - T_hold_ext - board_skew (e.g., 100ps-100ps-50ps = -50ps) meaning hold may be negative allowed. Step4: For system-synchronous (common board clock): output delay must include full period: set_output_delay -max = T_period - (T_setup_ext + board). Step5: Add margin 5% of period (confidence 0.6) for OCV.
data.wrong_way: Use same output delay for both source-sync and system-sync, ignoring that source-sync budget is board+setup only while system-sync includes period, causing either impossible timing (system-sync too tight) or under-constrained source-sync that fails on board due to unmodeled trace skew
data.defense: Provide board stackup and trace length report, external device datasheet with setup/hold numbers, and diagram showing clock-data alignment (center-aligned vs edge-aligned); show calculation spreadsheet with board min/max separate and justify margin from SI simulation
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: over-constrains output path, forces large drivers and hurts power, may still signoff but with SI issues; Too loose: chip passes STA but board fails because external setup/hold violated in corner, found only in lab with pattern-dependent failures
data.node_era_note: At 28nm board skew 50ps often negligible vs 2ns period; at 7nm-and-below with 1GHz+ source-sync, 50ps board skew is 5% of period and must be budgeted explicitly

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous handshake interface max/min delay constraint
data.situation: Asynchronous SRAM, flash, or custom handshake where request, address, data have no common clock, timing is relative between signals
data.derivation: Step1: Identify handshake: e.g., req launches, ack returns, data must be stable before ack. Step2: Do NOT use set_input_delay with period; use set_max_delay and set_min_delay between related signals. Step3: Example: req to data valid: set_max_delay -from [get_ports req] -to [get_ports data] = T_external_access_max + board_max = 10ns (confidence 0.6) (e.g., SRAM access 8ns (confidence 0.6) + board 2ns (confidence 0.5)). Step4: Hold: set_min_delay = board_min + hold requirement of external device = 1ns (confidence 0.5). Step5: For bidirectional, separate read and write constraints with -rise/-fall and case analysis on direction pin. Step6: False path all unrelated clocks to these IOs to avoid period-based analysis interfering.
data.wrong_way: Constrain async interface with create_clock + set_input_delay using arbitrary 10ns period, causing STA to check against non-existent clock edge and either miss true max-delay violation or create artificial multicycle; or apply set_false_path to entire async interface, allowing unbounded delay and silicon read failure
data.defense: Provide external device timing diagram showing req->data relationship without clock, and board trace delays; show that max-delay constraint directly models access time, not period; include protocol assertion that req de-asserts after ack, proven by formal
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (max-delay too small): implementation fails to meet impossible async timing, forces unnecessary pipelining and area; Too loose (false path): path can be 20ns but STA reports no violation, chip fails to read external memory at speed, caught only in system test
data.node_era_note: At 28nm async interfaces often handled with simple false path; at 7nm-and-below need explicit max/min delay plus SI-aware derating due to long board traces and on-die variation

data.title: Embrace speed-demon frequency design alongside braniac complexity
data.where_in_paper: Introduction and Guiding principles – Very-high-frequency design
data.decision: Revamp chip design with new transistor-level tools and regular dataflow constructs to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies (1.1 and 1.3 GHz initial), embracing high clock rate in addition to traditional complex-IPC approach
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Staying solely in braniac camp – more complex design but higher instructions-per-cycle rate without pursuing high clock rate – which IBM UNIX systems had traditionally followed
data.rationale: To maintain leadership position, need leadership operating frequencies; balanced design can achieve high frequency without sacrificing IPC, and system was designed to preserve balance as technology allows even higher frequencies
data.outcome: POWER4 introduced at 1.1 GHz and 1.3 GHz, surpassing other 64-bit microprocessors in key benchmarks, with path to increase frequency while preserving system balance
data.quote_as_recalled: With the POWER4, IBM opted to also embrace the speeddemon approach.
data.weakest_point: Exact initial frequencies 1.1 and 1.3 GHz may be from intro not guiding principles; page number may be 5 not 6

data.title: RAS beyond parts and ECC – transform checkstops to software interrupts
data.where_in_paper: Guiding principles – Leadership in reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS)
data.decision: Require RAS approach that eliminates outages and provides redundancy where errors cannot be eliminated, and where possible transform hard machine stops (checkstops) into synchronous machine interrupts to software to allow circumvention
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Achieving high levels of reliability only by choosing reliable parts and incorporating error-correction-code (ECC) logic into major arrays
data.rationale: Servers evolved toward continuous operation, needing mainframe-like RAS attributes; choosing reliable parts and ECC alone does not achieve high levels of reliability
data.outcome: POWER4 incorporates pervasive functions for first-failure data capture, BIST, performance monitoring, error detection/logging, and firmware/OS recovery that can restore and continue after errors such as L1 parity errors
data.quote_as_recalled: one does not achieve high levels of reliability only by choosing reliable parts and incorporating errorcorrectioncode (ECC) logic into major arrays.
data.weakest_point: Exact wording may have line-break hyphenation differences from OCR; transform checkstops sentence is separate but related

data.title: Full-system co-design of technology, packaging, and microarchitecture
data.where_in_paper: Guiding principles – Full-system design approach and POWER4 chip overview
data.decision: Design entire system together from processor to memory and I/O bridge chips as a synergistic architecture, not as isolated chip, leveraging process technology and packaging to optimize total system
data.rationale: One of IBM's major strengths is system expertise to design multiple parts consistently; a new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to feed it effectively, and POWER4 as used refers not only to chip but structure to interconnect chips
data.outcome: Resultant POWER4 chip family includes on-chip L2, L3 directory, fabric controller, GX controller, pervasive functions, and ability to build 8-way MCM and up to 32-way SMP systems with balanced buses
data.quote_as_recalled: POWER4 cannot be considered only a chip, but rather an architecture within which a set of chips are designed together to realize a system.
data.weakest_point: Attributing 8-way and 32-way outcome to this section may conflate chip overview section; directory vs data split belongs to later section

data.title: Two cores on one chip sharing unified L2 via CIU crossbar with three autonomous controllers
data.where_in_paper: POWER4 chip section – Chip logical view and L2 cache
data.decision: Place two identical processor cores on one POWER4 die sharing a unified second-level cache on same chip through a core interface unit (CIU) crossbar switch, with L2 implemented as three separate autonomous controllers each feeding 32 bytes per cycle
data.rationale: To optimize for SMP operation where large number of transistors can be used to improve total system performance for high-throughput multitasking, providing two-way SMP model to software on single chip and maintaining bandwidth to both cores
data.outcome: CIU connects each L2 controller to either data or instruction cache in either processor, accepts 8-byte stores, and supports more than 200 instructions in flight with up to eight instructions issued per cycle
data.quote_as_recalled: The two processors share a unified secondlevel cache, also on the same chip, through a core interface unit (CIU)
data.weakest_point: 32 bytes per cycle per controller detail may belong to later detailed L2 section not chip overview; three controllers vs three slices distinction

data.title: Distributed switch interconnect with frequency-scaled buses
data.where_in_paper: Interconnecting chips to form larger SMPs and System balance
data.decision: Use distributed switch interconnect topology new to industry where each chip writes to its own bus and snoops all buses, and make all chip-chip and fabric buses scale with processor frequency to preserve system balance as technology improves
data.rationale: To form systems up to 32-way SMP from 4-chip 8-way MCM building blocks while maintaining flat memory model with worst-case latency only slightly more than 10 percent over best-case, and to allow system balance to be maintained over time as frequencies increase
data.outcome: Four POWER4 chips on MCM form 8-way SMP; up to four MCMs interconnect in ring via inter-module buses acting as repeaters; bus speeds scale proportionately, maintaining balance and enabling larger caches and parallelism in future systems
data.quote_as_recalled: The interconnect topology, referred to as a distributed switch, is new to the industry.
data.weakest_point: Half-processor-speed for all buses and 10 percent latency figure may be from later system balance paragraph; alternative bus design not explicitly stated as rejected
