data.symptom: Congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: View layer-by-layer congestion heatmap (not just overall density map)
first_checks.why_first: overall density can look fine while a single metal layer is critically oversubscribed in a narrow region

first_checks.check: Check the congestion map against macro boundaries and high-pin-count cells in the hotspot region
first_checks.why_first: macro abutment zones and dense pin arrays are the single most common hidden congestion source behind clean-looking density

first_checks.check: Run the global router's congestion report (per-gcell overflow counts by layer) before looking at DRCs
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes genuine capacity problems from detailed-router path-finding failures, which have completely different fixes

first_checks.check: Check if hotspot region uses double-via or ECO cell insertions that consumed routing tracks
first_checks.why_first: post-ECO track starvation is a frequent late-stage surprise that looks like congestion but has a different fix

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Halve cell density in the hotspot gcell region via placement blockage and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if global-route overflow disappears, the congestion was genuine density-related and you need local cell spreading or halos
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, the issue is macro pin access or layer-direction conflict, not cell density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Flip the preferred routing direction of the offending metal layer in the hotspot region only and re-run global route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if overflow clears, you had a layer-direction conflict (typically near rotated macros or cross-boundary routes)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, direction was not the cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Route the hotspot region with cell-level pin-access (patch) turned off to see if pin-access alone creates the overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if overflow disappears, the issue is pin-access geometry consuming routing resources, not net congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, it is genuine net congestion

common_root_causes.cause: Macro adjacency: two large macros with complex pin interfaces placed too close, consuming all lower-metal routing resources in the channel
Huge netlist fanout nets (clock gating, resets, test) creating local routing demand spikes on a single metal layer
Standard-cell placement ignoring metal-layer direction constraints, creating layer-direction conflicts
Post-ECO routing track starvation from double-via insertion or ECO cell density

data.classic_trap: Engineers add halos or spread cells everywhere instead of checking per-layer congestion, which fixes nothing when the actual cause is a macro pin-access or layer-direction problem on a single metal layer.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, lower metal pitches mean macro pin-access congestion is far worse and appears at much smaller inter-macro gaps than at 28nm.
data.weakest_point: Frequency labels and discrimination logic are from general practice, not any single documented case. The node-era contrast is particularly approximate.

data.symptom: Setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check if violations are on paths sharing a single clock domain with excessive insertion delay or skew
first_checks.why_first: CTS-induced setup violations localized to one clock domain point to clock-tree structure problems, which are cheaper to fix than redesigning data paths

first_checks.check: Verify that clock latency is within the SDC target for each clock domain (compare post-CTS timing with post-placement pre-CTS timing)
first_checks.why_first: a jump in violations coinciding with CTS means clock insertion delay ate into setup slack, which is a different root cause than data-path issues

first_checks.check: Report whether the violations cluster near macro boundaries or in specific physical regions
first_checks.why_first: spatial clustering suggests placement or floorplan issues rather than logic or constraint problems

first_checks.check: Check for clock-gating cells with high output capacitance that the CTS engine struggles to buffer
first_checks.why_first: unusual clock-gate structures can silently create large insertion delays in one subtree

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run timing with the clock tree back-annotated to post-CTS parasitics but data-path still at placement-estimated parasitics
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations appear mainly on paths where clock latency increased, the CTS is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations existed before CTS with similar slack, the issue was already in the data path and CTS just exposed it

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check timing on the same failing paths with an ideal clock network (set_ideal_network on the clock root)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations vanish, the clock tree insertion delay or skew is the culprit, not the data path
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations remain, the data path itself is too slow regardless of clock quality

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate whether all failing paths share one clock subtree root (same clock buffer chain) versus spread across unrelated subtrees
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if they share one subtree root, a local CTS structural issue (bad pin, wrong NDR, congestion blocking buffer insertion) is likely
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if they spread across unrelated subtrees, the design simply has marginal timing that CTS latency pushes negative

common_root_causes.cause: CTS insertion delay consuming most of the setup slack because the design was marginally timed at placement (data paths slightly too slow, relying on optimistic clock model)
High-fanout clock sink group (e.g., large register bank near a macro) causing skew or insertion-delay overshoot in one subtree
Wrong or missing non-default routing rule (NDR) on clock nets causing the CTS router to use suboptimal routes with higher RC than expected
Cross-domain path where the launch and capture clocks have asymmetric latencies that were not visible in the pre-CTS ideal-clock analysis
Large combinational depth on critical paths that was hidden by overly optimistic wire-load models in synthesis

data.classic_trap: Assuming all post-CTS setup violations are 'the tools will fix them in optimization' and not checking whether one clock subtree is structurally broken. Many engineers run ECO synthesis blindly instead of checking if CTS itself has a problem on one domain.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, OCV (on-chip variation) derates are much more aggressive, making marginal paths fail much more frequently after CTS than at 28nm where derates were milder.
data.weakest_point: The discrimination between clock-tree cause and data-path cause is well-established, but my frequency estimates are subjective practice impressions. The NDR-related cause may be less common than I recall.

data.symptom: Hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Count total hold violations and check if they are on a handful of paths or thousands
first_checks.why_first: a few hold violations are routine post-CTS and will be fixed by hold buffers; thousands suggest a structural problem in the clock tree or constraints

first_checks.check: Check whether violations are concentrated on very short combinational paths (zero-delay paths) or on inter-clock-domain crossings
first_checks.why_first: zero-delay paths require a different fix (inserting delay buffers) than skew-caused holds (fixing clock tree), and cross-domain holds suggest constraint issues

first_checks.check: Verify set_min_delay and set_min_pulse_width constraints are not overly tight due to a constraint error
first_checks.why_first: an erroneously tight min-delay constraint on an IO port or clock pin generates spurious hold violations that look like a real problem but are not

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hold violations disappear when you relax hold derates (OCV factors) to zero and re-run timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if they disappear or reduce dramatically, the violations are OCV-induced marginal holds that buffer insertion will fix
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if most violations remain, the cause is genuinely short data-path delay or clock skew, not OCV

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hold violations are on paths whose data-path delay is less than one gate delay (essentially zero-delay wire-only paths between register pairs)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if yes, this is the classic fast-path hold problem requiring deliberate delay insertion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if data-path delay is substantial, the hold violation is caused by clock skew favoring the capture edge

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hold violations are concentrated on paths crossing between two specific clock domains
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if yes, the inter-clock timing relationship (especially if one clock is derived from the other) has a skew issue in one direction
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations spread evenly across all clock domains, it is generic post-CTS hold behavior

common_root_causes.cause: Routine post-CTS hold violations on short data paths — this is normal and expected; hold-fixing buffers will be inserted in the next step
Clock skew between launch and capture registers biased in the hold-unfavorable direction (capture clock arrives early relative to launch)
Overly aggressive OCV derates making otherwise-clean paths appear as hold violations
Constraint error: an incorrect set_min_delay or set_false_path annotation that should have excluded the path but did not

data.classic_trap: Panic over thousands of post-CTS hold violations when in fact a large hold violation count is completely normal after CTS and before hold optimization. The real trap is NOT running hold fix and instead trying to 'fix' the clock tree, which can break setup timing.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, OCV derates are larger and hold violations are more numerous post-CTS; at 28nm, hold violations are fewer and the typical reaction is calmer.
data.weakest_point: The 'routine hold violations are normal' point is so fundamental it borders on trivial, but the discrimination logic is real practice. Frequency estimates are my best recall.

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Run dynamic IR-drop simulation (or voltage-aware STA if available) and check if timing-failing instances map to high-current-density regions
first_checks.why_first: this is the cheapest way to confirm or deny IR-drop as the cause — if failing cells are not in drop hotspots, IR-drop is not the cause

first_checks.check: Check if the violations are on paths through high-activity cells (clock buffers, large combinational blocks with high toggle rates)
first_checks.why_first: high-activity cells are both timing-critical and IR-drop contributors, making them the prime suspects

first_checks.check: Compare STA timing with and without voltage-drop annotation (if the flow supports annotated voltage per instance)
first_checks.why_first: directly isolates the timing impact of voltage drop on specific paths

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run STA with the voltage set to nominal (Vdd = max) on all instances and check if violations disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations vanish, they were voltage-drop-induced
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations remain, the timing failure has another cause (logic, placement, clock)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at the power-rail IR-drop map and check if violating paths share the same power stripe or via as a high-current block (e.g., SRAM macro IO ring)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violating cells sit on the same power stripe as a high-current sink, IR-drop on that stripe is likely the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violating cells are on well-powered stripes with minimal drop, IR-drop is not the cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Increase the number of power vias or widen the power stripe in the hotspot region and re-run timing + IR-drop jointly
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if timing violations clear, the power grid was insufficient in that region
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations persist, the power grid was adequate and the timing issue has a different root cause

common_root_causes.cause: Power grid insufficient in a localized region, often near large SRAM macros or high-activity register banks
Simultaneous switching of a large bus (e.g., data bus between a processor core and L2 cache) causing localized dynamic IR drop
Missing or insufficient decoupling capacitance near high-current blocks
Static IR drop on a long power stripe with too few vias connecting to the upper metal power grid

data.classic_trap: Assuming timing violations that appear late in the flow (post-route or signoff) are always routing-RC or OCV problems and never checking IR-drop. Engineers will re-run timing ECO and closure loops repeatedly before someone suggests running IR-drop analysis, wasting days.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, IR-drop effects are proportionally worse because Vdd is lower and a 50mV drop is a larger fraction of the supply; at 28nm, IR-drop was less frequently the root cause of timing failures.
data.weakest_point: IR-drop-induced timing failure is less common as a first-encountered symptom than the other entries; my frequency estimates for root causes are based on general practice impressions rather than measured data.

data.symptom: Clock skew / CTS divergence — sinks missing insertion-delay targets

first_checks.check: Run the CTS timing report and check if skew exceeds the target, and whether it is one subtree or globally bad
first_checks.why_first: identifies if the problem is localized (one subtree) or systemic (entire clock tree), which determines the fix approach

first_checks.check: Check the CTS log for warnings about congestion, blocked buffer locations, or pin-access failures that prevented optimal buffer placement
first_checks.why_first: CTS tools log their difficulties explicitly; these warnings are often the direct explanation of skew problems

first_checks.check: Verify the clock constraints (SDC): are clock targets realistic given the number of sinks and physical spread of the design?
first_checks.why_first: an overly tight insertion-delay target that is physically impossible will cause CTS to fail to converge without an obvious error

first_checks.check: Check if any clock sink has an unusual pin position (deeply buried inside a hard macro with long internal routing)
first_checks.why_first: a single hard-to-reach sink can dominate the entire subtree's insertion delay and skew

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Isolate the worst subtree and run CTS on it alone with relaxed skew/latency targets to see if it converges
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if it converges with relaxed targets, the problem was an overly tight constraint for that subtree's physical geometry
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if it still fails to converge, there is a physical-access problem (congestion, macro blockage) that prevents good buffer placement

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the same subtree achieves acceptable skew when you temporarily remove one specific sink (the one farthest from the center of the sink cluster)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if skew improves dramatically, that outlier sink is the problem — you may need to relocate the sink or add an NDR route
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if skew is still bad, the problem is the overall physical distribution of sinks, not one outlier

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare CTS results with a manual H-tree or fishbone topology versus the tool's auto-generated tree for the problematic domain
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if the manual tree achieves better skew, the tool's algorithm is failing on this particular sink distribution
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if both perform similarly, the problem is fundamental to the physical layout (sinks are too spread out)

common_root_causes.cause: Large number of physically dispersed sinks in one clock domain making it geometrically impossible to achieve tight skew targets
Macro blockage or congestion preventing the CTS engine from placing buffers in optimal locations
An outlier sink (e.g., inside a deep-hard-macro pin or at a chip boundary far from the clock root) dominating skew for its subtree
Clock-gating cell with high output capacitance creating an RC bottleneck in the clock tree
Missing or wrong non-default routing rule on clock nets causing the CTS router to use high-RC routes

data.classic_trap: Blaming the CTS tool settings (buffer list, max_transition) before checking physical feasibility. Many skew problems are caused by placement decisions (macro locations, register cluster assignments) that cannot be fixed by tweaking CTS parameters — the fix requires moving registers or modifying the floorplan.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, CTS must handle much more aggressive max_transition constraints and metal-layer resistance, making skew convergence harder; at 28nm, the tool has more margin on transition time and can use larger buffers more freely.
data.weakest_point: My recall of CTS divergence as a distinct symptom (versus just 'skew too high') may conflate two slightly different failure modes. The discrimination experiments are sound practice logic but I am not certain the H-tree/fishbone comparison is commonly done in automated flows.

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Look at the LVS report to determine if the mismatch is classified as short, open, or missing net — each has different dominant causes
first_checks.why_first: the classification immediately narrows the search space: shorts are almost always geometric, opens are often connectivity errors, and missing nets are usually abstract-level mismatches

first_checks.check: Check if the mismatch involves a power/ground net or a signal net — P/G mismatches are almost always via or stripe problems, signal mismatches are routing or cell-level
first_checks.why_first: P/G and signal mismatches have disjoint root-cause sets; checking this splits the problem immediately

first_checks.check: Run ERC (Electrical Rule Check) independently to see if there are connectivity anomalies that precede the LVS failure
first_checks.why_first: ERC violations often reveal the geometric cause of an LVS short or open before you need to visually inspect layout

first_checks.check: Check the LVS report for the specific cell instance or via structure involved and cross-reference with the extracted netlist
first_checks.why_first: identifying the specific physical structure narrows inspection to a small layout region rather than searching the whole chip

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract the layout of the mismatched region standalone and compare the extracted netlist to the expected netlist for that region alone
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if the standalone extraction also shows the mismatch, the problem is in the physical layout of that region
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if standalone extraction is clean, the mismatch is caused by connectivity between this region and the surrounding layout (via overlap, abutment error)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the shorted or missing net involves an auto-generated filler cell, endcap, or tap cell — remove the filler region and re-run LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if the mismatch disappears, the filler/endcap/tap cell is creating an unwanted connection or covering a needed connection
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if the mismatch remains, the problem is in the standard cells or routing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For a missing-net case: check if the net exists in the GDS but connects to the wrong pin or if it is entirely absent from the physical database
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if it connects to the wrong pin, the error is a pin-assignment or routing-layer mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if it is entirely absent, the error is in the netlist-to-GDS translation (missing wire, deleted by DRC fix, or tool bug)

common_root_causes.cause: Geometric short between two signal nets caused by routing DRC violation that the detailed router missed or that a post-route ECO introduced
Filler cell or endcap cell shorting to adjacent routing due to incorrect metal-fill rules or missing keep-out around special cells
Abutment error: two hard macros or blocks whose boundary metal layers overlap, creating an unintended short at the boundary
Pin-access layer mismatch: the standard cell pin is on a different metal layer than the router expects, creating an open
Manual ECO that was implemented in the netlist but not correctly reflected in the physical database (or vice versa)

data.classic_trap: Spending hours inspecting the signal routing when the actual short is between power stripes or filler cells. Engineers often assume signal-level causes before checking the most mechanically likely geometric cause: metal fill, endcaps, or abutment boundaries.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, metal fill is much denser and fill-rule-driven, making fill-related shorts more common than at 28nm where fill was simpler and less likely to cause LVS issues.
data.weakest_point: The filler-cell cause frequency may be inflated in my recall because fill-related LVS failures are memorable and annoying, biasing my frequency estimate upward.

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Verify that the schematic netlist used for LVS comparison matches the physical implementation version (correct library version, correct ECO level)
first_checks.why_first: version mismatch between netlist and layout is the most common cause of systematic device-size mismatches and is trivially checkable

first_checks.check: Check if the mismatch is in an analog or mixed-signal block where device sizes are drawn (not from standard cells) — these have different verification flows
first_checks.why_first: drawn device-size errors are a completely different category from digital standard-cell errors and require the analog layout extraction flow

first_checks.check: Check if the extra devices are substrate/well taps or guard-ring structures that the extraction tool counts but the schematic does not include
first_checks.why_first: extraction-counted parasitic devices (taps, guard rings) that are absent from the schematic are a very common 'extra device' false alarm

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the library cell masters used in the physical layout against the library version in the netlist — check for cell name suffix differences (e.g., _V2 vs _V3)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if cell masters differ, the layout was built from a different library version than the netlist, causing device-size mismatches
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if they match, the library version is consistent and the error is elsewhere

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For extra-device mismatches: check if the devices are diodes or substrate structures that the extraction tool generates by default and that can be excluded with a filter rule
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if they are diodes/substrate devices and the filter rule was missing, the 'extra devices' are a false alarm from the extraction settings
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if the extra devices are real transistor-level structures, there is a genuine layout-vs-schematic error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS in 'device-property' mode to identify which specific transistor parameters (W, L, fingers) differ, and compare those against the cell's GDS view in the standard-cell library
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if the GDS view itself has wrong dimensions, the library cell is corrupted
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if the GDS view matches but the extracted instance does not, the error is in how the tool handles the cell (e.g., duplicate instantiation, mirrored cell error)

common_root_causes.cause: Version mismatch between the netlist (from synthesis or P&R) and the physical layout database (GDS/OASIS), often due to an incomplete design database handoff
Extra devices from substrate diodes, well taps, or guard rings that the extraction tool generates but the schematic does not represent
Corrupt or mismatched standard-cell library GDS that differs from the library used for netlist generation (different library drop or corrupted file)
Analog block device-size error from manual layout modification that was not back-annotated to the schematic

data.classic_trap: Assuming 'extra devices' means the layout has unwanted transistors when in fact they are extraction-generated substrate devices that simply need a filter rule. Engineers can waste days looking for 'phantom' transistors in the layout that are not real layout errors.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, FinFET device counting is different from planar MOSFET counting, and the extraction tool may count fins rather than full transistors, leading to more confusing device-count mismatches if the LVS rule deck is not correctly configured.
data.weakest_point: My experience with wrong-device-size LVS errors is more limited than with other symptoms; frequency estimates carry lower confidence. The analog-block case in particular may be less common than I recall.

data.symptom: Antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Check the antenna violation report for the violating metal layer and the gate oxide area ratio exceeded
first_checks.why_first: the layer identifies whether the fix needs metal-jumper insertion (lower layers) or diode insertion (any layer), and the ratio tells you how severe the violation is

first_checks.check: Check if the violations are on nets that connect directly to gate inputs without passing through any buffer (long unbroken metal runs into a gate)
first_checks.why_first: these are the classic antenna-prone nets; if violations cluster here, the fix is straightforward antenna-diode insertion or metal jumpering

first_checks.check: Verify that the antenna rule deck is the correct one for the target process node and metal stack — wrong rule deck can generate false violations
first_checks.why_first: using the wrong antenna rules is a surprisingly common signoff-setup error, especially on multi-site projects with multiple process options

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run antenna check with and without the 'protected' flag on existing antenna diodes in the standard cells — check if violations appear only when diode protection is ignored
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations vanish when cell diodes are acknowledged, the issue was the antenna tool not recognizing cell-internal protection diodes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations remain even with cell diodes acknowledged, the cell diodes are insufficient for the metal area involved

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For each violating net, check if the metal area is accumulated across one very long wire (intra-route) or across many fanout branches (tree-route) — this determines whether metal-jumper insertion or antenna-diode insertion is the better fix
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if area accumulates on one long wire, inserting a metal jumper (via to upper metal, back down) breaks the area in half and fixes it
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if area is distributed across a fanout tree, only per-leaf antenna diodes will fix it

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the violating nets were recently added in an ECO (post-CTS or post-route) that was routed without antenna-aware routing enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations are all on ECO-added nets, the ECO routing step needs antenna-aware routing rules
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations are on original-design nets, the issue is in the initial routing or CTS

common_root_causes.cause: Long unbroken metal runs (especially on lower metals M1-M3) connecting to unprotected gate inputs — the classic antenna effect
CTS clock nets with large metal area and insufficient antenna diode protection in the clock buffers
ECO nets routed without antenna-aware routing rules, violating antenna limits on newly added routes
Standard-cell library lacking built-in antenna diodes on sensitive gate inputs, requiring external diode insertion

data.classic_trap: Inserting antenna diodes everywhere without checking whether metal-jumper insertion (via to upper metal and back) would be a smaller area and timing impact fix. Also, running antenna checks without the correct process antenna model (especially the metal-to-diffusion area ratio) and getting false positives.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, antenna rules are more complex with per-layer ratios and different oxide thicknesses per layer; at 28nm, the rules are simpler and fewer layers have critical ratios.
data.weakest_point: I am not fully confident in the frequency of the ECO-related cause — it may be more or less common than I recall. The metal-jumper vs diode discrimination is real practice but I may be overstating how often engineers actually make this choice versus just inserting diodes.

data.symptom: Detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Examine the DRC violation types (spacing, width, via enclosure, cut spacing) — each type points to a different root cause
first_checks.why_first: a spacing violation and a via-enclosure violation have completely different causes and fixes; knowing the type eliminates half the search space

first_checks.check: Check if the violating region has an unusual number of non-default routing rules (NDRs) or special net constraints that restrict the router's solution space
first_checks.why_first: NDRs and special constraints (shield, match-length, max-length) can make a globally feasible route infeasible in detail, and this is the most common cause of global-clean/detail-fail

first_checks.check: Check the global-route congestion map for the violating region — even if it looked clean, look at per-layer (not aggregate) congestion
first_checks.why_first: aggregate congestion can mask a single-layer overflow that the global router handled by deferring to detail, where it then fails

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax the violating metal layer's minimum spacing rule by one grid unit and re-run detail routing only in the hotspot region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if the violations disappear, the tool cannot meet spacing at the current grid for that local density — the fix is cell spreading or track offset
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations persist, the problem is not basic spacing but something more structural (pin access, via stacking)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if violations are exclusively at standard-cell pin-access points (where routes must enter a cell boundary) versus mid-route
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if all violations are at pin access, the issue is cell pin accessibility — check pin geometry, cell orientation, or add pin-access blockages
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations are mid-route, the issue is general congestion or routing-resource conflict in that gcell

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run detail routing with the global-route guide fixed (no re-optimization allowed) versus with guide re-optimization enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if violations disappear with guide re-optimization, the global router's guides were suboptimal for the detail router
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if violations persist regardless, the physical configuration genuinely prevents legal routing

common_root_causes.cause: Pin-access geometry on standard cells that the detail router cannot legally reach within spacing/width rules — especially on cells with pins on lower metals in dense regions
Non-default routing rules on special nets (clock, high-speed) constraining the detail router into a conflict with neighboring regular nets
Via enclosure or cut-spacing violations at metal-layer transitions where the router must stack vias through a tight region
Macro pin geometry on a lower metal layer that is inaccessible due to dense standard-cell placement blocking all approach paths

data.classic_trap: Assuming that clean global routing means the detailed router should succeed and blaming the detail router algorithm. In reality, the global router often produces guides that are marginally feasible, and the fix is usually to adjust placement (spread cells), change macro pin access, or relax an NDR — not to tune the detail router.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, double-patterning (SADP) constraints add a coloring dimension to detail routing that does not exist at 28nm, creating an entirely new category of detail-only DRC violations (color-conflict DRCs).
data.weakest_point: The via-enclosure cause frequency may be under-represented; I associate detail-only DRCs mostly with pin access and NDRs, which may bias my frequency estimates.

data.symptom: Unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check the placement log for the density target used and whether the tool reports a utilization percentage above 75-80%
first_checks.why_first: above ~80% utilization, standard-cell placement routinely overflows; this is the simplest and most common cause

first_checks.check: Examine macro placement: are macros taking up too much area or poorly positioned, leaving fragmented pockets of standard-cell space?
first_checks.why_first: fragmented free area from bad macro placement can make utilization look low in aggregate while being effectively unplaceable locally

first_checks.check: Check if the netlist has very high-fanout nets or extremely wide cells (e.g., large muxes, wide adders) that create local density spikes regardless of global utilization
first_checks.why_first: a few very wide cells or high-fanout nets can overflow a single gcell even at moderate overall utilization

first_checks.check: Verify that the placement constraints (blockages, region constraints, fence regions) are not over-constraining the tool
first_checks.why_first: over-constrained placement (e.g., too many fence regions or too-tight region assignments) can make placement infeasible even at low utilization

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all placement blockages (except hard macro boundaries) and re-run placement to see if the tool converges
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if it converges, the blockages are over-constraining the problem — reintroduce them one by one to find the culprit
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if it still overflows, the problem is utilization or netlist structure, not blockages

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Place only the top 50% of cells by instance count (leave the rest unplaced) and check if that partial placement overflows
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if even the partial placement overflows, the netlist is genuinely too dense for the die area in the macro configuration
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if partial placement is fine, the overflow is caused by interaction between specific cell groups (likely driven by one or two high-fanout nets)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if removing one or two specific high-fanout nets (by temporarily setting them as ideal) eliminates the overflow
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: if it does, those nets are creating a localized density spike that the placer cannot distribute — the fix is to buffer/split the net or restructure the netlist
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: if overflow persists, the problem is global density or macro placement, not specific nets

common_root_causes.cause: Die area too small for the netlist: utilization exceeds ~80% and the placer cannot find a legal solution
Poor macro placement creating fragmented or L-shaped free regions that are effectively lower utilization than the aggregate number suggests
Over-constrained placement (too many fence regions, too-tight region constraints, or misplaced halos) that eliminates enough legal locations to make placement infeasible
Extremely high-fanout nets (control signals, test buses) that the placer cannot distribute and that create local density hotspots
Netlist restructuring during synthesis that created very wide cells (complex combinational blocks) without breaking them into smaller, more placeable units

data.classic_trap: Immediately asking for more die area or reducing blockages when the real fix is to improve macro placement. Macro placement is the single highest-leverage intervention for unroutable placement, but engineers often treat macros as fixed and try to squeeze the standard cells into the leftover space.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, standard cells are much narrower (fin-pitch height) so utilization percentage is higher for the same logical complexity; the practical overflow threshold is different from 28nm, and tools handle it differently.
data.weakest_point: I am most confident about this symptom's diagnosis flow because it is the most fundamental P&R problem. The frequency of over-constrained placement as a cause may be under-represented because it is often caught and fixed early, so it may be less memorable.

data.pattern_name: Block-Boundary Output/Input Delay Budget Split
data.situation: Two blocks (A and B) share a clock and are being implemented independently. Block A feeds data to Block B through top-level routing. Each block needs its own SDC with boundary delay constraints.
data.derivation: 1. Combinational-path budget = T_period - T_setup - T_clock_uncertainty.  Example at 500 MHz: 2000ps - 50ps (confidence 0.5) - 120ps (confidence 0.6) = 1830ps.  2. Estimate interconnect delay from floorplan: T_inter ≈ 300-500ps for a moderate top-level route (confidence 0.5).  3. Split remaining time by estimated block complexity: T_A_budget / T_B_budget proportional to each block's combinational-depth × gate-delay estimate.  4. set_output_delay on A = T_inter + T_B_budget.  5. set_input_delay on B = T_A_budget + T_inter.  6. Verify self-consistency: A's available = budget - output_delay = T_A_budget; B's available = budget - input_delay = T_B_budget.
data.wrong_way: (a) set_output_delay = T_inter only, ignoring capture-block share → A is under-constrained internally and B is over-constrained by the amount of B's budget that A silently consumed.  (b) 50/50 split regardless of complexity → one block starved, the other has excessive slack.  (c) Forgetting clock_uncertainty → budget is 100-200ps optimistic, and the error accumulates silently through integration.
data.defense: Present the floorplan-derived interconnect estimate, each block's gate-equivalent count or combinational depth, and the resulting slack distribution. If one block's initial implementation shows very negative or very positive slack, adjust the split and re-budget.
data.signoff_risk: Too-tight output delay on A: Block A over-designed (area/power bloat) and may still fail, blocking integration. Too-loose output delay on A: A finishes easily but the interconnect + B path overflows the period at integration, requiring either interconnect buffering (area + power) or A re-implementation (schedule risk).
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, interconnect RC is much higher so the interconnect share of the budget grows from roughly 20-25% to 30-40% (confidence 0.6), changing the typical split ratio.

data.pattern_name: False Path vs Multicycle Path Decision for Inter-Clock Paths
data.situation: Two clock domains exist in the design. The engineer must decide whether paths between them should be set_false_path, set_multicycle_path, or constrained as single-cycle.
data.derivation: 1. Determine if clocks share a common root (same PLL or oscillator).  2. If NO common root → clocks are asynchronous → false-path the data paths, but constrain synchronizer paths separately (see Synchronizer Max-Delay pattern).  3. If common root with different frequencies → compute LCM period: LCM(T_A, T_B). MCP_setup = LCM / T_capture.  4. Always set MCP_hold = MCP_setup - 1 to move the hold check to the correct launch-capture edge pair.  5. If same frequency with known phase offset → model with set_clock_latency -source and constrain as single-cycle with the offset accounted for.
data.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on a path whose clocks share a root → real timing violation ignored, silicon failure.  (b) set_multicycle_path N -setup without also setting set_multicycle_path (N-1) -hold → tool performs hold check on wrong edge: either generates false hold violations (area waste from unnecessary buffers) or misses real hold violations.  (c) Blanket set_false_path between two domains to 'clean up reports' → masks paths that should be timed, including paths through combinational logic between domains that bypass the synchronizer.
data.defense: Show the clock-generation schematic (PLL → divider → clock tree) proving the relationship. Present the LCM edge diagram with launch and capture edges marked. Demonstrate the hold-edge adjustment is correct by showing the actual waveform.
data.signoff_risk: False path too aggressive: real path untimed, functional silicon failure. False path too conservative (should be false but isn't): wasted optimization cycles and area, but functionally safe. Multicycle without hold adjustment: false hold violations waste area, or real hold violations on the wrong edge escape to silicon.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled — the logical decision tree is the same regardless of process node.

data.pattern_name: set_max_delay on Synchronizer Clock-Domain Crossing
data.situation: A signal crosses from clock domain A to domain B through a 2-FF synchronizer. The path to the first synchronizer flop needs a real timing constraint, not a false-path.
data.derivation: 1. The path from the source register in domain A to the D pin of the FIRST synchronizer flop in domain B IS timed.  2. set_max_delay on this path = T_capture_period (ensures data arrives within one capture cycle without demanding single-cycle tightness).  3. set_false_path -hold on this same path (hold timing is meaningless through a synchronizer because metastability makes the capture-edge relationship non-deterministic).  4. Paths through the second synchronizer flop onward: set_false_path (data is now synchronized).  5. Identify each synchronizer instance explicitly by cell name or by hierarchical path — do not rely on clock-domain crossing auto-detection.
data.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on the entire crossing including the path to the first flop → path can be arbitrarily long, widening the metastability window and degrading MTBF.  (b) Apply normal set_max_delay without setting -hold false_path → tool inserts hold buffers on the synchronizer path, adding latency that may exceed the max_delay target or defeat the purpose.  (c) set_max_delay globally to all paths between the two domains instead of targeting the synchronizer flop → over-constrains data paths that should be false-path'd.
data.defense: List each synchronizer instance by hierarchical name. Show the set_max_delay value justified as one capture-clock period. Reference the MTBF requirement (from reliability spec) that justifies the synchronizer depth. Show that hold-false-path is applied to prevent buffer insertion.
data.signoff_risk: Too-tight max_delay: unnecessary optimization on synchronizer paths, area waste, possible routing congestion near synchronizer cells. Too-loose max_delay: data arrives late, first flop samples transitioning data, MTBF degrades or functional failure. Missing hold false-path: tool inserts delay buffers that increase latency on the synchronizer path, partially defeating the max_delay constraint.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, faster clock frequencies mean the absolute max_delay value is smaller, making the path-to-synchronizer constraint tighter and increasing the chance that even a modest-length route violates it.

data.pattern_name: Over-Constraining at Synthesis with Gradual Relaxation Toward Signoff
data.situation: Starting implementation of a new block. Target clock period is known, but the design will degrade during CTS (insertion delay), routing (parasitics), and signoff (OCV, IR-drop). The constraint must leave room for this degradation.
data.derivation: 1. At synthesis: target period × (1 - early_margin). Typical early_margin = 25-30% (confidence 0.6). At 500 MHz (2ns): synthesize to ~1.4-1.5ns.  2. After placement: relax to period × (1 - mid_margin). Typical mid_margin = 10-15% (confidence 0.5). Target ~1.7-1.8ns.  3. After CTS: relax to period × (1 - late_margin). Typical late_margin = 3-5% (confidence 0.6).  4. At signoff: use full period with all parasitics, OCV, IR-drop annotated.  5. The margin values are calibrated from prior tapeouts at the same node on the same team's designs.
data.wrong_way: (a) Synthesize to 100% of period from the start → after CTS and routing add 200-400ps of degradation, design is significantly negative → many ECO iterations, schedule risk.  (b) Synthesize to 50% of period → massive over-design: area 20-40% larger than necessary (confidence 0.5), power significantly higher, and the tool optimizes paths that don't need it.  (c) Relax constraints too aggressively between stages (e.g., jump from 70% to 100% after placement) → catch timing problems too late when they're expensive to fix.
data.defense: Present the empirical degradation curve from the team's prior designs at the same node: average insertion-delay as % of period, average routing-parasitic impact, typical OCV impact. Show the margin schedule matches this historical data.
data.signoff_risk: Over-constrained at synthesis: area and power waste but functionally safe — expensive chip, meets schedule. Under-constrained at synthesis: area-efficient but timing closure becomes a multi-iteration nightmare at signoff — tapeout delay risk, possible missed market window.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, OCV derates and IR-drop effects are larger, so the early margin typically needs to be 35-40% versus 25-30% at 28nm (confidence 0.6). The relaxation schedule has more stages.

data.pattern_name: Async FIFO Gray-Code Pointer Synchronization Constraints
data.situation: An asynchronous FIFO bridges two clock domains. Gray-code pointers cross from write domain to read domain (and vice versa) through synchronizer chains. The constraint must protect data integrity while bounding pointer propagation delay.
data.derivation: 1. Data path through FIFO: set_false_path from write-clock domain to read-clock domain on data bits (FIFO depth protects data — no timing constraint needed).  2. Gray-code pointer bits from write side to read side: set_max_delay = T_read_period per bit (ensures each pointer update arrives within one read-clock cycle).  3. Similarly for read-to-write pointer: set_max_delay = T_write_period.  4. set_false_path -hold on all pointer synchronizer paths (hold timing meaningless through synchronizers).  5. Each pointer bit gets an independent set_max_delay to ensure all bits of the same pointer arrive within the same capture window.
data.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on everything including pointer bits → pointer propagation is unconstrained, may take many cycles, FIFO full/empty detection becomes unreliable, data corruption through read-before-write-complete or write-before-read-complete.  (b) set_max_delay on pointer bits to a value much larger than the capture period → pointer update delayed by multiple cycles, requiring deeper FIFO than implemented, functional overflow/underflow.  (c) Using set_multicycle_path on pointer bits instead of set_max_delay → meaningless for truly asynchronous clocks with no fixed phase relationship.
data.defense: Show the FIFO depth analysis: depth must be greater than 2 × (max_delay / period) for safe full/empty detection. List each pointer bit's max_delay constraint. Reference synchronizer MTBF analysis for the chosen synchronizer depth. Show waveform diagram of pointer update timing.
data.signoff_risk: Unconstrained pointer (false path): subtle data corruption when write side overwrites data before read side consumes it — extremely hard to reproduce in simulation, manifests as rare data errors in silicon. Over-constrained pointer (max_delay too tight): area waste from buffer insertion on pointer paths, possible routing congestion near synchronizers, but functionally safe.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, faster clock frequencies mean the absolute max_delay is smaller and FIFO depth requirements are proportionally larger for the same synchronization latency budget.

data.pattern_name: Generated/Divided Clock Constraint Derivation
data.situation: A flip-flop or latch divides the master clock by N, producing a slower clock that drives downstream logic. The SDC must correctly define the generated clock and its relationship to the master.
data.derivation: 1. Define master clock first: create_clock -name mclk -period T [get_ports mclk_pin].  2. Define generated clock: create_generated_clock -name gclk -source [get_pins div_reg/CK] -divide_by N [get_pins div_reg/Q].  3. Generated period = N × T.  4. Source pin MUST be the clock-input pin of the divider register (CK), not the data-output pin (Q). The tool traces from source to output automatically.  5. Set clock uncertainty on the generated clock domain: includes master PLL jitter + divider-edge jitter + guard band.  6. For paths between master and generated domains: compute edge relationships and determine if multicycle constraints are needed (fast-to-slow may need MCP; slow-to-fast is typically single-cycle).
data.wrong_way: (a) create_clock on the divider output with a manually specified period instead of create_generated_clock → the tool does not know the master-generated relationship, cannot compute inter-domain timing, latency and insertion delay are wrong.  (b) Specify -source as div_reg/Q (output pin) instead of div_reg/CK (clock pin) → tool fails to trace through the divider correctly, latency calculation wrong by the divider's clock-to-Q delay.  (c) Forgetting clock uncertainty on the generated clock → zero jitter assumed, timing too optimistic by the jitter amount.  (d) Not handling the edge relationship between master and generated clocks → hold violations on fast-to-slow crossings that are invisible in single-edge analysis.
data.defense: Show the clock-generation RTL or schematic. Present the waveform diagram with master and generated edges aligned. Prove the edge relationship (which master edge corresponds to which generated edge). Demonstrate that uncertainty is set for both domains.
data.signoff_risk: Wrong generated period: all downstream timing wrong — paths either over-constrained (area waste) or under-constrained (silicon failure). Missing inter-domain constraints: paths between master and generated clock untimed, functional failure. Wrong source pin: latency off by the divider's clk-to-Q delay, setup/hold margins incorrect.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled — the SDC construct is identical; at 7nm jitter is proportionally larger relative to the period, making the uncertainty setup more critical but not changing the pattern.

data.pattern_name: Virtual Clock and IO Delay Budgeting for External Interfaces
data.situation: Chip IO ports interface with external components (memory, PHY, other chips). The internal clock tree does not reach the IO, and the external timing reference may differ from the internal clock.
data.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock matching the external reference: create_clock -name virt_clk -period T_ext (no physical pin, or on a reference clock input).  2. For input ports: set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -max D_in [get_ports data_in].  D_in = T_ext_clk2q (from external chip datasheet) + T_board_trace (from PCB extraction) + T_margin.  3. For output ports: set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -max D_out [get_ports data_out].  D_out = T_board_trace + T_ext_setup (from external chip datasheet) + T_margin.  4. T_margin = 10-15% of T_ext (confidence 0.6).  5. T_board_trace = from PCB team's post-layout extraction or pre-layout estimate: typically 0.5-3ns depending on board (confidence 0.5).  6. Internal clock defined separately on the actual clock input pin of the chip.
data.wrong_way: (a) set_input_delay relative to the internal clock instead of the virtual clock → tool includes internal clock-tree latency in the IO timing calculation. The external device does not see the internal clock tree, so this is wrong by the clock-tree latency amount.  (b) Forgetting the board trace delay → timing optimistic by 0.5-3ns, silicon works in the lab but fails on the actual board with real trace lengths.  (c) Using the internal clock period when it differs from the external period → constraining to the wrong frequency, either over- or under-constraining IO paths.
data.defense: Present the external chip datasheet with highlighted timing parameters (clk-to-output, setup time). Show the PCB team's trace-delay extraction report. Display the resulting IO timing budget with the margin clearly separated. Show a timing diagram with external and internal clock edges.
data.signoff_risk: Input delay too tight: internal paths to IO registers over-designed, area/power waste. Input delay too loose: data arrives at IO register too late, IO interface fails on actual board. Output delay too tight: output path over-designed. Output delay too loose: data arrives at external receiver too late, external device fails to capture.
data.node_era_note: At lower nodes with multi-GHz SerDes IO, the trace delay is a much larger fraction of the period and jitter is more significant, making the IO budget much tighter and the margin more critical (confidence 0.7).

data.pattern_name: Clock Uncertainty Budget Decomposition
data.situation: Setting set_clock_uncertainty for a clock domain. The value must aggregate multiple real-world sources of timing variation, and the correct value changes as the design progresses through the flow.
data.derivation: 1. Total uncertainty = T_jitter + T_skew + T_guard.  2. T_jitter (PLL output jitter): from PLL datasheet or PLL team characterization. Typically 2-5% of period (confidence 0.6). At 500 MHz: 2ns × 3% ≈ 60ps.  3. T_skew (clock tree skew): before CTS, use an estimate based on design size — typically 50-150ps (confidence 0.5). After CTS, use the actual reported skew from CTS timing reports.  4. T_guard (margin): 5-15% of (jitter + skew) (confidence 0.5).  5. Apply at each flow stage: (a) Pre-CTS synthesis/implementation: set_clock_uncertainty = jitter + skew_estimate + guard. (b) Post-CTS: set_clock_uncertainty = jitter + guard (remove skew_estimate since actual skew is now known). (c) Inter-clock crossings: add additional inter-clock uncertainty on top (typically larger, covering both PLLs' jitter).
data.wrong_way: (a) Single flat uncertainty value for the entire flow → too optimistic before CTS (skew unknown), too pessimistic after CTS (estimated skew still in the number).  (b) Forgetting to reduce uncertainty after CTS → design over-constrained by the estimated-skew amount, unnecessary buffering and area waste.  (c) Using PLL jitter alone without skew → underestimate by 50-150ps, silicon fails under clock-tree skew conditions especially at worst-case PVT corners.  (d) Same uncertainty for intra-domain and inter-domain paths → inter-domain uncertainty should be larger because it covers jitter from two independent PLLs.
data.defense: Show the PLL jitter specification (datasheet excerpt). Show the CTS skew report (or estimation methodology if pre-CTS). Present a table of uncertainty values at each flow stage. Demonstrate that inter-clock uncertainty is appropriately larger than intra-clock.
data.signoff_risk: Uncertainty too large: over-designed clock tree, extra buffers and area, power waste — functionally safe but expensive. Uncertainty too small: timing violations under real jitter + skew conditions, functional failure at high temperature or low voltage corners — these failures are often intermittent and hard to diagnose.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm, PLL jitter is a larger fraction of the period (faster clocks, similar absolute jitter), and OCV derates effectively increase the skew component, so total uncertainty is a much larger fraction of the period than at 28nm (confidence 0.7).

data.title: Clock frequency philosophy and pipeline depth
data.decision: Pursued a balanced design optimizing both IPC and clock frequency rather than maximizing clock frequency through an ultra-deep pipeline
data.alternatives_or_rejected: A deeper pipeline to achieve higher clock frequency, with correspondingly greater branch misprediction penalties and latch-power overhead
data.rationale: Higher frequency alone does not yield proportional performance gains once pipeline depth penalties (branch misprediction recovery, latch power, diminishing per-stage work) are accounted for; a balanced approach yields better overall throughput
data.outcome: POWER4 achieved competitive frequencies for its era while maintaining high IPC, delivering strong single-thread and multi-thread performance for server workloads
data.weakest_point: I am not fully certain the paper explicitly names an ultra-deep pipeline as a rejected alternative versus presenting the philosophy as a positive design principle only

data.title: Dual-core on a single die
data.decision: Integrate two complete processor cores on a single chip die to improve throughput for commercial multi-threaded workloads
data.alternatives_or_rejected: A single-core design devoting all transistor budget to one wider or deeper core, or using a multi-chip module for multi-processor configurations
data.rationale: Commercial server workloads exhibit significant thread-level parallelism; two cores on-die share the memory subsystem efficiently and avoid inter-chip latency
data.outcome: POWER4 became one of the first commercial dual-core server processors, significantly improving throughput on enterprise workloads
data.weakest_point: I am not certain the paper frames the dual-core choice as a decision with explicitly discussed rejected alternatives; it may simply present it as an architectural given

data.title: RAS (Reliability, Availability, Serviceability) design approach
data.decision: Embed extensive hardware-level RAS features throughout the design: ECC on caches and buses, instruction retry, error containment, and sparing mechanisms
data.rationale: Enterprise/server customers require extremely high availability; hardware-level error detection and recovery mechanisms minimize silent data corruption and unplanned downtime
data.outcome: POWER4-based systems achieved very high availability metrics suitable for mission-critical enterprise and commercial deployments
data.weakest_point: I cannot verify whether the paper names a specific rejected alternative for RAS or simply describes the chosen approach; I have marked alternatives as not-stated-in-paper to be safe

data.title: Scalable interconnect for multi-chip SMP configurations
data.decision: Use a scalable point-to-point interconnect fabric to link multiple POWER4 modules into larger SMP configurations rather than a conventional shared bus
data.rationale: Point-to-point interconnects scale with increasing chip count without the bandwidth saturation and arbitration delays that degrade shared buses at high processor counts
data.outcome: POWER4-based systems scaled to configurations supporting up to 32 processors in a single system image
data.weakest_point: The specific framing of the interconnect decision (shared bus as rejected alternative) may come from general POWER4 knowledge rather than this paper's exact text; the paper may describe the fabric without contrasting it against a shared-bus alternative

data.title: Cache hierarchy with shared on-chip L2 and off-chip L3
data.decision: Implement a large shared on-chip L2 cache accessible by both cores, backed by a large off-chip L3 cache on the multi-chip module
data.rationale: A shared L2 facilitates inter-core data sharing and coherence efficiency; a large off-chip L3 provides capacity for server workloads with large memory footprints that would not fit on-die
data.outcome: The hierarchical cache structure reduced average memory latency for enterprise workloads and supported efficient inter-core data sharing
data.weakest_point: I am not fully certain whether the L2 was shared between cores or partitioned per core in the paper's description; I believe it was shared but may be conflating with general knowledge. Also, specific rejected alternatives for the cache hierarchy are likely not discussed in the paper.

assumptions_invoked: Arrangement fee of EUR 100 treated as financed charge added to amount financed (per EU CCD Annex I: all charges relating to the credit agreement are included in the total charge for credit, and financed charges are added to the amount financed rather than deducted as upfront cash outflows)
Repayments of EUR 450 per month commence one month after drawdown (t=1 through t=24)
No other charges; loan is fully drawn at t=0
APRC expressed as nominal annual rate = 12 x monthly rate (EU CCD Annex I method)
data.equation: 10 100 = 450 * a_bar(24|i_monthly) where a_bar(24|i) = (1 - (1+i)^-24) / i; APRC = 12 * i_monthly
data.iterations: Iter1: i=0.005, a_bar=22.5629, PV=10 153.29 (PV > 10 100, rate too low). Iter2: i=0.006, a_bar=22.2899, PV=10 030.47 (PV < 10 100, rate too high). Iter3: i=0.0055, a_bar=22.4258, PV=10 091.62 (PV < 10 100, bisection midpoint). Convergence: i_monthly=0.0054326, APRC=6.519% -> 6.5%
data.weakest_point: Whether the arrangement fee is a financed charge (added to amount_financed=10 100, giving APRC=6.5%) or an upfront cash fee (consumer net-receives 9900, giving APRC=8.7%). EU CCD Annex I includes all charges in the total cost of credit; the financed treatment is the standard interpretation, but implementations vary on whether upfront fees reduce the amount received vs. inflate the repayment stream. The APRC differs by ~2.2 percentage points between the two treatments.

assumptions_invoked: Full credit limit of EUR 3000 assumed drawn for the whole duration (EU CCD Article 6.2 overdraft provision: when the amount or date of drawings cannot be determined, the full limit is assumed to be drawn in full at the start)
Duration of 3 months used because the agreement has no fixed duration and no repmt schedule (EU CCD Art. 6.2 default assumption)
Nominal rate 12% p.a. charged monthly = 1% per month on outstanding balance
Monthly account fee of EUR 25 treated as recurring charge included in repayment stream (Annex I: all charges consumer is required to pay in connection with the credit agreement are included)
Principal repaid in 3 equal monthly instalments of 3000/3 = 1000; interest = 1% x 3000 = 30/month; total monthly payment = 1030 + 25 = 1055
data.equation: 3000 = 1055 * a_bar(3|i_monthly) where a_bar(3|i) = (1 - (1+i)^-3) / i; APRC = 12 * i_monthly
data.iterations: Iter1: i=0.027, a_bar=2.8450, PV=3001.48 (PV > 3000, rate too low). Iter2: i=0.028, a_bar=2.8395, PV=2995.70 (PV < 3000, rate too high). Iter3: i=0.0273, a_bar=2.8434, PV=2999.74 (very close, rate slightly low). Convergence: i_monthly=0.027255, APRC=32.706% -> 32.7%

If excluded from the APRC calculation and treated as a separately-charged fee, the monthly payment for APRC purposes would be 1030 (interest+principal only) and the APRC would be significantly higher. Additionally, the 3-month duration is a default assumption; a longer assumed duration would lower the APRC substantially.

assumptions_invoked: Full limit of EUR 1500 drawn immediately at t=0 (open-end credit, drawdown date not specified, worst-case full draw assumed)

Repayment assumed as 12 equal monthly instalments (EU CCD Art. 6.2 open-end credit provision: where repayment structure cannot be determined, 12 equal monthly instalments are the standard default assumption based on typical annual credit cycle)
Rate 18% nominal p.a. monthly compounding: i_monthly_stated = 0.18/12 = 0.015
No other fees per problem statement
Monthly payment computed as standard amortising PMT: 1500 x 0.015 x (1.015)^12 / ((1.015)^12 - 1) = 137.52
data.equation: 1500 = 137.52 * a_bar(12|i_monthly); APRC = 12 * i_monthly (or equivalently (1+i_monthly)^12 - 1 for effective annual)
data.weakest_point: EU CCD APRC can be expressed as nominal annual (12 x monthly rate = 18.0%) or as effective annual rate ((1+i_monthly)^12 - 1 = 19.6%). The directive does not always make the distinction explicit in consumer-facing materials; some member-state implementations use nominal, others effective. The difference is 1.6 pp. Additionally, the 12-instalment default for open-end credit is a reasonable inference from Art. 6.2 but the directive does not explicitly mandate this figure.

assumptions_invoked: Full credit limit of EUR 5000 assumed drawn at t=0 (EU CCD Art. 6.2: when drawdown date cannot be ascertained, full amount drawn at commencement is assumed; the alternative would be to use average existing practise, but full immediate drawdown is the conservative default)
EUR 200 broker fee financed into the credit balance (added to amount financed, not deducted as upfront cash payment)
Amount financed = 5000 + 200 = 5200
Single repayment at 12 months: 5200 x (1 + 0.08) = 5616 (interest = 416)
Rate 8% nominal annual, monthly charging: i_monthly_stated = 0.08/12

Financed fee treatment: the fee is added to the balance (not paid separately at t=0), so the consumer pays interest on the fee for 12 months; this differs from an upfront cash fee which would reduce the net amount received without inflating the repayment amount
data.weakest_point: Whether the broker fee is financed into the balance (APRC=7.7%) or paid as an upfront cash fee (APRC=8.0%). If paid as a cash fee at t=0, the consumer net-receives 4800 and repays 5400 at month 12, giving APRC = 8.0% (the stated rate). The financed treatment lowers the APRC because the fee is spread over 12 months. The distinction is the single most consequential assumption in this case, producing a 0.3 pp divergence. Directive Art. 19 requires all charges to be included, but does not universally mandate financed treatment for all fee types.
