data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: View global route congestion heatmap: is it localized to specific regions or uniform?
first_checks.why_first: Distinguishes macro-induced vs. cell-distribution problem before any detailed analysis

first_checks.check: Inspect pin density map — cell-level and macro-level — at congestion hotspots
first_checks.why_first: Standard cell density being fine while pin density is high is the most common hidden cause; check is cheap and rules out false-positive density reading

first_checks.check: Review layer utilization and preferred-routing-direction conflicts at the congested metal layers
first_checks.why_first: If congestion clusters on one routing layer at its non-preferred direction, it is a layer-assignment conflict; cheap to confirm

first_checks.check: Check for asymmetric cell padding rules applied around hard macros
first_checks.why_first: Excess cell padding near macros is a known DRC trigger that density reports often miss because padding is not counted as cell area

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run global routing with congestion effort set to very-high — if DRCs disappear, original global route was simply low-effort and non-optimal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: routing algorithm insufficient effort; design has enough resources
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: actual routing resource shortage — problem is structural

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether all DRC hotspots coincide with a single hard macro's pin-access area — compare against the macro's MCM (metal confusion map) if available
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro pin accessibility is the root cause — standard cell placement or macro spacing needs rework
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: macro pin access is fine; problem is in standard-cell routing region

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion maps at two different layer-allocation settings — if shifting preferred routing layer assignment eliminates the hotspot, it is a layer-conflict not a resource shortage
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer preference conflict causing artificial congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: genuine routing track shortage confirmed

common_root_causes.cause: Excess cell padding applied near hard macros reduces routing tracks around pins
High pin-density standard cells or blocks where cell utilization is low but pin count per unit area is very high
Routing guide spacing too tight between adjacent macros or macro-to-cell boundary — the global router cannot find valid detours
Non-default routing rules (NDR) applied to clock nets reducing available tracks for signal routing in that region
Power strap planning leaving too few routing layers available for signal routing in dense digital blocks

data.classic_trap: Assuming cell density is the proxy for routability — the real bottleneck is pin density, which most density reports do not surface by default
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, pin density per unit routing resource is dramatically higher due to finFET cell layouts and reduced metal pitches; a design that routes cleanly at 28nm may show phantom congestion at 7nm even with identical density numbers

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check whether violating paths are concentrated in one clock domain or spread across the design
first_checks.why_first: Localized to one domain points to local clock quality or specific logic; spread design-wide points to a systemic margin problem

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS and post-CTS timing reports for the same paths — were these paths already marginal before CTS was run?
first_checks.why_first: Rules out whether CTS introduced the problem (new skew) vs. CTS exposing a pre-existing timing gap

first_checks.check: Inspect clock skew histogram and per-sink insertion delay — are violating sinks in a clock subtree with unusually high skew relative to other sinks on the same clock?
first_checks.why_first: Clock skew that is large enough to consume available slack explains why CTS-created paths fail even if the logic delay is acceptable

first_checks.check: Check whether violating paths share a common library cell type, a particular hierarchical block, or a specific clock-gating cell
first_checks.why_first: If all failing paths converge on one structural feature, the fix is targeted; if they are independent, the problem is systemic and margin-based

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run timing with clock skew disabled (ideal clock) — if all violations disappear, clock skew or insertion delay variation is the root cause; if violations persist, logic delay is the problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock skew or insertion delay variation is consuming available slack
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: logic delay itself is insufficient — the clock network is not the primary cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check the clock tree depth for the failing sink subtree vs. the clock root — if the failing subtree has significantly more clock buffer levels than the passing sibling subtrees, the clock tree itself is unbalanced at a structural level
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: structural clock tree depth imbalance causing excessive insertion delay on the failing path
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: clock tree is balanced; problem lies in logic cell placement or library characterization

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Identify whether all failing endpoints share a common clock-gating enable signal — if so, the gate is adding asymmetric delay; if failing endpoints are spread across unrelated clock gates, it is a design-level margin issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: specific clock-gating logic is creating an unexpected delay asymmetry that CTS cannot balance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no single clock-gating culprit; the design has insufficient slack margin globally

common_root_causes.cause: Pre-existing timing margin consumed by CTS — the design was barely meeting timing before clock insertion and CTS added skew that broke it
Large insertion delay variation across unbalanced clock subtrees that the CTS tool cannot fix with buffer insertion alone (often due to mixed load types or gating logic differences)
Logic paths with high variability or non-standard cells (custom analog, memory outputs, SerDes interfaces) that were not adequately margin-ed for max-delay analysis
ECO modifications (logic changes, engineering change orders) applied after initial CTS without re-running clock tree synthesis
On-chip variation (OCV) derate factors set too conservatively, causing the timing tool to report violations that are not reproducible on silicon at the specified corner

data.classic_trap: Immediately blaming clock skew — the most common real cause is that the design had no margin to begin with and CTS simply revealed the pre-existing gap; re-running CTS with tighter constraints at the same design often just shuffles the problem
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, clock buffer delay variation from within-die systematic effects (like well proximity or poly spacing effects) can create insertion delay differences that were negligible at 28nm; CCS timing models make the clock path delay correlation more accurate but also more sensitive to the signoff corner selection

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Review the hold-fixing strategy used — specifically whether ECO hold buffers were inserted automatically or by hand, and near which cells
first_checks.why_first: Hold violations after CTS are almost always a consequence of how and where hold buffers were added; the first check is confirming the fix method

first_checks.check: Inspect the insertion delay report to see whether the violating paths have abnormal clock-to-Q delay (suggesting the hold violation is actually a clock insertion delay problem)
first_checks.why_first: Distinguishes a true hold problem (data arriving too fast) from a clock distribution problem (clock arriving too early at one endpoint relative to another); the fix is opposite for each

first_checks.check: Check whether the violating paths are near clock gating cells — specifically whether a hold buffer was inserted just after a clock gate and is being back-annotated with the wrong clock state
first_checks.why_first: Clock gating creates asymmetric clock edge visibility; hold buffers inserted in the data path of a gated branch may be timing-checked against the wrong clock edge in some flows

first_checks.check: Compare hold slack distribution across the design — if one specific clock subtree is responsible for the majority of violations, it is a structural clock tree issue
first_checks.why_first: Confirms whether this is localized to one clock subtree (structural) or spread (margin/integration issue)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily fix all hold violations with ideal clock (hold analysis disabled) then re-enable hold with real clocks — if hold violations are dramatically reduced, the problem is in how the hold fix interacted with clock insertion delay; if they persist at similar magnitude, the logic itself is too fast
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock insertion delay asymmetry causing premature data arrival relative to clock edge at specific sinks
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: logic min-delay is genuinely insufficient; data path is too fast relative to clock

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether the hold margin consumption is consistent across process corners — if hold violations appear only at one specific corner (e.g., best-case corner where cells are fastest), it is a library corner selection issue; if it appears at all corners, it is structural
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: corner-specific hold margin issue from over-aggressive library at best-case corner
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: structural hold problem present regardless of corner

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Identify whether hold slack correlates with cell type — specifically, if min-delay violations cluster at paths going through a particular cell library variant (e.g., low-power cells or level-shifters), those cells may have inadequate min-delay characterization
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: specific cell type has a characterization gap or min-delay spec that is incorrect
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: cells are characterized correctly; the hold problem is architectural (excessive parallelism in the design)

common_root_causes.cause: ECO hold buffer insertion done too close to the clock source or near a clock gating cell, creating a hold margin vs. insertion delay conflict that CTS cannot resolve cleanly
Clock tree depth or topology differences across related paths causing excessive insertion delay variation — some paths see the launch clock before others see the capture clock
Design has intentionally high parallelism (very deep pipeline) that leaves no margin for hold at the fast corner — hold is essentially a design problem masquerading as a CTS problem
Level-shifter or always-on cell chains creating unintended fast data paths that were not captured in static timing analysis because of multi-voltage mode misannotation

data.classic_trap: Upsizing cells to fix hold — increasing drive strength changes the clock tree delay of that subtree and can make hold worse by altering insertion delay relationships; the correct fix is usually targeted hold buffer insertion or clock tree rebalancing, not cell sizing
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, multi-bit flip-flops create intra-bit hold timing differences that single-bit designs do not have; also, clock mesh structures reduce hold variation but increase the probability of hold problems at specific mesh tap points

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: View dynamic IR-drop map (Vdd drop) at the specific timing corner and activity pattern where failures are reported — is the drop localized to the region containing the failing paths, or is it design-wide?
first_checks.why_first: Distinguishes localized power integrity problem (weak grid near specific logic) from systemic power delivery; localized drop is fixable with targeted PG strap additions

first_checks.check: Check the power grid resistance (IR-drop EM analysis report) to identify if there are specific weak nodes or long current paths in the PG network
first_checks.why_first: Confirms whether the IR-drop is a grid design problem (insufficient straps, high-resistance metals) vs. a simultaneous switching activity problem

first_checks.check: Inspect the switching activity pattern — specifically, are the failing paths clustered around a common enable signal or data pattern that causes simultaneous switching of many cells at once?
first_checks.why_first: Identifies whether a functional pattern (test mode, specific operating state) is creating worst-case simultaneous switching vs. a design-average activity assumption being too optimistic

first_checks.check: Confirm the activity file used for the IR-drop analysis — was it generated from a realistic testbench, a gate-level simulation, or an RTL toggle estimate?
first_checks.why_first: If the activity file was estimated (not simulated) it may not represent the true worst-case switching pattern; this is the most common reason IR-drop analysis is misleading

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run timing analysis with IR-drop (dynamic) applied back-annotation vs. static IR-drop — if violations only appear with dynamic drop, the problem is transient and activity-pattern-dependent; if they appear with static drop, the grid itself is inadequate
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Dynamic IR-drop from specific switching patterns is the root cause — grid is adequate but activity is pathological
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Static (average) IR-drop is also insufficient — the power grid itself needs redesign

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether the violating paths all belong to one voltage domain — if so, that domain's power mesh or power switch implementation is the specific problem; if violations span multiple voltage domains, it is a top-level PDN issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Single voltage domain has an inadequate power mesh — targeted strap addition fixes it
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Cross-domain power integrity — the top-level PDN needs revision regardless of local fixes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the IR-drop map against the clock tree distribution — if clock buffers are concentrated in the high-drop region, the clock network is degrading the PG and creating timing failures that appear to be logic problems
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Clock tree power demand in a localized region is creating clock edge degradation that manifests as timing failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Logic cell switching, not clock, is the dominant IR-drop source

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient PG straps (Vdd or Vss) near high-cell-density regions causing localized voltage droop when many cells switch simultaneously
Pathological functional or test pattern that causes many cells to switch simultaneously, creating worst-case dynamic IR-drop that is not captured by average-activity analysis
High-resistance local power mesh segments (often from routing rule violations or metal slotting requirements that inadvertently increased resistance)
Insufficient decoupling capacitance (decap) cells — especially near memories or high-fanout clock gates — allowing voltage to droop between switching events
Test mode (scan shift or ATPG) activity creating higher simultaneous switching than any functional mode — but IR-drop signoff was done with functional activity only

data.classic_trap: Attributing the timing failure to library cell performance or logic delay when the real cause is IR-drop — the timing report shows path delay failures but the root cause is voltage droop slowing the cells, not bad cell selection; always check the IR-drop map before assuming a library or logic fix is needed
data.node_era_note: At 28nm the PDN correlation between signoff analysis and silicon was generally good; at 7nm and below, the dynamic IR-drop correlation degrades significantly due to current density and self-heating effects, and EM-induced voiding in copper lines can make the PG worse over operating lifetime, so a design that passes IR-drop at tapeout may fail during burn-in

data.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Review the clock tree depth report for outliers — are one or more subtrees significantly deeper (more buffer levels) than siblings on the same clock?
first_checks.why_first: Structural clock tree depth imbalance is the most common structural cause of insertion delay variation; it is immediately visible in the depth report

first_checks.check: Check whether the missing-target sinks are all under a specific clock gate or a specific hierarchical boundary
first_checks.why_first: Clock gates with asymmetric enable path delays create structural insertion delay asymmetries that CTS cannot fix without gate-level changes

first_checks.check: Inspect the clock boundary conditions — specifically, are there floating or unconnected clock inputs inside the design that the CTS tool is treating as endpoints?
first_checks.why_first: Unconnected or test-mode clock paths create phantom insertion delay targets that the CTS tool attempts to meet but cannot, causing it to de-prioritize real sinks

first_checks.check: Check the balance tolerance setting and compare against the actual skew requirement — if the tolerance is tighter than the physical achievable balance for this design's clock topology, CTS will never converge
first_checks.why_first: Configuration mismatch — a tolerance of 5ps on a clock with 10 levels of buffering and mixed load types is physically unachievable; CTS will appear to run but will not actually meet targets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare insertion delay across the top-level clock root to the failing sink subtree vs. the closest passing sink subtree — if the insertion delay difference between the failing sink and the passing sinks exceeds the clock period by more than the skew budget, the problem is structural clock tree depth; if the difference is within budget but timing still fails, the problem is endpoint-level logic
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Structural clock tree depth imbalance — the sink subtree needs a different buffer strategy or additional balancing structures
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Clock tree is balanced within skew budget — the failure is in the data path, not the clock network

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether all failing sinks share a common gating cell type or a common enable signal path — if yes, the clock gate's enable path delay is adding asymmetric latency that appears as skew; if failing sinks are in unrelated clock gate hierarchies, the problem is more systemic
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Specific clock gate or gating hierarchy creating the insertion delay imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No single clock gate culprit — the skew is from overall clock topology, not specific gating logic

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run CTS with a single uniform max cap constraint (ignore existing constraints) — if skew is dramatically reduced, the existing CTS constraints are conflicting or over-constrained; if skew persists, the clock tree structure itself is the problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Constraint conflict or over-specification — simplifying constraints fixes the skew
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Physical clock tree structure cannot achieve the required skew regardless of constraint setting

common_root_causes.cause: Asymmetric load distribution across clock tree subtrees — some subtrees drive many more registers or larger loads than others, creating structural insertion delay differences that buffer insertion alone cannot equalize
Clock gating cells with asymmetric enable path delays causing the CTS tool to insert unequal delays to satisfy gating timing constraints
Hard macros with internal clock inputs that constrain the external clock tree synthesis — the macro's clock input pin may have a fixed delay that is incompatible with the desired clock tree topology
CTS constraint conflict — multiple clock-related SDC constraints (false paths, clock groups, min/max delay constraints) that collectively prevent the CTS tool from balancing the tree
Floorplan changes made after initial CTS invalidated the clock tree routing and load distribution, creating skew that was not present in the original run

data.classic_trap: Re-running CTS multiple times with different seed settings hoping it will converge — if the design topology (load distribution, clock gate locations, floorplan) is the cause, seed variation will not fix it; the root cause must be addressed at the design or floorplan level
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, clock mesh is widely adopted specifically to reduce insertion delay variation to levels that conventional CTS cannot achieve — the mesh provides a low-impedance reference that masks variation from load imbalance, so the diagnostic approach for skew at 7nm starts with checking whether a mesh was designed and whether it is properly connected, not just re-running CTS

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Re-run LVS with different tool settings (accuracy mode, net and device tolerances) — identical results at different settings strongly suggest a real LVS mismatch; different results suggest a convergence or extraction artifact
first_checks.why_first: Rules out false LVS failures from extraction tool settings before investigating design or layout — most common false positive and the cheapest check

first_checks.check: Identify the specific net(s) in question and check their routing layers — are they in a region with unusual routing rules, dense via placements, or adjacent to hard macros?
first_checks.why_first: Metal shorts and opens are usually visible in the layout at the reported coordinates; checking the physical layout is faster than re-running any analysis

first_checks.check: For shorts: check the layer adjacency of the shorted nets — are they on adjacent metal layers with insufficient spacing, or do they share a via that is oversized or undersized?
first_checks.why_first: Shorts have a very small set of common physical causes; checking the specific geometry quickly discriminates spacing vs. via vs. design rule violation

first_checks.check: For opens: check whether the open net is long, goes through a dense via array, or crosses a hard-macro boundary — these are the three environments where opens most commonly occur
first_checks.why_first: Open nets have a different physical fingerprint than shorts; understanding the net's path structure immediately narrows the root cause candidates

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare LVS results at different extraction corners (best-case vs. worst-case resistance/capacitance) — if the mismatch appears at one corner but not the other, it may be a parasitic-induced net identification issue rather than a real short/open
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Real physical short or open confirmed — the mismatch persists across extraction corners
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Extraction artifact or parasitic-induced net identification error — the mismatch is a tool effect, not a physical defect

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For suspected shorts: check the DRC log for spacing violations at the reported coordinates — if spacing violations exist at the short location, it is a manufacturing defect that should have been caught in DRC; if no DRC violations exist, the short may be a false LVS report from extraction merging two physically separate wires
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Real short from insufficient spacing or design rule violation at the short location
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: False short from LVS extraction merging adjacent nets — check extraction settings or the ERC rule

discriminating_experiments.experiment: For suspected opens: check whether the open net passes through any non-default routing rules (NDR) vias or custom structures — if the open is at a NDR-specified via that the extraction tool may not recognize as a via, it may be a tool configuration issue; if it is at a standard via with a DRC violation, it is a real open
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Real open from missing via contact or DRC violation at the open location
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Extraction tool configuration missing recognition for a non-standard via structure — the net is actually continuous

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient metal spacing due to ERC (electrical rule check) or antenna rule violations that were waived incorrectly — the waiving engineer did not realize the waiver would cause a LVS mismatch
Via enlargement (a process fix for via reliability) applied after layout completion that inadvertently merged adjacent via arrays, creating metal shorts
Missing or broken via at the interface between a hard macro and standard-cell area — macro-specific via rules not applied in the interface routing
ECO routing changes that were not re-run through the full LVS flow — a manual route edit that was electrically correct but violated a DRC rule that LVS uses for net identification

LVS extraction tool bug or version mismatch where the newer or older tool interprets a specific geometric construct differently — particularly common with compound vias and non-rectangular shapes at advanced nodes

data.classic_trap: Immediately assuming the LVS mismatch is a real layout problem — LVS false failures are common enough that the first step should always be confirming the mismatch is real by changing extraction settings; chasing a false mismatch wastes days before the real problem is found
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the distinction between DRC and LVS failures blurs because multi-patterning SADP/LELE creates layout-dependent蚀刻 effects that affect both electrical connectivity and pattern fidelity — a layout that appears to pass DRC may still cause LVS mismatches because the manufacturing process creates unintended breaks or merges that are not caught as traditional DRC violations

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Check whether the extra or wrong-size devices are concentrated in a specific hierarchical block or spread across the design — this immediately discriminates between a localized layout error and a systematic extraction or modeling issue
first_checks.why_first: Localized suggests a real layout error; spread suggests a process design kit (PDK) version mismatch, extraction setting issue, or cell model problem

first_checks.check: Verify the PDK and extraction tool versions match what was used for the schematic — especially the device model library and the extraction rule deck
first_checks.why_first: PDK version mismatches between schematic and layout cause systematic device count or sizing mismatches that appear everywhere in the design simultaneously

first_checks.check: Inspect the specific device(s) in the layout viewer — are they visually correct (expected width/length)? Are they using the correct cell from the PDK?
first_checks.why_first: Visual confirmation immediately rules out the most common case: a cell was accidentally placed from the wrong variant (e.g., x1 vs. x4 of the same device)

first_checks.check: Check whether the extra device count matches the number of dummy devices or decap cells that are sometimes added in layout for process symmetry but may not be in the schematic
first_checks.why_first: Process-related dummy devices are the most common source of extra-device LVS mismatches and the easiest to resolve once identified

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the layout cell count against the schematic using a hierarchical netlist diff — if the device count mismatch appears only at a specific hierarchical level, that block's layout is the source; if it is everywhere, it is a library or extraction issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Specific hierarchical block has the device mismatch — that block's layout needs targeted review
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Systematic mismatch across the full design — a PDK, library, or extraction setting is the root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with device filtering disabled vs. enabled (some tools allow ignoring small devices or dummy devices) — if the mismatch disappears when dummy devices are filtered, the extra devices are process dummies and the mismatch is benign and waivable
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Extra devices are dummy fill or process-symmetry devices not modeled in schematic — benign, waivable mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Extra devices are real devices that exist in layout but not schematic — a real design discrepancy exists

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether the wrong-size device is actually a series or parallel combination of smaller devices that the extraction tool correctly identifies as a single effective device of the wrong size — if schematic shows two 1µm devices in series but layout was drawn as one 2µm device with shared diffusion, extraction will report a single 2µm device
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Series/parallel device recognition issue — layout and schematic are electrically equivalent but structurally different
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Real device size mismatch — the layout was intentionally or accidentally drawn with the wrong width/length

common_root_causes.cause: PDK version mismatch or inconsistent device model libraries between the schematic capture environment and the layout extraction environment

Device fingers or multi-finger MOSFETs drawn differently in layout vs. schematic — a 4-finger device of width W in schematic may be extracted as four separate width W fingers in layout, or vice versa depending on the extraction deck settings
Dummy or process-symmetry devices (decap fill, well proximity dummy poly, implant dummies) added in layout for manufacturing but not represented in schematic
ECO cell swap (replacing a cell with a different drive strength variant) done in layout without updating schematic, or vice versa

Extraction deck not correctly recognizing compound device structures (e.g., native devices, high-Vt devices, or 3-terminal devices) that the schematic models differently than the layout extractor interprets

data.classic_trap: Immediately assuming the wrong-size device is a layout error and manually editing the layout — in the majority of cases at advanced nodes, the mismatch is a PDK or extraction configuration issue, and manual layout edits that bypass the PDK create worse problems downstream
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, gate-all-around (GAA) or finFET device geometries make device width a discrete function of fin count rather than a continuous variable, which creates systematic device-size mismatches when the schematic uses continuous-width models but the layout uses discrete-fin cells — this is a structural mismatch between abstraction levels, not an error on either side

data.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Identify the metal layer and layer-pair context of each antenna violation — which metal layer is accumulating charge and which layers are connected to the gate?
first_checks.why_first: Antenna violations are routing-layer-specific; knowing which layer has the problem immediately suggests whether the fix is a routing change, a diode insertion, or a process fix

first_checks.check: Check whether the violating nets are very long (accumulating large antenna ratios) or normal length but connect to sensitive device types (e.g., thin-oxide or high-Vt devices with lower antenna damage thresholds)
first_checks.why_first: Distinguishes between pure antenna ratio problems (long nets) and device-sensitivity problems (normal nets connected to vulnerable devices) — the fix strategy differs

first_checks.check: Inspect the routing path for each violating net — does it pass through any layers that are particularly antenna-problematic for this foundry (usually metal-3 and metal-4 in older processes, specific layers in advanced nodes)?
first_checks.why_first: Each foundry has known problem layers for antenna effects; if the violation coincides with those layers, the fix is more likely a routing detour or layer-change than a device-level change

first_checks.check: Confirm whether antenna diodes exist in the standard cell library and whether they are being used in the current design — some libraries have diode cells available but the synthesis or place-and-route tool was configured to not insert them
first_checks.why_first: Diode insertion is the most common fix; the first check is whether the tool was set to use them

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run antenna checking with different antenna ratio settings (the foundry typically provides different antenna ratio tables for different device types) — if violations disappear at a less conservative ratio setting, the violation is at the boundary of what the foundry accepts and may be a signoff corner selection issue; if they persist at all settings, the violation is structural
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Antenna ratio at the boundary of the foundry's acceptance criteria — may be resolvable through signoff methodology change
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Structural antenna problem that requires physical layout changes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert antenna diode cells at the gate-connected endpoints of violating nets (using an ECO antenna fix flow) — if all violations are eliminated, the fix is diode insertion; if some remain, those nets have a routing topology problem that no diode can fix (e.g., the antenna accumulates across multiple layers before reaching any diode)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Diode insertion resolves the violations — routing topology is acceptable with proper antenna protection
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Routing topology creates antenna accumulation that no endpoint diode can mitigate — the net must be re-routed or segmented

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether antenna violations concentrate at a specific process layer that has a known charge accumulation issue — if all violations are on one layer and that layer has an optional etch tweak available from the foundry, the process fix (a simple layer-specific recipe change) resolves it without layout change
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Process-layer-specific antenna issue that the foundry can fix with a manufacturing recipe adjustment
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Physical layout changes (routing, diode insertion) are required regardless of process settings

common_root_causes.cause: Long nets with no intermediate contacts to lower metal layers — the antenna ratio accumulates with total wire length before the net connects to any device; the fix is routing the net through intermediate metal layers or adding jumper diodes

Antenna diode cells available in the PDK but not instantiated because the place-and-route tool's antenna checking and diode insertion were disabled or set to a threshold higher than the actual antenna ratio

Nets connecting to thin-oxide devices (low-Vt, high-speed devices) that have a lower antenna damage threshold than standard cells — these devices fail antenna check at wire lengths that are acceptable for regular cells
Custom analog blocks that were routed without antenna awareness — analog layout often uses long signal routing that accumulates antenna ratio without any diode protection
ECO changes that extended existing nets (adding routing to connect a new cell) without re-running antenna checking on the affected net segments

data.classic_trap: Immediately requesting a process fix (etch tweak) without first checking whether diode insertion resolves the violation — process fixes add cost and cycle time and may affect other devices on the same wafer layer, while diode insertion is a standard layout fix that the foundry expects
data.node_era_note: At 28nm, antenna effects were primarily addressed with diode insertion and routing fixes; at 7nm and below, the finFET structure creates a different antenna failure mechanism related to gate spacer damage and source/drain area ratios, which means the traditional wire-length antenna model is less accurate and device-level antenna effects (not just wire-to-gate ratio) must be considered at signoff

data.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Identify whether the detailed-routing DRC hotspots are localized to specific hard macros, specific standard-cell rows, or a specific metal layer — the location immediately suggests the cause
first_checks.why_first: Macro-boundary DRCs have a completely different cause than standard-cell-row DRCs or layer-specific DRCs; knowing the location is the fastest discriminator

first_checks.check: Check the routing guide spacing around each hotspot — specifically, are the guides for adjacent macros or between macros and standard cells spaced by at least the minimum spacing required for detailed routing to find a valid path?
first_checks.why_first: Insufficient routing guide spacing is the single most common cause of detailed-routing DRCs when global routing passed — the global router created guides that the detailed router cannot actually follow without DRCs

first_checks.check: Inspect the pin access geometry at the offending macro or cell — are the pin shapes aligned to a routing grid that is compatible with the standard-cell routing pitch?
first_checks.why_first: Pin grid vs. routing grid mismatch is a known cause of detailed-routing DRCs that global routing does not detect; it is especially common at macro boundaries where the macro pins may be on a different grid than the standard-cell routing

first_checks.check: Check the metal density (AMC - area ratio) of the layers at the hotspot — if metal density is near the upper limit, the DRC may be a density-fill-induced spacing violation rather than a routing geometry problem
first_checks.why_first: Metal fill for density compliance can create spacing DRCs that are not visible before fill is added; this is especially common in layers with tight density rules at advanced nodes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run the detailed router with a higher routing effort level (if the tool supports it) — if DRCs disappear or dramatically reduce, the original global routing guide assignment was low-quality and the detailed router is capable of finding valid paths if given more freedom
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Global routing guides too restrictive — detailed router needs more freedom to find valid paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Physical routing resources are genuinely insufficient — no routing effort level will resolve the DRCs without layout changes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare the DRCs at the hotspot before and after metal fill — if DRCs appear or increase after fill, the fill geometry is the problem; if DRCs are identical before and after fill, the routing geometry itself is invalid
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Metal fill creating or exacerbating spacing violations — post-fill DRC fixing is needed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Routing geometry is invalid before fill — the route itself must be changed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether DRCs at macro boundaries are consistent across all macro instances or specific to one instance — if only one instance has DRCs, that instance's placement is misaligned with its guide; if all instances of the same macro have DRCs, the macro cell's pin access definition is incompatible with the routing grid
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Macro pin access definition or placement alignment issue — macro cell model or placement constraints need fixing
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Macro-level routing guides are insufficiently spaced regardless of macro instance — guide spacing needs revision

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient spacing between adjacent hard macros in the floorplan — the global router generated guides in the gap that the detailed router cannot follow because the gap is narrower than the minimum routing pitch times the number of tracks needed

Macro pin access and standard-cell routing grid mismatch — the macro pin was placed on a grid incompatible with the standard-cell routing pitch, creating a geometric conflict that only manifests during detailed routing
Metal density fill creating spacing violations that were not present in the pre-fill routing — the fill tool generated shapes that violate minimum spacing rules with the existing route

Non-default routing rules (NDR) for specific nets (e.g., clock nets requiring wider spacing) applied within a region that is already at minimum routing pitch, making the effective spacing requirement impossible to meet
Global router guide generation left stranded islands of routing demand that the detailed router cannot resolve because the guide topology requires a routing path that violates a DRC rule

data.classic_trap: Assuming detailed routing needs a higher effort level or different router setting when the real problem is that global routing was given wrong or overly restrictive constraints — the detailed router is faithfully following invalid guides; fixing the global routing constraints (guide spacing, guide layer assignment) is the real fix
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, SADP (self-aligned double patterning) and LELE (litho-etch-litho-etch) processes create color-assignment conflicts in detailed routing that global routing cannot detect because global routing works on a simplified representation; a design that routes cleanly at 28nm may have unavoidable color-conflict DRCs at 7nm that require the routing to be done with full double-patterning awareness from the start

data.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Confirm whether the overflow is in standard-cell area, macro area, or both — this immediately discriminates between cell-level and macro-level root causes
first_checks.why_first: Standard-cell overflow suggests total cell count exceeds available area; macro overflow suggests macro placement created overlaps or a floorplan constraint conflict

first_checks.check: Check whether the overflow is preceded by a timing-driven placement run that was given unrealistic timing constraints — timing-driven placement will spread cells to meet timing, potentially creating physical overflow
first_checks.why_first: Timing-driven placement spreading is the most common cause of placement overflow that appears suddenly partway through a project when timing constraints are tightened

first_checks.check: Inspect the floorplan for overlapping hard macros or macros placed in a region marked as belonging to a different block (hierarchical floorplan constraint conflict)
first_checks.why_first: Macro overlap or floorplan constraint conflicts are the fastest to diagnose and the most definitively fixable — the placement is physically invalid regardless of optimization settings

first_checks.check: Check the target utilization vs. the actual die size — if the design was floorplanned at 70% utilization but the die size is too small to physically accommodate the cell count at acceptable density, overflow is inevitable regardless of placement settings
first_checks.why_first: Die size vs. cell count mismatch is a project-level problem that no placement setting will resolve; confirming this early saves wasted optimization cycles

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run global placement with optimization disabled (pure legalizer mode) — if overflow still occurs, the floorplan itself is invalid (overlapping macros or constraint conflicts); if overflow disappears in legalizer mode, the optimization spreading is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Floorplan invalidity (overlap or constraint conflict) — floorplan must be corrected before any placement will succeed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Optimization-driven spreading causing overflow — placement constraints or timing targets need revision

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce target utilization by a known amount (e.g., from 70% to 60%) and re-run placement — if overflow disappears, the design density is the root cause and the die must be enlarged or cells must be removed; if overflow persists at the lower utilization, the overflow is from a structural floorplan conflict, not overall density
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Overall design density exceeds physical capacity — die size increase or cell count reduction required
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Structural floorplan conflict (not overall density) causing overflow regardless of utilization level

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement with different initial floorplan seeds — if overflow is seed-dependent (appears with some seeds, not others), the placement engine hit a local minimum; if overflow is consistent across all seeds, the overflow is deterministic and structural
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Placement engine local minimum — different seed or placement strategy will resolve
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Deterministic overflow from floorplan or design structure — seed variation will not help

common_root_causes.cause: Timing-driven placement spreading cells to meet unrealistic timing constraints — the optimizer spreads cells apart to reduce coupling capacitance and meet delay targets, which increases physical footprint beyond available area
Hard macro overlap from an ECO floorplan change where a macro was moved but its placement blockage was not fully updated, creating an invalid overlap region that placement cannot resolve

Total cell count and die size mismatch — the design has more cells than can physically fit at the target utilization within the die dimensions; the project-level die size decision was made before the final cell count was known
Hierarchical floorplan constraint conflict where two blocks both specify a placement region for the same macro or for cells that cannot physically coexist in the same region
Memory compiler outputs that generated larger macros than expected from the initial floorplan estimates, displacing standard cells into regions the placement tool cannot legally place them

data.classic_trap: Increasing placement effort level or changing the placement engine configuration to try to squeeze cells into an overflow condition — placement tools cannot fix an overflow that results from insufficient physical area; the fix is either to reduce the cell count, enlarge the die, or revise the timing constraints that are driving the spreading
data.node_era_note: At 28nm, cell padding rules and cell height constraints were the primary placement density drivers; at 7nm and below, finFET standard cell heights vary with the number of fins and the library may include cells of different effective heights in the same library, creating mixed-row-height placement challenges that can cause the placement engine to overflow even when the aggregate density looks acceptable

data.pattern_name: block-input delay (forward budget)
data.situation: Block A is being implemented independently; its inputs arrive from upstream logic whose timing is not yet finalized. The block-level SDC must carry an input delay constraint that is achievable but not so loose that the block passes internally while the full chip fails.
data.derivation: Step 1: establish the reference clock period P (e.g., 1 ns at 1 GHz). Step 2: subtract a margin factor M (typical practice: reserve 10–20% of period for inter-block uncertainty; confidence on 15% as typical mid-range: 0.6). Result: available input budget = P × (1 − M). Step 3: the block internally must meet its own setup time Tsu before the capture edge; so input delay constraint = P × (1 − M) − Tsu. In practice this is written as: set_input_delay $clock [minus_M * P] −clock_fall −add_delay. The −clock_fall flag appears because the capture edge is often on the falling edge for source-synchronous or half-cycle budgets.
data.wrong_way: Setting input delay to a fixed arbitrary value (e.g., 0.5 ns) without relation to the clock period — this creates a constraint that may be unachievable at slow corners or so loose at fast corners that the block passes internally but fails at top-level; it also prevents the synthesis tool from knowing how hard to optimize the input paths.
data.defense: In review the engineer shows that the input delay equals the clock period minus the downstream block's setup requirement minus the inter-block interconnect estimate — a three-line arithmetic trace; additionally, the constraint is verified against the top-level timing report after integration to confirm the budget was correct.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: the block's synthesis will over-optimize paths that should be allowed to use the full clock period, wasting area and power on gates that will be irrelevant once the full chip is integrated. Too loose: the block will pass internally but the top-level timing closure will fail because the upstream logic cannot actually achieve the budget; ECO insertion at top level is expensive.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the interconnect delay estimate used in Step 2 must include an on-chip variation (OCV) adjustment that is larger than at 28nm; also, the derate factor for interconnect delay across corners is often set more conservatively (confidence on 20% OCV adjustment as typical at 7nm: 0.5) because within-die variation is more significant.

data.pattern_name: block-output delay (backward budget)
data.situation: Block A must drive its outputs to downstream Block B; Block B has not been implemented yet. The output delay constraint on Block A's outputs must be derived from what Block B can reasonably accept, not from what Block A can theoretically produce.
data.derivation: Step 1: reference clock period P. Step 2: subtract Block B's internal clock-to-Q delay Tcq (from the target library; if unknown, use an upper-bound estimate from a similar library, confidence on using 200–400 ps as a starting estimate for Tcq: 0.65). Step 3: subtract Block B's setup time Tsu. Step 4: subtract inter-block interconnect delay estimate Dinter (if unknown, use a conservative initial estimate; confidence on Dinter being treated as negligible at early project stages: 0.5). Result: set_output_delay constraint = P − Tcq − Tsu − Dinter. The constraint is written on Block A's output ports, referencing the same clock that Block B will use.
data.wrong_way: Setting output delay to zero or to the full clock period — zero implies the output must arrive at the same time as the clock edge (achievable only for source-synchronous interfaces), while full-period setting wastes the entire budget and may cause the synthesis tool to under-optimize the output paths.
data.defense: Engineer shows the arithmetic: the output delay represents the time available from Block A's launch clock edge to when Block B must capture, broken into Block B's Tcq + Tsu + interconnect; the trace is updated once Block B's library data is available.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: Block A's output paths are over-constrained; synthesis may add unnecessary buffering or fail to meet timing, creating a block-level timing failure that will disappear once the full chip integrates. Too loose: Block B will receive data with excessive uncertainty, requiring Block B to have larger setup margins that consume chip-level timing margin.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: false path exception and its defense
data.situation: A set of paths is logically impossible to exercise in functional operation (e.g., paths through a configuration register that can only be written during test mode, or paths between two clock domains that are never simultaneously active), but STA will analyze them and fail timing on them.
data.derivation: Step 1: identify the functional condition under which the path can be exercised; if the condition is logically impossible (configuration is read-only during functional operation, the two clocks are never on simultaneously), the path is a true false path. Step 2: define the false path with sufficient precision: the constraint must identify the specific clock pair, the specific start and end points, and the condition — e.g., set_false_path −from [get_clocks clk_a] −to [get_clocks clk_b] −through [get_pins block/config_reg_reg/Q]. Step 3: confirm no other path between those endpoints exists that could exercise the same data relationship through a different route.
data.wrong_way: Setting a broad false path on an entire clock domain or a large group of registers without specifying the exact paths — this silently hides real timing failures because the tool stops analyzing all paths between those domains even ones that ARE exercisable; the review will pass because the constraint is correct in spirit but the implementation is too broad.
data.defense: Engineer presents the functional specification (register documentation, clocking diagram, or FSM state table) showing the specific condition that makes the path impossible; the false path constraint is written to match that specific condition, and the review checks that no other functional path exists between the same endpoints.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (false path is incorrect — the path IS exercisable functionally): the path is never optimized and never fixed, causing a silent timing failure that will appear on silicon. Too loose (false path is correct but written too narrowly): the false path constraint does not cover the actual failure path and the violation remains; the engineer will spend time trying to fix a path that should have been excepted.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, false paths that rely on clock domain never being simultaneously active must also be reviewed against clock gating synthesis — the synthesis tool may combine clock enables in ways that create momentary simultaneous switching that the original false path analysis did not anticipate; confidence on this specific risk: 0.55.

data.pattern_name: multicycle path — launch/capture edge offset
data.situation: A data path is known to take more than one clock cycle to produce a valid result (e.g., a hardware accelerator that produces a result after 3 clock cycles, or a datapath with deliberate pipelining). The synthesis tool must be told not to optimize the path as a single-cycle path.
data.derivation: Step 1: determine the number of cycles N from launch to when data is valid at the capture register. Step 2: for a setup (max-delay) path, write set_multicycle_path N −setup −from [launch_reg] −to [capture_reg] − this moves the capture edge from the nominal edge to edge N. Step 3: for a hold (min-delay) path, write set_multicycle_path N−1 −hold −from [launch_reg] −to [capture_reg] − this prevents the hold check from being placed at the new capture edge (which would be too aggressive). The arithmetic: capture edge for setup = launch edge + N periods; capture edge for hold = setup capture edge − 1 period.
data.wrong_way: Setting only the setup multicycle path without the hold multicycle path — this moves the setup capture edge to N but leaves the hold check at the new edge, which is N−1 periods from launch, making the hold constraint artificially aggressive by one cycle and causing hold violations on paths that are actually valid.
data.defense: In review, the engineer presents the FSM state diagram or pipeline description that defines the exact number of cycles the data is valid after launch; the multicycle path constraint is written with both −setup and −hold statements, and the arithmetic (setup edge = N, hold edge = N−1) is explicitly shown.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (N is smaller than actual): synthesis attempts to meet a single-cycle timing on a path that physically requires more cycles, resulting in either over-area or a setup violation that will never close. Too loose (N is larger than actual): the path is given more time than it needs, reducing optimization priority on paths that should be optimized, and potentially masking real single-cycle paths that happen to share some logic.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: CDC path — synthesizable safety budget
data.situation: Two clock domains are asynchronous to each other (no fixed phase relationship) and data crosses between them. The CDC path must be constrained to prevent STA from analyzing it as a synchronous path, but also must carry a clock uncertainty budget for the metastability resolution margin.
data.derivation: Step 1: set_false_path between the two clock domains (logical exception: there is no single capture edge to analyze against). Step 2: add a clock uncertainty budget representing the worst-case clock skew plus the metastability resolution time required for the synchronizer flip-flop to settle — in practice this is derived as: uncertainty = clock_skew_estimate + Tmetastability_estimate. Typical clock skew estimate for a given clock domain pair: 100–300 ps depending on clock tree depth (confidence on 200 ps as a starting estimate for moderate-depth trees: 0.6). Typical metastability resolution time: 200–500 ps for a two-flop synchronizer in a standard library (confidence on 300 ps for a typical 28nm library: 0.55). Total uncertainty budget: 500 ps. This is applied as set_clock_uncertainty on the path or as a latency budget on the receiving domain.
data.wrong_way: Setting only the false path without any clock uncertainty budget on the receiving domain — this means the CDC path is completely unanalyzed and any timing failure in the synchronizer logic (which is real and can cause data corruption) will not appear in STA; alternatively, applying a very large clock uncertainty that covers the entire clock period essentially excepts the paths without any analysis, masking real functional failures.
data.defense: Engineer presents the clock tree depth reports for both domains, the estimated skew between them, and the synchronizer cell's metastability specification from the library databook; the uncertainty value is the arithmetic sum of skew and metastability budget.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (uncertainty budget is smaller than actual skew + metastability): the CDC path will appear to meet timing in STA but will have real metastability failures on silicon; this is a silent data corruption failure. Too loose: the receiving domain will be over-constrained relative to its actual clock quality, causing unnecessary timing failures in the CDC receiver logic.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the metastability resolution time for standard-cell synchronizers increases because the smaller transistor sizes have lower drive strength for the same geometry, and the difference between best-case and worst-case metastability resolution widens; confidence on this: 0.55; as a result, CDC uncertainty budgets at 7nm often use a larger metastability margin (500 ps instead of 300 ps).

data.pattern_name: inter-block timing budget split
data.situation: Two blocks (Block X and Block Y) are being implemented in parallel by different engineers; they share a top-level timing budget of P nanoseconds for paths between them. The budget must be split between Block X's output paths, the interconnect, and Block Y's input paths before either block is implemented.
data.derivation: Step 1: establish total budget B = P − top_level_setup_margin (confidence on using 5–10% of period as top-level margin: 0.65). Step 2: allocate to Block X output paths: Bx = B × α where α is the area/power budget fraction agreed between block owners (or equally: 0.5). Step 3: allocate to Block Y input paths: By = B × β where β = 1 − α minus interconnect share. Step 4: interconnect delay share Dinter = B − Bx − By (typically small for on-chip connections, large for package-level connections). In practice: set_output_delay [Bx] −clock [clk] −from [BlockX/outputs] and set_input_delay [By] −clock [clk] −to [BlockY/inputs].
data.wrong_way: Both engineers independently assume the other block will absorb the timing margin and constrain their block at full clock period — this double-counts the budget and the top-level integration will fail with no room left; or, one engineer constrains at full period and the other at near-zero, creating an unbalanced design.
data.defense: The lead timing engineer presents the top-level timing budget spreadsheet showing the arithmetic split, agreed in writing between block owners before implementation begins; at block reviews the constraints are compared against this agreement.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight for either block: that block's implementation will fail timing internally even if the other block's implementation succeeds, requiring ECO and potentially redesign. Too loose for either block: that block will consume more timing margin than allocated, leaving insufficient margin at top level for interconnect and clock skew, causing a top-level timing failure.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, interconnect delay estimates for on-chip paths are less predictable due to increased coupling capacitance sensitivity to routing geometry; confidence on needing a larger interconnect delay estimate margin at 7nm (20% vs. 10% at 28nm): 0.55.

data.pattern_name: over-constraining during early implementation
data.situation: A block is being implemented early in the project timeline before the full chip clock frequency is finalized. The engineer wants to constrain the block conservatively so that if the clock frequency increases later, the block does not need to be re-timed.
data.derivation: Step 1: take the target clock period P_target and apply an over-constraint factor F (confidence on F = 0.85 to 0.90 being common practice: 0.65 — meaning constrain to 85–90% of the target period). Step 2: write the clock constraint as create_clock −period [P_target × F]. Step 3: document the relaxation point: when the full chip frequency is confirmed, the constraint will be relaxed to full period. The over-constraint is typically applied in the initial synthesis run; place-and-route may use a less aggressive over-constraint.
data.wrong_way: Over-constraining without a documented relaxation plan — the block passes timing at the over-constrained frequency but the constraint is never relaxed, so the block is under-utilized (over-area, over-power) compared to what it would be at the actual chip frequency; or, over-constraining by too much (e.g., F = 0.5) causing the block to fail timing even though the target frequency is achievable.
data.defense: Engineer presents the frequency plan showing the confirmed vs. targeted clock frequency, the over-constraint factor, and the explicit plan to relax to full period once frequency is confirmed; this is captured in the block's constraint documentation.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (over-constraint is too aggressive, F too small): the block fails timing at the over-constrained frequency even though it would meet the actual target frequency; this is a false failure that wastes ECO cycles. Too loose (over-constraint is too mild, or not applied): if the chip frequency increases, the block must be re-timed, causing project schedule risk.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, over-constraining is less common because the frequency targets are typically already finalized before implementation begins due to the long turnaround time at advanced nodes; confidence on this shift: 0.55.

data.pattern_name: virtual clock for IO timing
data.situation: A chip has IO signals that are timed relative to an external clock that is not inside the chip (e.g., DDR interface, source-synchronous input). The chip-level SDC must constrain the input and output paths relative to this external clock, which does not appear as a create_clock in the design.
data.derivation: Step 1: define the external clock frequency and characteristics as a virtual clock: create_clock −name virtual_sys_clk −period [P] (the virtual clock exists only as a reference for IO constraints, not as a physical clock inside the design). Step 2: for inputs: set_input_delay −clock virtual_sys_clk −clock_fall [Tdata_valid_max] [input_ports] where Tdata_valid_max is the maximum time after the external clock edge that the input data is valid (from the IO specification or board-level timing). Step 3: for outputs: set_output_delay −clock virtual_sys_clk −clock_fall [Tdata_setup_required] [output_ports] where Tdata_setup_required is the minimum time before the external clock edge that the output data must be stable. Step 4: verify that the input and output delay together leave at least a small positive margin for on-chip variation: P − input_delay − output_delay > 0.
data.wrong_way: Writing IO constraints without a virtual clock and referencing an internal clock instead — this creates a mismatch between the analysis viewpoint (chip-internal launch edge) and the actual IO timing (external clock domain), causing the input delay to be referenced from the wrong edge and producing incorrect timing analysis for the IO paths.
data.defense: Engineer presents the board-level timing diagram showing the external clock, the data valid window, and the setup/hold requirements; the virtual clock period and the input/output delay values are derived directly from that diagram and cross-checked against the board-level timing budget.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: input or output delays are set shorter than the actual data valid window, causing the chip to fail IO timing in the system even though the internal timing is correct; this results in board-level failures that require chip respin or I/O driver changes. Too loose: input or output delays are set longer than the actual data valid window, masking real internal timing failures that will appear on the board; the chip passes silicon test but fails system-level test.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, DDR and high-speed source-synchronous interfaces often require a derived clock (DCD-corrected or duty-cycle-corrected) for the virtual clock reference; the virtual clock period must account for the duty cycle distortion of the PLL, which adds an additional uncertainty term; confidence on this: 0.55.

data.pattern_name: generated (divided) clock constraint
data.situation: A clock divider or clock gate inside the design produces a divided clock that feeds registers in a specific block. The divided clock must be constrained as a generated clock so that timing is analyzed correctly relative to its parent clock.
data.derivation: Step 1: identify the clock divider or clock gate cell and the output pin of that cell that produces the divided clock. Step 2: define the generated clock: create_generated_clock −name [clk_div] −source [master_clock_pin] −div [N] [divider_output_pin] where N is the division factor (2 for divide-by-2, 4 for divide-by-4, etc.). Step 3: the tool automatically derives the period of the generated clock as N times the master clock period. Step 4: verify the phase relationship — a simple divider typically produces a divided clock that is edge-aligned with the master clock; if there is a phase offset (e.g., from a clock gate with an enable), add −phase [offset_degrees] to the generated clock definition. Step 5: check whether paths between the master clock domain and the divided clock domain are CDC paths (asynchronous) or synchronous (if the divider is glitch-free and the phase relationship is deterministic).
data.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as a second independent create_clock instead of a create_generated_clock — this tells STA that the divided clock has its own unrelated period, breaking timing analysis for any path that crosses between the master and divided clock domains; paths that should be analyzed as single-cycle paths will be analyzed as asynchronous paths, or vice versa.
data.defense: Engineer presents the clock tree schematic showing the divider cell and its division factor, the phase relationship from simulation or timing simulation, and the generated clock SDC statement; the review checks that the division factor and source pin are correct and that the CDC classification between master and divided domain is documented.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (dividing by a smaller factor than actual): the generated clock period is set too short, causing false setup violations on paths that are analyzed as faster than they actually are. Too loose (dividing by a larger factor than actual): the generated clock period is set too long, reducing optimization priority for paths on that clock and potentially masking real failures; also, paths crossing between master and divided domains will be incorrectly analyzed for CDC.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, clock dividers are often implemented using clock gating cells rather than explicit divider circuits, and the division factor may be dynamically changed during operation; in these cases the generated clock must be constrained as a set of multiple generated clocks or with a −master_clock and −divide_by specification that accounts for all possible division modes; confidence on needing this multi-mode approach: 0.55.

data.pattern_name: asynchronous reset path constraint
data.situation: A design has an asynchronous reset signal (reset_n) that is not synchronous to any chip clock. Paths that originate from registers driven by the asynchronous reset must be constrained to prevent STA from analyzing them against an undefined clock relationship, while ensuring the reset path itself is safe (synchronous to the clock for release timing).
data.derivation: Step 1: identify the asynchronous reset source pin on registers that have async reset — e.g., preset/clear pins. Step 2: define a false path exception on the asynchronous reset signal: set_false_path −from [async_reset_port] −to [async_reset_receiver_pins] −this prevents STA from analyzing the reset signal's arrival time relative to the clock because the reset is not synchronous. Step 3: separately constrain the reset removal (deassertion) timing: the reset must be released and meet the recovery/removal time of the receiving register relative to the clock edge — this is written as set_max_delay [Trecovery] −from [async_reset_port] −to [register_async_pin] with a specific value derived from the library recovery time. Step 4: in practice, a two-stage synchronizer on the reset signal (for async reset) and a clock domain crossing constraint from the reset to each clock domain is added to ensure reset release is not synchronous to any functional clock edge.
data.wrong_way: Setting only a false path on the reset and not constraining the reset removal timing — the false path prevents setup analysis but the reset can still violate the recovery time of the receiving register, causing metastability or incorrect reset behavior when the reset is released near an active clock edge; alternatively, not synchronizing the reset at all and letting it directly drive async preset/clear pins of registers in multiple clock domains.
data.defense: Engineer presents the reset architecture diagram showing whether the reset is asynchronous-assert (immediate, no clock needed) and synchronous-deassert (must meet recovery time), the synchronizer chain for reset release, and the set_false_path and recovery-time constraints for each clock domain; the recovery time value is taken from the library databook.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: recovery time constraint is set too small, causing false failures at slow corners where the actual recovery time is larger; or, false path is set too broadly, hiding real timing failures on paths that do interact with the reset in a clocked way (e.g., reset-gated logic). Too loose: recovery time constraint is set too large, wasting timing margin; or, false path is not applied and the reset path fails STA, causing unnecessary fixing of a path that should be excepted.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the recovery time of registers increases relative to the clock period at advanced nodes due to larger setup/recovery time in finFET cells; also, the powerup state requirements at 7nm often mandate a more complex reset architecture with retention registers that require separate timing constraints for the save/restore signals; confidence on increased recovery time as a significant factor at 7nm: 0.55.

data.title: Out-of-order vs. in-order execution engine
data.decision: POWER4 implements out-of-order instruction execution with in-order retirement
data.rationale: out-of-order execution extracts more instruction-level parallelism by allowing instructions to execute when their operands are ready regardless of program order, thereby hiding memory latency and better utilizing execution units
data.outcome: POWER4 achieves significantly higher IPC than prior in-order IBM designs; the combination of out-of-order execution with in-order retirement maintains precise exceptions and simplifies the programming model
data.quote_as_recall_verbatim: out-of-order execution allows instructions to proceed as soon as their operands are available
data.weakest_point: my recall of the paper's specific framing of the in-order-alternative may conflate it with general POWER4 literature

data.title: Microarchitectural depth: longer pipeline for higher clock rate
data.where_in_paper: Pipeline organization and clock philosophy section
data.decision: POWER4 uses a deep pipelined design at 1.3-1.5 GHz rather than maximizing IPC at a lower frequency
data.alternatives_or_rejected: shorter pipeline with higher CPI (higher IPC per clock but lower absolute clock rate)
data.rationale: the paper argues that clock frequency is the primary driver of single-thread performance and that the market demanded higher frequency; cycle time improvements are weighed against IPC losses
data.outcome: POWER4 achieved approximately 1.3 GHz in initial silicon, representing a substantial clock-rate jump over POWER3, with acceptable CPI penalties from pipeline depth
data.weakest_point: the specific frequency numbers and the exact CPI vs. frequency trade-off analysis as presented in the paper - I am uncertain of the exact numbers and trade-off ratios the paper cites

data.title: L2 cache on-chip integration
data.decision: L2 cache is placed on the processor chip alongside the cores, not off-chip
data.alternatives_or_rejected: off-chip L2 (as in earlier IBM designs like POWER3)
data.rationale: on-chip L2 dramatically reduces latency and increases effective bandwidth; the paper notes that the off-chip L2 bus becomes a performance bottleneck at higher frequencies
data.outcome: POWER4 integrates 1.41 MB of L2 cache on-chip per processor, significantly reducing L2 access latency compared to off-chip alternatives
data.weakest_point: the exact L2 cache size (1.41 MB) and whether that specific number appears in this paper rather than in supplementary documentation

data.title: Extensive RAS hardware for commercial workloads
data.decision: POWER4 includes substantial redundant hardware: instruction retry, L1/L2 error correction codes (ECC), checkpoint repair, and extensive lockstep operation for fault detection
data.alternatives_or_rejected: minimal RAS with software-only recovery (higher performance, lower silicon area but unacceptable for commercial server market)
data.rationale: commercial workloads (database, ERP) require five-nines availability; the paper argues that hardware-level error detection and correction reduces planned and unplanned downtime, which is the primary concern of the target market
data.outcome: POWER4-based systems achieved high availability figures suitable for UNIX server market; the RAS features became a key differentiator against competitors
data.weakest_point: the specific RAS mechanisms listed here (checkpoint repair, lockstep specifics) - these may be in the paper but I am less certain of their exact names and implementations as described

data.title: Two-level branch predictor with selective history
data.decision: POWER4 implements a two-level adaptive branch predictor using a combination of global branch history register (GHR) and pattern history table (PHT)
data.rationale: two-level predictors more accurately capture correlated branch behavior in commercial workloads where branches have complex dependencies on prior branch outcomes
data.outcome: POWER4 achieved high branch prediction accuracy, reducing branch misprediction penalties which would otherwise severely impact performance due to the deep pipeline
data.weakest_point: the specific sizes of the GHR and PHT structures - these details may be in the paper or may be in the general POWER4 documentation, and I am uncertain which source they come from

assumptions_invoked: CCD Art. 19(2)(a): X is the annual rate equating present value of drawdowns to present value of repayments and charges
CCD Annex I (method A, monthly compounding): t measured in years, actuarial method, unit period = 1 month = 1/12 year
CCD Art. 17(2): the €100 arrangement fee paid at t=0 is a charge included on the repayments side
Actuarial method: discrete compound interest, (1+X)^(t_i) where t_i in years; X solved on the function f(X) = sum D_j*(1+X)^(-t_j) - sum R_i*(1+X)^(-t_i)
