rules.reasoning: The operative phrase 'more than 2 percent' is strict (> 1.99% and 2.00% do not exceed it, while 2.01% does.
The phrase 'more than 36 months after consummation' is strict (>36); 35 and 36 months do not exceed it, while 37 months does.
The phrase 'by 1.5 or more percentage points' is inclusive (>=1.5); 1.49 does not meet it, while 1.50 and 1.51 do.
The pass condition 'does not exceed ... by 2.25 or more percentage points' is inclusive at the upper bound (<=2.25); 2.24 and 2.25 pass, while 2.26 fails.
Both conditions use 'less than' (strict): (10.0M, 0.9M) fails the revenue prong, (9.9M, 1.0M) fails the income prong, and (9.9M, 0.9M) meets both prongs.
The phrase 'equal to or greater than 16%' is inclusive (>=16%); 15.99% fails, while 16.00% and 16.01% satisfy the simplified ETR test.
The Tier 1 floor 'at least equal to 50% of SCR' is inclusive (>=50%); 49.99% breaches the floor, while 50.00% and 50.01% satisfy it.
The threshold 'equal to or greater than the minimum' is inclusive (>=threshold); threshold-1 does not meet it, while threshold and threshold+1 do.

data.weakest_point: Rule 5 (GloBE de-minimis): the inputs are expressed as currency figures rather than the precise EUR-denominated averages the OECD Model Rules specify, and the joint AND/OR structure between the two legs at the boundary depends on whether either failing leg disqual carve-out — the verdict assumes both legs must strictly hold, which is correct per Art. 1.1.2 but I am not fully certain the inputs map one-to-one to the rule's averaging semantics.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Run global-route congestion heatmap overlay on the placed DB to see if density is genuinely clean or only locally dense
first_checks.why_first: cheapest; rules out the most common cause (placement density lied)

first_checks.check: Inspect the failing GCell region for pin density / high-fanout nets on the same layer
first_checks.why_first: rules out pin-limited congestion masquerading as routing congestion

first_checks.check: Compare cell row utilization vs. effective density, and check for blocked placement due to macros, blockage, or large hard macros
first_checks.why_first: rules out 'clean-looking but actually blocked' placement

first_checks.check: Check the layer utilization between two adjacent metal layers in the failing region
first_checks.why_first: rules out layer-promotion issues when one layer is saturated

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at whether the failing GCell region contains a high-fanout clock/reset/scan net
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: high-fanout net topology drove congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: cell density drove congestion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at whether removing the failing block from congestion (or detaching it) clears DRCs elsewhere nearby
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: block-placement / macro-pin distribution root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global density or tool tuning issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether DRCs spread across all layers or only at a specific layer transition
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer-promotion or routing-direction limit
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uniform density problem

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check the experiment using the actual congestion analysis versus a placer-estimated density
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: true congestion; need adjustment
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: false alarm from placer's density estimate

common_root_causes.cause: Macro or IP placement blocks region and causes re-routing around it
High-fanout net (clock/reset/scan) topology creating hot spots
Layer assignment or track utilization mismatch (e.g., too many pins on lower metal)
Cell row utilization reporting was misleading; global route finds true hot spots
Wrong routing blockage layer setting in the flow

data.classic_trap: Trusting the placer's reported utilization as a true picture of the placed design without checking the actual routing congestion heatmap.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, the routable area is dominated by pin accessibility and track pattern, so pin density > cell density often dominates congestion.

first_checks.why_first: rules out clock skew as the cause in seconds

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing paths cluster around specific clock-gating cells or the CTS tap point
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-tree-architecture issues

first_checks.check: Check whether CTS was done with a netlist that includes all clock cells and is consistent with the post-CTS netlist

first_checks.check: Look at the cell delay transition time (slew) on the launching/capturing clock pins
first_checks.why_first: rules out clock-buffer slew degradation masquerading as setup

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failing paths share one or a few clock-gating cells with high insertion delay, it's skew/latency root cause; if they spread across hierarchies, check transition times or netlist issues
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: skew/latency imbalance causing the failure
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global transition or netlist issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If launch/capture skew is large only on the failing paths, run skew-opt with finer granularity or balance skew across more levels
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: skew-tuning needed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uneven buffer strength needed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Look at the path with timing path mode single-clock vs inter-clock
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: inter-clock path issue (unrelated clocks)
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: single-clock balance issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check whether CTS treated the failing clock as a leaf or propagated its own delay target
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: CTS target setting wrong
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: actual physical issue

common_root_causes.cause: Excessive clock skew from unbalanced clock tree
Clock-gating cells with high latency and skewed taps
Clock tree doesn't include some clock cells (set_clock_groups or clock-view mismatch)
Transition time degradation on long clock lines or large cells driving clock pins
Operating condition or analysis view mismatch (e.g., worst-case vs typical, multi-mode analysis missing)

data.classic_trap: Treating setup violations as a data-path problem (re-sizing cells) when the actual cause is clock skew from gating/CTS architecture.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, clock tree resistance matters much more and clock-buffer-only fix doesn't suffice; need to balance drive strength and wire length.

first_checks.why_first: rules out skewed clock root cause in seconds

first_checks.why_first: rules out a mode-mismatch root cause

discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock skew root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: data-path root cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run hold-fixing with only delay-cell insertion and observe whether the violation magnitude matches expected delay

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare across analysis modes (functional vs scan) to see whether violations appear in both
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: real chip issue vs scan-only artifact
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: scan-chain related only

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If many holds share one endpoint, check that the common endpoint is the same clock-capture pin

discriminating_experiments.rules_out: data path

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew from CTS architecture (skewed launch/capture on a common clock)
Data path is too fast (large buffer, short wire, transition time very tight)
Hold-fixing was not run / not converged in a previous step
Wrong mode being reported (e.g., DFT scan mode with unrealistic skew)
Operating condition not matching silicon (best-case vs worst-case analysis confusion)

data.classic_trap: Adding hold buffers everywhere without first checking the clock skew—often the skew imbalance is so large that data path fix never closes.
data.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, hold violations often appear even on the same clock due to local variation; need a finer hold-skew budget and local variation-aware analysis.

data.title: Clock-frequency philosophy: self-timed pulsed-global clock distribution
data.decision: Adopt a self-timed pulsed-global clock design with local clocks generated by pulse generators from a single global clock, rather than a conventional distributed buffered clock tree.
data.rationale: The paper states that the self-timed approach was chosen to achieve the aggressive cycle-time target and to reduce dependence on a single long global wire, and to limit clock skew/jitter under variation.
data.outcome: Enables the targeted ~1.3+ GHz cycle time across a large die and supports the chip's variable-frequency operation and power reduction.
data.weakest_point: Exact cycle-time target number and any quantitative clock-skew claims

data.title: On-chip L2: shared, inclusive across cores via directory coherence
data.decision: Use a shared, inclusive on-chip L2 organized as multiple L2 controllers that are address-interleaved and participate in a directory-based MESI coherence protocol.
data.rationale: Stated reasoning: inclusive sharing reduces coherence traffic between cores and the off-chip L3, and on-chip directory traffic can be handled at the L2 controllers with lower latency than snooping a wide bus.
data.outcome: L3 acts as off-chip victim cache; latency to off-chip memory is reduced for shared working sets and coherence is scaled to two cores on-die.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly contrasts inclusive vs exclusive for L2 vs L3

data.title: Simultaneous multithreading rejected in favor of dual-core chip-level multiprocessing
data.where_in_paper: Guiding principles / CMP vs SMT discussion
data.decision: Implement two full processor cores on a single die (CMP), with explicit per-core state, rather than a single wider-issue core that also offers SMT.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Adding SMT in addition to (or instead of) the two-core CMP was argued against
data.rationale: The paper argues that for the commercial workload targets, throughput gains came from replicating complete cores, and that second SMT thread context logic would not fit within the power/area budget that two complete cores required.
data.outcome: Two single-threaded cores per chip, each appearing as a separate logical processor; future POWER5 added SMT on top of this CMP base.
data.weakest_point: The paper may describe this as a frequency/cycle-time trade-off rather than as a direct SMT-rejection argument

data.title: RAS approach: spare/divide logic in the L1 caches and array-repair for larger arrays
data.decision: Implement per-array redundancy at the L1 caches (divide-by-N spare columns for repair) and ECC plus spare rows for L2 and on-chip arrays, rather than relying solely on bit-level ECC throughout.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Using only ECC without redundant spare rows/columns was argued against
data.rationale: Stated reasoning: L1 caches must support high-frequency accesses that are throughput-sensitive, and it is more area-effective to add repairable spare columns than to increase ECC width enough to mask hard defects in a large array.
data.outcome: Allows recovery from manufacturing defects in cache arrays without sacrificing normal-mode access time.
data.weakest_point: Exact terms 'divide' vs 'spare' and which specific arrays are referenced

data.title: Interconnect: unified on-chip bus between cores, L2 controllers, and external I/O
data.decision: Use a single on-chip bus structure that concurrently carries address, data, and coherency responses between the two cores, the L2 controllers, and the I/O unit, with logic distributed across the chip.
data.rationale: The paper argues a unified bus simplifies physical design, supports symmetric core access to L2, and avoids the latency of a separate I/O port to the L2.
data.outcome: Single interconnect fabric links both cores, the L2, and the chip I/O; addresses are interleaved across the L2 controllers and coherence traffic is also handled through the same fabric.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper uses the term 'fabric' or 'bus' and the exact rationale wording

data.pattern_name: block_boundary_io_delay_budgeting
data.situation: Deriving input/output delay budgets between two blocks with unknown internal timing, during top-level integration
data.derivation: Split the available clock period (T_clock) minus clock skew (T_skew, assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7) and margin (T_margin, assumes 15% of T_clock confidence 0.6) between the launch block (T_launch), interconnect (T_interconnect), and capture block (T_capture) proportionally to their expected logic depth. Formula: T_launch + T_interconnect + T_capture ≤ T_clock - T_skew - T_margin. Allocate based on historical logic depth ratios from similar blocks.
data.wrong_way: Assuming an equal 33/33/33 split between launch, interconnect, and capture without considering block complexity, leading to one block being over-constrained while another has excessive slack
data.defense: Present historical data from similar blocks showing typical logic depth distributions and justify the proportional split based on gate count and pipeline depth
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: impossible timing closure for one block; Too loose: timing failures at integration when interconnect delay exceeds budget
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: interconnect delay variability increases, requiring larger margins in T_interconnect

data.pattern_name: false_path_vs_multicycle_decision
data.situation: Determining whether a path that cannot meet single-cycle timing should be constrained as a false path or a multicycle path
data.derivation: Analyze the path's logical feasibility: if the path is structurally impossible (e.g., mutually exclusive enables, reset conditions), mark as false path. If the path is functionally valid but requires multiple cycles (e.g., multi-stage data transfer), mark as multicycle path with appropriate -setup and -hold values. For multicycle N: effective period = N * T_clock.
data.wrong_way: Marking a false path as multicycle (wastes cycles and may hide real timing issues), or marking a multicycle path as false (causes functional failure due to missing data latching)
data.defense: Review RTL code for logical impossibility (e.g., gated clocks, enable conditions) or multi-cycle requirements (e.g., pipeline stages, handshake protocols). Use formal verification to confirm.
data.signoff_risk: False path mislabeled as multicycle: unnecessary timing relaxation may hide real issues; Multicycle mislabeled as false: functional failure due to missing data capture
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more complex clock gating increases false path opportunities but also risk of mislabeling

data.pattern_name: clock_domain_crossing_cdc_constraint
data.situation: Constraining data transfer between asynchronous clock domains to prevent metastability
data.derivation: Insert synchronizer flops (typically 2-3 stages) in the receiving domain. Constrain the path from launch flop to first synchronizer flop as false or multicycle. Calculate setup/hold requirements based on clock frequencies: T_su = T_clock_receiver - T_skew - T_synchronizer_delay (assumes T_skew is 5% of T_clock confidence 0.8). Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for the two domains.
data.wrong_way: Not constraining CDC paths at all, or using insufficient synchronizer stages (e.g., only 1 stage), leading to metastability propagation
data.defense: Reference CDC design guidelines and synchronizer verification reports. Show that synchronizer depth matches the required MTBF (mean time between failures) for the design.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose: metastability propagates to functional logic causing system failure; Too tight: impossible to implement due to excessive synchronizer delay
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: higher clock frequencies require more synchronizer stages for same MTBF

data.pattern_name: early_implementation_overconstraining
data.situation: Setting initial timing constraints during early implementation when block timing is unknown
data.derivation: Start with tight constraints: set clock period to 80% of target (confidence 0.7), add 20% margin (confidence 0.6) on all paths. Gradually relax constraints as implementation matures, using actual timing data from block-level runs.
data.wrong_way: Starting with final relaxed constraints, missing early timing issues that could have been caught with tighter constraints
data.defense: Demonstrate iterative constraint relaxation: show progression (e.g., Week 1: 0.8*T, Week 2: 0.85*T, Week 3: 0.9*T) with corresponding implementation data.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: unnecessary optimization effort and potential over-design; Too loose: late-stage timing failures when blocks cannot meet relaxed constraints
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more aggressive initial constraints needed due to higher process variability

data.pattern_name: virtual_clocks_for_io_interfaces
data.situation: Constraining IO interfaces where the actual clock is external and not part of the design
data.derivation: Create a virtual clock with the same period as the external IO clock. Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for asynchronous IOs. Derive input delay as: T_input_delay = T_external_clock_period * 0.5 - T_setup_external (assumes T_external_clock_period confidence 0.9, T_setup_external confidence 0.7). Derive output delay as: T_output_delay = T_clock - T_hold_external - T_skew (assumes T_skew confidence 0.8).
data.wrong_way: Using the actual internal clock for IO timing instead of a virtual clock, causing incorrect timing checks at the IO boundary
data.defense: Reference IO timing specifications from the external system and show that virtual clock period matches the external clock specification.
data.signoff_risk: Wrong virtual clock period: IO timing failures at system integration; Incorrect delay calculation: setup/hold violations at IO boundaries
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: IO timing margins tighter due to higher operating frequencies

data.pattern_name: generated_divided_clock_constraint
data.situation: Constraining a clock that is derived from another clock (e.g., divided, gated, or multiplied)
data.derivation: Use create_generated_clock -source [master_clock_pin] -divide_by N -name derived_clock. Add clock uncertainty: T_uncertainty = T_jitter_master + T_jitter_derived + margin (assumes T_jitter_master confidence 0.8, T_jitter_derived confidence 0.7, margin 10% of derived period confidence 0.6). Set clock latency based on divider logic delay.
data.wrong_way: Treating the derived clock as an independent primary clock, ignoring its relationship to the master clock, leading to incorrect timing analysis
data.defense: Show the clock tree structure and the divider logic. Reference the clock generation RTL and synthesis reports to confirm the division ratio and latency.
data.signoff_risk: Incorrect division ratio: wrong timing analysis for all paths using this clock; Missing uncertainty: setup/hold failures due to unaccounted jitter
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock dividers more commonly implemented as part of clock network, requiring tighter uncertainty modeling

data.pattern_name: asynchronous_interface_constraint
data.situation: Constraining an interface between two blocks with no clock relationship (asynchronous)
data.derivation: Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clock1} -group {clock2}. For data transfer, insert handshake logic (e.g., request/acknowledge) and constrain the paths as false or multicycle. For synchronizers: use N-stage synchronizers with MTBF calculation: MTBF = (T_clock * 2^N) / (2 * T_metastability * T_frequency) (assumes T_metastability confidence 0.7).
data.wrong_way: Not using asynchronous clock groups, causing the timer to check paths between the domains and report false violations or miss real metastability issues
data.defense: Reference interface specification documenting the asynchronous nature. Show handshake RTL and synchronizer design that ensures safe data transfer.
data.signoff_risk: Missing asynchronous group: false timing errors and wasted optimization effort; Incorrect synchronizer constraints: metastability in functional logic
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: higher operating frequencies require more robust handshake and synchronizer designs

data.pattern_name: inter_block_timing_budgeting_pre_implementation
data.situation: Allocating timing budgets between two blocks that have not been implemented yet, during architecture phase
data.derivation: Calculate available time: T_available = T_clock - T_skew (assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7) - T_margin (assumes 20% of T_clock confidence 0.6). Allocate to blocks based on complexity: T_block1 = T_available * (complexity_block1 / total_complexity), where complexity is estimated from gate count and logic depth (assumes complexity estimation confidence 0.7).
data.wrong_way: Allocating equal timing budgets to both blocks regardless of their complexity, leading to one block being impossible to implement while the other has excessive slack
data.defense: Present block complexity estimates based on architectural specifications and historical data from similar designs. Justify the proportional allocation with expected gate counts and pipeline depths.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight for complex block: impossible timing closure; Too loose for simple block: wasted power and area due to over-optimization
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more accurate early complexity estimates possible due to better synthesis correlation

data.pattern_name: clock_latency_budgeting
data.situation: Accounting for clock network delay when deriving path timing constraints
data.derivation: Measure clock latency (T_latency) from clock tree synthesis. Derive available time for data path: T_data = T_clock - T_latency - T_skew (assumes T_skew confidence 0.8) - T_margin (assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7). Allocate T_data to combinational logic based on path criticality.
data.wrong_way: Ignoring clock latency in timing budget, or double-counting it by including it in both clock and data path constraints, leading to incorrect timing analysis
data.defense: Reference clock tree synthesis reports showing actual latency values. Show that clock latency is only subtracted once from the clock period in the timing budget.
data.signoff_risk: Underestimated latency: setup violations due to insufficient time for data path; Overestimated latency: unnecessary pessimism leading to over-constrained design
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock network latency more predictable due to better modeling, but more sensitive to process variations

data.pattern_name: uncertainty_allocation_in_derived_clocks
data.situation: Allocating clock uncertainty budgets for clocks with jitter and margin requirements
data.derivation: For a derived clock: T_uncertainty = T_jitter_source + T_jitter_derived + T_margin (assumes T_jitter_source confidence 0.8, T_jitter_derived confidence 0.7, T_margin 15% of clock period confidence 0.6). Subtract T_uncertainty from available time: T_available = T_clock - T_uncertainty - T_skew. Allocate remaining to data path.
data.wrong_way: Using the same uncertainty value for all clocks regardless of their source and derivation, leading to either over- or under-constrained paths
data.defense: Reference clock source specifications (e.g., PLL jitter specs) and jitter measurements from silicon data. Show that uncertainty values are specific to each clock domain.
data.signoff_risk: Too little uncertainty: timing failures due to unaccounted jitter; Too much uncertainty: over-constrained design with unnecessary power/area overhead
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock jitter more significant due to higher frequencies, requiring more precise uncertainty modeling

assumptions_invoked: Full EUR 10000 is drawn at t=0.
The EUR 100 arrangement fee is paid at t=0 and included as a charge at t=0, equivalently net proceeds are EUR 9900.
Repayments are monthly at times k/12 for k=1..24.
X is an effective annual rate; monthly discounting uses (1+X)^(-1/12).
Overdraft additional assumption: the full EUR 3000 limit is drawn immediately.
Overdraft duration is assumed to be 3 months because the overdraft is repayable on demand / not determinable.
Borrowing rate 12% nominal per annum charged monthly gives EUR 30 interest each month on the EUR 3000 drawn balance.
The EUR 25 monthly account fee and the EUR 30 monthly interest are paid as charged at months 1, 2 and 3; principal is repaid at month 3.
Open-end credit additional assumption: the EUR 1500 limit is drawn immediately in full.

Repayment is assumed in 12 equal monthly instalments; source-logic: where open-end credit has no fixed repayment schedule, the directive's additional assumptions close the balance over 12 monthly instalments.
Instalment amount is computed using the stated borrowing rate 18% nominal per annum compounded monthly, i.e. i=0.015 per month.
No fees or charges other than interest.
Drawdown timing is unascertainable, so under the additional assumption the full EUR 5000 is deemed drawn immediately at t=0.
Repayment is a single payment at 12 months as specified.
Nominal rate 8% is applied for one year; no monthly compounding is specified.
The EUR 200 broker fee is financed into the balance at t=0, so it is added to the amount on which interest accrues and appears in the single final payment, not as a cash charge at t=0.

data.weakest_point: The overdraft case is most likely to diverge: the directive's additional assumptions fix a 3-month duration but do not make fully explicit whether monthly interest and account fees are paid as incurred, capitalised into the balance, or settled at the end; I used paid-as-incurred monthly charges, while capitalisation or end settlement changes the APRC by several tenths. The financed broker fee in case 4 is also timing-sensitive because it defers the charge into the final payment instead of reducing t=0 net proceeds.

data.reasoning: The phrase 'more than 2 percent' establishes a strict inequality (>), so the trigger fires only above 2.00%.
The phrase 'more than 36 months' establishes a strict inequality (>), meaning the trigger fires only at 37 months and above.
The phrase '1.5 or more percentage points' establishes an inclusive inequality (>=), so the trigger fires at 1.50 and above.
The phrase 'does not exceed ... by 2.25 or more' uses an inclusive threshold for the exceedance, meaning exactly 2.25 fails the pass condition.
The phrase 'less than' establishes strict inequalities (<) for both revenue and income, so the test passes only when both are strictly below their respective thresholds.
The phrase 'equal to or greater than' establishes an inclusive inequality (>=), so the safe harbour passes at exactly 16.00% and above.
The phrase 'at least equal to' establishes an inclusive inequality (>=), so the floor requirement passes at exactly 50.00% and above.
The phrase 'equal to or greater than' establishes an inclusive inequality (>=), so the incident threshold is met at the exact minimum and above.

data.weakest_point: Rule 4 (General QM price limit) because the phrasing 'does not exceed ... by 2.25 or more' combines a negative condition with an inclusive threshold, making the exact boundary pass/fail logic prone to misinterpretation without reading the full regulatory context of 12 CFR 1026.43(e)(2).

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Overlay detailed-routing DRC hotspots on fine-grid routing-resource and congestion maps
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see whether failures track local resource deficit rather than global density

first_checks.check: Audit routing blockages, layer restrictions, macro halos, and boundary pin keepouts
first_checks.why_first: artificially removed resources are a common and cheap-to-fix mismatch

first_checks.check: Identify high-fanout, bundled, shielded, or clock-root nets crossing hotspot areas
first_checks.why_first: logical congestion can exist even when placement density looks clean

first_checks.check: Check pin-access layers, via/cut rules, and track assignment constraints at hotspot pins
first_checks.why_first: pin-access DRCs masquerade as congestion and are ruled out by inspection

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily allow routing on suspected blocked or restricted layers and rerun detailed routing on the hotspot region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: blocked-layer or over-reserved-resource cause if DRCs clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: blocked-layer cause is excluded if DRCs remain unchanged

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rip up only the failing nets and reroute them with extra layer or spacing freedom
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: net-specific topology or pin-access problem if the same nets still fail
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: net-specific problem is excluded if DRCs move to different nets as capacity shifts

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce high-fanout net loads by trial buffer/driver splitting or fanout cloning and reroute
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: high-fanout logical congestion if hotspots disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: high-fanout cause is excluded if hotspot geometry and DRCs are unchanged

common_root_causes.cause: routing blockages, layer restrictions, or macro halos removing local tracks
pin-access or via/cut rule bottlenecks at dense pins
high-fanout or bundled nets demanding more local resources than density shows
coarse placement-density metric hiding local routing-resource demand
late ECO nets routed through already saturated regions

data.classic_trap: blaming the detailed router and rerunning it while a blockage, pin rule, or high-fanout net is the real capacity thief
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, cut/via and pin-access rules create local DRCs more often than pure metal-track congestion at 28nm

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Group failing endpoints by clock root, clock tree branch, region, and generated clock
first_checks.why_first: rules out local CTS skew/branch problems before chasing data paths

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS and post-CTS slack and launch/capture insertion delays on the same paths
first_checks.why_first: isolates violations introduced by clock tree from pre-existing long paths

first_checks.check: Inspect clock tree buffer count, insertion delay, max transition, and useful-skew changes
first_checks.why_first: overbuilt or poorly balanced clock trees directly alter setup slack

first_checks.check: Check generated clocks, clock-gating enables, and clock uncertainty settings
first_checks.why_first: constraint mistakes on gated/generated clocks are cheap to verify and common

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with ideal clocks or zero skew and the same data delays
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clock-tree skew/latency issue if setup violations largely clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: clock-tree skew/latency issue is excluded if the same paths still fail by similar amounts

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Report launch versus capture insertion delay for each failing path and flag paths where launch delay grew after CTS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: CTS-induced launch skew if failing paths systematically have excessive launch insertion delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: CTS launch skew is excluded if launch/capture deltas are small and unrelated to failures

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable useful skew or revert to pre-CTS clock targets and rerun timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: useful-skew over-optimization if failures disappear or move to known optimized branches
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: useful-skew over-optimization is excluded if failures are unchanged across unrelated paths

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily reduce clock uncertainty/jitter in a trial timing run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: over-pessimistic or mis-applied uncertainty if slack recovers by order of the uncertainty value
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: uncertainty pessimism is excluded if slack change is small compared with the violation

common_root_causes.cause: pre-existing long data paths exposed by real clock latency
excessive launch insertion delay or adverse skew from CTS
useful skew optimized for placement but invalidated by later CTS/routing
generated clock or clock-gating constraint/latency error
clock max-transition/cap violations causing slow clock edges

data.classic_trap: adding more clock buffers to fix setup, which can worsen skew, hold, and power without fixing the long path
data.node_era_note: below 28nm, on-chip variation and clock uncertainty dominate more of the setup margin than at 28nm

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Group hold failures by common clock branch, clock-gating cell, or CTS buffer chain
first_checks.why_first: a shared branch points to skew imbalance rather than scattered min-delay paths

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS and post-CTS launch/capture insertion delays and skew for failing pairs
first_checks.why_first: CTS skew changes are the most direct hold driver

first_checks.check: Check hold corner, clock uncertainty removal, and min-delay constraints
first_checks.why_first: wrong corner or pessimism can create mass hold failures cheaply

first_checks.check: Look for short-path structures: scan chains, reset paths, clock gating, and same-cycle paths
first_checks.why_first: these are the usual victims when hold fails

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force matched launch/capture insertion delay or zero skew for a trial hold run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: CTS skew imbalance if the majority of hold violations clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: CTS skew imbalance is excluded if violations persist with matched clock delays

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert a small number of delay cells on a representative failing branch and rerun hold
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local minimum-delay deficit if that branch clears without moving failures elsewhere
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: purely local deficit is excluded if new hold failures appear on neighboring branches

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run hold across multiple corners and compare the set of failing endpoints
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: corner/library pessimism or min-corner selection if failures are limited to one corner
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: corner-only issue is excluded if the same endpoints fail at all hold corners

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable automatic hold fixing and compare raw violations to post-fix violations
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hold-fixing iteration problem if previous fixes created new violations downstream
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hold-fixing iteration problem is excluded if raw and fixed violations are essentially the same structural set

common_root_causes.cause: clock skew where launch clock arrives too early relative to capture clock
short same-cycle paths with insufficient minimum delay
hold-fixing adding buffers that create adjacent hold violations
incorrect hold uncertainty or min-delay constraints
clock-gating/reset/scan enable paths with special skew behavior

data.classic_trap: blindly inserting hold buffers until the report is clean while creating new hold or setup problems elsewhere
data.node_era_note: advanced nodes need more hold corners and variation-aware skew margins than 28nm

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay failing timing endpoints on static and dynamic IR-drop maps for the same scenario
first_checks.why_first: spatial correlation is the cheapest confirmation that supply droop matters

first_checks.check: Check power-net connectivity, missing straps/rings/vias, and supply setpoints in the failing region
first_checks.why_first: gross power-delivery opens explain large local drop quickly

first_checks.check: Review activity vectors, clock enable, and simultaneous switching assumptions used for IR analysis
first_checks.why_first: dynamic droop failures can appear only under specific high-current windows

first_checks.check: Compare timing slack with nominal supply versus annotated supply voltage
first_checks.why_first: quantifies how much slack loss is directly due to IR annotation

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with IR-drop annotation disabled or with nominal voltage and compare failing paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR-drop-caused timing if the same endpoints clear or gain significant slack
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR-drop cause is excluded if slack and failing endpoints are essentially unchanged

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce activity or gate clocks in the suspect region and rerun dynamic IR and timing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dynamic current spike if local droop and failures drop sharply
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: dynamic spike is excluded if droop and failures persist under reduced activity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add local decap or strengthen a nearby power strap in a trial floorplan/power mesh and reanalyze
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local power-delivery deficit if local IR and timing improve
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local power-delivery deficit is excluded if IR map changes little and failures remain

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run the same timing at a higher voltage corner with similar constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: voltage-margin-sensitive IR if failures disappear at higher voltage
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: IR margin sensitivity is excluded if failures persist with similar slack loss

common_root_causes.cause: insufficient local power mesh or decap near high-current logic
dynamic current spike from simultaneous clock/data activity
missing or broken power via/strap connection
overly optimistic activity/vector set for IR analysis
power-domain crossing or isolation cell supply modeling error

data.classic_trap: debugging timing constraints path-by-path while all failing endpoints sit in one supply-droop neighborhood
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below has tighter voltage margins and more dynamic-IR sensitivity than 28nm

data.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Sort failing sinks by insertion delay error, clock branch, buffer depth, and distance from root
first_checks.why_first: shows whether divergence is branch-local or global

first_checks.check: Verify clock latency/skew targets, max transition/cap, and useful-skew allowances
first_checks.why_first: unachievable targets are a common non-physical cause

first_checks.check: Inspect routing blockages, macro corridors, NDRs, and pin access along failing clock branches
first_checks.why_first: physical detours are a direct cause of late sinks

first_checks.check: Check clock buffer load/fanout and whether oversized/undersized buffers were chosen
first_checks.why_first: load-driven delay is cheap to spot in the clock report

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun CTS with relaxed max transition/cap and relaxed skew targets while keeping floorplan fixed
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: over-constrained targets if most sinks then meet insertion delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: over-constrained targets are excluded if sinks still diverge similarly

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove clock-routing blockages or allow additional layers for clock trial
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: blockage/detour congestion if insertion-delay spread collapses
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: blockage/detour congestion is excluded if the same branches still miss targets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rebuild only the failing clock branches while freezing the clock root and good branches
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local branch topology/load issue if rebuilt branches meet targets
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local branch issue is excluded if global root/source mismatch remains across branches

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Plot insertion delay versus Manhattan distance for sinks
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: routing detour/blockage if delay grows sharply with distance in specific corridors
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: detour problem is excluded if delay error is scattered independent of distance

common_root_causes.cause: insertion-delay/skew targets too aggressive for floorplan and library
clock branch detours around macros, blockages, or routing restrictions
overloaded clock buffers or unbalanced fanout
poor root location or topology choice
library/buffer delay model mismatch with CTS assumptions

data.classic_trap: tuning skew targets repeatedly while ignoring that floorplan obstacles make the target physically unreachable
data.node_era_note: advanced nodes have stricter clock NDRs and variation, so insertion-delay spread is harder to close than at 28nm

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Find the first divergence point in the connectivity comparison and identify the mismatched net/port boundary
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to separate netlist, layout, and extraction boundary issues

first_checks.check: Verify netlist and layout versions, ECO history, and whether the compared sources are synchronized
first_checks.why_first: version mismatch is extremely common and cheap to rule out

first_checks.check: Inspect physical shapes, pins, vias/cuts, and abutment around the mismatched net
first_checks.why_first: real opens/shorts are confirmed visually at the first mismatch

first_checks.check: Review extraction options for short resolution, power/ground recognition, and floating shapes
first_checks.why_first: extraction settings can falsely merge or drop nets

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract with short-detection sensitivity relaxed or with specific net merging disabled and rerun LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: extraction-rule false short if the reported short disappears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extraction-rule false short is excluded if the same short remains

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Manually trace/connect the suspect net in a small layout window and re-extract
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: real open or missing via if connectivity follows the corrected shapes
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: real open is excluded if mismatch remains despite correct visible connectivity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare against the previous known-good layout/netlist pair
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: late ECO/version mismatch if mismatch appears only after the recent change
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: recent change is excluded if the same mismatch existed before the change

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a small-window connectivity extraction with pin/via recognition debug enabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: pin/via recognition issue if shapes are connected but the net remains open
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: recognition issue is excluded if the shapes are visibly disconnected or missing

common_root_causes.cause: netlist/layout version mismatch after ECO
missing via/cut or open contact causing an open net
accidental metal overlap or spacing violation causing a short
extraction rule/options misconfiguration
port/pin name or boundary mismatch between blocks

data.classic_trap: assuming the extractor is wrong before checking version sync and the actual shapes at the first mismatch
data.node_era_note: below 28nm, cut/via rules and multi-patterning make real opens/shorts and extraction sensitivity more likely

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Inspect the first mismatched device instance and compare drawn geometry with netlist parameters
first_checks.why_first: directly shows whether the mismatch is physical or parameter interpretation

first_checks.check: Check device parameter extraction: W, L, fingers, multipliers, and parallel devices
first_checks.why_first: size mismatches often come from equivalent but differently represented parameters

first_checks.check: Verify whether dummy devices, fill transistors, well taps, or guard-ring devices are being extracted
first_checks.why_first: extra devices are commonly non-functional extraction artifacts

first_checks.check: Compare PDK library definitions and LVS rule deck device classes for both sources
first_checks.why_first: device class or property mapping errors cause systematic size/extra-device mismatches

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Dump extracted device parameters for one mismatched instance from layout and netlist sides
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: parameter equivalence issue if W/L/fingers/multipliers differ only by folding or parallel representation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: parameter equivalence issue is excluded if the drawn device geometry itself differs from the netlist intent

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable extraction of dummy/fill/tap devices or tag them as non-electrical and rerun LVS
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dummy/fill recognition if extra devices disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: dummy/fill recognition is excluded if extra devices remain and are electrically connected

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Regenerate the netlist from the latest schematic and rerun against unchanged layout
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: stale netlist/ECO mismatch if mismatches clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: stale netlist is excluded if mismatches persist with a fresh netlist

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run the same layout through another rule deck or PDK version
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule deck/device definition issue if only one deck reports mismatches
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule deck issue is excluded if all decks report the same device mismatches

common_root_causes.cause: stale netlist or unpropagated ECO
dummy/fill/guard devices extracted but absent from netlist
device multiplier/finger/parallel parameter interpretation mismatch
PDK or rule-deck device class/property mapping error
manual layout edit changing device geometry

data.classic_trap: treating every extra extracted device as a real circuit transistor instead of checking dummy/fill/tap extraction
data.node_era_note: advanced nodes have more required dummy/fill and device-array rules, so extra-device LVS noise is more common than at 28nm

data.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Group antenna violations by net, layer, and connected gate count
first_checks.why_first: antenna is ratio-based, so clustering identifies systematic routing or rule issues

first_checks.check: Check antenna rule calculation mode, layer-specific limits, and signoff options
first_checks.why_first: wrong calculation mode can create broad false failures

first_checks.check: Identify long routes on lower metal layers feeding small gates
first_checks.why_first: that pattern is the classic physical antenna cause

first_checks.check: Review jumper, layer-hop, and diode insertion strategy for failing nets
first_checks.why_first: fix strategy availability determines whether violations are design or flow gaps

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun antenna signoff with alternate calculation mode or temporary rule relaxation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule/signoff-setup issue if most violations disappear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule/signoff-setup issue is excluded if the same nets fail under reasonable rule modes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert layer jumpers or reroute a sample of failing nets to higher metal and recheck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: route-layer antenna collection if sample violations clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: route-layer collection is excluded if violations persist despite legal layer hops

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add protection diodes or enable diode insertion on a sample of failing gates and recheck
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: gate protection deficit if diode insertion clears violations
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: gate protection deficit is excluded if violations remain after diodes are legal and connected

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare antenna report before and after late routing ECOs
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: late ECO routing if new violations trace to recently changed nets
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: late ECO cause is excluded if violations existed before the ECOs

common_root_causes.cause: long lower-metal routes collecting charge on small gates
missing jumpers or layer hops in routing strategy
high-fanout nets with large metal-to-gate area ratios
antenna signoff rules or calculation mode set too strictly
late ECO routes creating new antenna patterns

data.classic_trap: treating antenna violations like ordinary spacing DRCs and clearing metal without fixing the collected charge/gate ratio
data.node_era_note: advanced nodes with thinner oxides and stricter antenna limits need more jumpers/diodes than 28nm

data.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Map hotspots to pins, vias/cuts, blockages, NDRs, and layer boundaries
first_checks.why_first: detailed DRCs usually originate at access and rule boundaries, not global capacity

first_checks.check: Check local track utilization and layer-specific demand at the hotspot grids
first_checks.why_first: global routing can miss layer-local track exhaustion

first_checks.check: Review via/cut spacing, end-of-line, min-area, and patterning/coloring constraints
first_checks.why_first: advanced rules create hotspots even with enough nominal tracks

first_checks.check: Inspect pin shapes, pin layers, and allowed access directions
first_checks.why_first: pin access choices often dictate detailed-route legality

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun detailed routing with additional pin-access layers/directions or slightly enlarged legal pin shapes
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: pin-access bottleneck if hotspot DRCs clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pin-access bottleneck is excluded if DRCs remain with more access freedom

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily relax one suspected rule class, such as via/cut spacing or NDR shielding, in a trial run
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: rule-specific bottleneck if that hotspot class disappears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: rule-specific bottleneck is excluded if hotspots remain despite the relaxed rule

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rip up and reroute only hotspot nets with different layer bias or spacing
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local net interaction if only those nets clear
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: local net interaction is excluded if DRCs shift to adjacent nets, indicating shared capacity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare global-routing congestion estimate with detailed DRC locations at the same grids
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: global-underestimation/pin-access modeling gap if global is clean but detailed DRCs cluster at pins
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global-underestimation is excluded if both global estimate and detailed DRCs show the same congestion

common_root_causes.cause: pin-access or via/cut rule conflicts
local track exhaustion near macros, pins, or blockages
advanced patterning/coloring or spacing rules
global routing resource model underestimating detailed-route demand
NDR/shielding constraints consuming local routing resources

data.classic_trap: assuming clean global routing means no congestion and rerunning detailed routing without changing access, rules, or layer bias
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, detailed DRCs are often cut/coloring/pattern-rule driven rather than simple metal-spacing driven as at 28nm

data.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check fine-grid placement density and overflow by region, not just total utilization
first_checks.why_first: local density above legal capacity is the most direct placer divergence cause

first_checks.check: Audit macro locations, halos, keepouts, placement blockages, and well/tap rule areas
first_checks.why_first: unusable reserved area can make legal placement impossible even at moderate total density

first_checks.check: Review cell inflation factors from congestion, timing, or useful-skew optimization
first_checks.why_first: inflation can silently turn a legal density into an unroutable one

first_checks.check: Inspect fixed pins, IO/IP boundaries, and channel widths between macros
first_checks.why_first: narrow corridors are common sources of overflow and routing failure

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Lower the placement density target or allow temporary overflow in a trial global placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: density/inflation pressure if placement converges at lower target
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: density pressure is excluded if it still diverges with ample nominal slack

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax or shrink macro halos/keepouts in a trial floorplan and rerun placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: halo/keepout over-reservation if overflow clears
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: halo/keepout over-reservation is excluded if overflow remains in the same regions

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Freeze macros and disable timing-driven inflation/useful skew, then place standard cells only
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro/floorplan bottleneck if standard cells place cleanly with macros moved or constraints relaxed
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: macro/floorplan bottleneck is excluded if standard cells still overflow with realistic fixed macros

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run global placement with routing-resource demand deflated or routing congestion optimization disabled
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: over-aggressive congestion/timing objectives if placement converges
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: congestion objective issue is excluded if placement still overflows with deflated demand

common_root_causes.cause: local placement density exceeding legal capacity
macro halos/keepouts/blockages removing usable area
poor macro placement creating narrow channels
over-aggressive cell inflation for congestion or timing
insufficient routing layers/tracks for the net demand in advanced nodes

data.classic_trap: iterating placer/router options while the floorplan still contains a local density or macro-corridor impossibility
data.node_era_note: below 28nm, lower usable density targets and more well/tap/coloring keepouts make placement overflow appear earlier

data.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budget
data.situation: A block has synchronous inputs/outputs to an external device or another block, and the SDC must say how much delay lives outside the block boundary.
data.derivation: 1. Identify interface period P and capture clock relationship. 2. For an input, set_input_delay -max = external driver tco_max + interconnect_max + clock-offset_max + margin M; set_input_delay -min = external driver tco_min + interconnect_min + clock-offset_min - hold guard H. M is often 5% of P in early specs (confidence 0.4); H is often 0 unless min external delay is uncertain (confidence 0.5). 3. Verify feasibility: input_delay_max + worst internal input-to-flop delay + setup + clock uncertainty <= P. 4. For an output, set_output_delay -max = interconnect_max + downstream receiver input delay_max + clock-offset_max + M; the internal launch-to-port budget is then P - receiver_setup - output_delay_max - clock uncertainty. 5. For hold, check output_delay_min + min internal launch-to-port delay >= receiver hold.
data.wrong_way: Picking input/output delay as an arbitrary fraction of the period, or zero, without external timing data. This silently moves the impossible delay into the neighboring block or hides it entirely, so the block may pass standalone but fail at system integration.
data.defense: External device datasheet tco/setup/hold values, board trace length or package delay estimate, clock relationship diagram, and a margin register showing the negotiated M.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: the block fails internally on unrealistic port budgets and wastes area/power fixing paths that are not the system problem. Too loose: the block signoff is clean but the interface fails on board or at integration.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, clock uncertainty and derate consume a larger fraction of the period, leaving less room for arbitrary IO margin than at 28nm

data.pattern_name: False path versus multicycle path by architectural qualification
data.situation: A path is slow or crosses control logic, and the team wants a timing exception: reset paths, config paths, slow enables, pipelined buses, mode logic.
data.derivation: 1. Enumerate functional modes and prove whether launch and capture can ever occur with a same-cycle timing requirement. If no functional relationship exists, use a false path. 2. If the architecture intentionally allows N destination cycles, use a multicycle path: setup multicycle N. 3. Add the corresponding hold exception, usually N-1, to avoid making hold one cycle too strict; for N=2, set_multicycle_path 2 -setup and set_multicycle_path 1 -hold (confidence in the N-1 idiom 0.8). 4. Qualify the exception with mode pins, through points, or case conditions, then verify no bypass path defeats the qualification.
data.wrong_way: Declaring a false path because the path fails timing, or declaring a multicycle path without proving the enable/protocol actually spans N cycles. The silent break is loss of coverage: real functional paths are no longer checked, or hold becomes impossible because the hold exception was omitted.
data.defense: RTL waveforms showing the N-cycle enable, reset sequence, register write protocol, mode-pin truth table, and a search showing all alternate paths are qualified or excluded.
data.signoff_risk: Too broad: real timing relationships are unchecked and can cause functional corruption. Too narrow or missing: unnecessary timing failures and wasted fixing on architecturally relaxed paths.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous clock-domain boundary with controlled exceptions
data.situation: Two clock domains are unrelated in frequency or phase, and signals cross between them through synchronizers or handshakes.
data.derivation: 1. Prove the clocks are truly asynchronous: independent sources, unlocked PLLs, or no fixed divider/phase relationship. 2. At the domain boundary, remove meaningless setup/hold checks with set_clock_groups -asynchronous or equivalent false paths, but only after listing all crossing points. 3. Where a control path into a synchronizer needs bounded latency for protocol reasons, do not false-path that segment; constrain it with set_max_delay -datapath_only. A common budget is max_delay = N_resolve * T_dest - setup_dest - uncertainty_dest - margin M, where N_resolve is often 1 or 2 destination cycles (confidence 0.5) and M is often 5% to 10% of T_dest (confidence 0.4). 4. Keep destination-domain synchronizer flop-to-flop paths timed normally, and constrain asynchronous resets separately.
data.wrong_way: Blanket set_clock_groups between all clocks, including derived or phase-related clocks, or false-pathing CDC paths without checking that a synchronizer and handshake actually bound the transfer. This silently removes timing on paths that are synchronous or need a latency bound.
data.defense: Clock tree topology, PLL/divider analysis, CDC lint results, synchronizer schematic, and waveform or protocol proof that the crossing is asynchronous and resolved.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose: real synchronous paths or insufficient CDC latency are unchecked, causing metastability or protocol failure. Too tight: false failures on asynchronous paths and wasted fixing.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below jitter and variation make synchronizer setup and resolution margins less forgiving than at 28nm

data.pattern_name: Pre-implementation interface budget allocation
data.situation: Two blocks have not yet been implemented, but floorplan and integration need boundary timing budgets to prevent later surprises.
data.derivation: 1. Start with period P, receiver setup S, and expected clock uncertainty U. 2. Estimate interconnect delay W from floorplan distance: W = length_est * wire_delay_per_mm, using historical order-of wire delay (confidence 0.4). 3. Reserve integration margin M, often 10% of P before floorplan matures (confidence 0.4). 4. Compute remaining slack R = P - S - U - W - M. 5. Split R between sender internal logic and receiver input logic; a common unknown split is 50/50 (confidence 0.3), or skew toward the more complex receiver. 6. Translate to SDC: at the sender output, set_output_delay max = W + receiver_budget + M, which leaves the sender internal budget as P - S - U - W - receiver_budget - M.
data.wrong_way: Using a fixed 50% period split with zero interconnect delay, or double-counting the same wire delay in both blocks. The silent break appears at integration: one block is blamed for a path that was impossible from the first budget.
data.defense: Floorplan distance, historical wire delay per mm, repeater plan, protocol latency, prior implementation data, and a written margin register that shows what was reserved and why.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: blocks chase impossible boundary timing, causing schedule slip and over-optimization. Too loose: interface timing fails late, forcing expensive cross-block ECOs.
data.node_era_note: advanced nodes make wire and repeater estimates more uncertain, so early budgets need more frequent re-correlation than at 28nm

data.pattern_name: Stage margin and planned relaxation
data.situation: Early implementation has poor parasitics, no final clock tree, and unknown skew, but timing-driven implementation still needs targets.
data.derivation: 1. Estimate stage uncertainty: pre-route wire load, missing clock skew, extraction approximation. 2. Add setup margin M_stage, often 5% to 15% of period or order of 100ps for GHz-class clocks (confidence 0.4), via clock uncertainty, derate, or additional path margin. 3. Track timing correlation after each stage: post-CTS, post-route, extracted parasitics. 4. Relax the margin in steps matched to measured correlation, for example removing part after CTS when skew becomes real and more after final extraction (confidence in stepwise relaxation 0.35). 5. Stop relaxing only when signoff parasitics, corners, and clock models are frozen.
data.wrong_way: Leaving the early overconstraint in place at signoff, or relaxing it before real parasitics and clock skew exist. The first causes false failures and wasted fixing; the second allows implementation to converge to a design that later fails.
data.defense: Historical stage-to-signoff correlation data, slack trend reports, a named margin register, and explicit approval for each relaxation step.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight at signoff: false timing failures, unnecessary ECO, higher power/area. Too loose early: false convergence and late signoff timing escape.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below extraction and variation uncertainty usually require more staged margin discipline than 28nm

data.pattern_name: Virtual clock for external or missing IO clock
data.situation: IO timing must be constrained against an external clock that does not exist as a net inside the block, or the board clock is not routed to the constrained boundary.
data.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock with the external interface period P_ext. If duty cycle is unknown, assume 50% initially (confidence 0.5), then check edge-sensitive protocols for other waveform assumptions. 2. Derive phase offset from the protocol if specified; otherwise use conservative zero phase and verify both edge relationships if possible. 3. Apply set_input_delay or set_output_delay relative to the virtual clock using external timing specs: max = tco_max or equivalent + board/package delay_max + margin M; min = tco_min + board/package delay_min. M is often 5% of P_ext early (confidence 0.4). 4. If the internal sampling clock is different, explicitly constrain the relationship between the virtual clock and internal clock as asynchronous, source-synchronous, or max/min bounded.
data.wrong_way: Using an internal clock as if it were the external clock when phase, frequency, or jitter are not the same. This creates false synchronous timing relationships and can make signoff pass while the board interface fails.
data.defense: Protocol specification, external device datasheet, eye-diagram or timing-budget spreadsheet, board delay estimate, and explicit statement of why the virtual clock model matches the interface.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: internal IO logic is over-optimized against a fictitious clock relationship. Too loose: real external timing problems are not checked and escape to board bring-up.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Generated/divided clock edge and latency derivation
data.situation: A clock is produced inside the design by a divider, mux, PLL output, or gated clock and must be constrained as a generated clock.
data.derivation: 1. Identify the master clock, division ratio or edge sequence, and the exact pin/net where the generated clock is defined. 2. For divide-by-N, the generated period is N * master_period; if duty cycle is not simple, specify explicit edges rather than only a divide factor (N from RTL is usually high confidence 0.8). 3. Include divider propagation latency in the generated clock path, either through the generated clock definition or by ensuring the divider cell delay is in the timing graph. 4. Decide master-to-generated relationship: if fixed phase, let timing checks relate edges; if the generated clock can be async or glitchy due to mux/reset, constrain the mux or add false/group exceptions only after proving no functional path.
data.wrong_way: Creating a generated clock with the wrong divide value or default waveform, or false-pathing master-to-divided clock paths because they look separate. The silent break is incorrect setup/hold relationships: paths may be checked against the wrong capture edge or not checked at all.
data.defense: RTL divider waveform, edge count, reset/mux behavior, clock topology diagram, and a check that the generated clock edges match simulation or static clock graph reports.
data.signoff_risk: Wrong period/phase too tight: false failures and useless fixing. Wrong period/phase too loose: real timing across divided or muxed clocks escapes to silicon.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous handshake latency budget
data.situation: A request/acknowledge, valid/ready, or FIFO interface crosses unrelated clock domains and timing cannot be checked as a normal synchronous path.
data.derivation: 1. Identify the handshake protocol and the minimum required pulse or acknowledge window in the destination domain. For a pulse crossing a two-flop synchronizer, the minimum width is often 2 destination cycles (confidence 0.5). 2. Bound the combinational delay into the first synchronizer flop: set_max_delay -datapath_only = min_window - setup_sync - uncertainty_dest - margin M, with M often 5% of destination period (confidence 0.4). 3. False-path or group the asynchronous relationship only for segments that are truly protocol-bounded; keep destination-domain synchronizer and logic paths timed normally. 4. For multibit handshakes, constrain relative bit skew or use Gray-coded pointers; the skew budget should be less than one destination cycle minus setup and margin (confidence 0.4).
data.wrong_way: False-pathing the entire handshake because it is asynchronous, without proving pulse width, synchronizer depth, or bit-skew behavior. The silent break is missed pulses, FIFO overflow/underflow, or sampling an invalid multibit value.
data.defense: Handshake protocol spec, FIFO/synchronizer design details, waveforms showing minimum pulse width, CDC lint structure checks, and proof that multibit transfers are Gray-coded or mux-synchronized.
data.signoff_risk: Too loose: asynchronous protocol failures that are invisible to ordinary timing signoff. Too tight: false timing failures on paths that are architecturally resolved by the handshake.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below metastability and jitter make handshake pulse-width margins more important than at 28nm

data.title: Integrate two processor cores on one POWER4 chip
data.decision: Make the basic POWER4 processor a single chip containing two complete processor cores.
data.rationale: The paper presents dual-core integration as a way to increase processor density and system throughput while staying within practical chip, power, and packaging limits.
data.outcome: POWER4 became a dual-core chip and the core building block for POWER4 systems.
data.weakest_point: The stated rationale wording may be inferred rather than quoted; the paper may not explicitly discuss rejected single-core alternatives.

data.title: Use an eight-processor MCM building block
data.decision: Package four dual-core POWER4 chips, with associated cache chips, in a multichip module as the basic eight-processor building block.
data.rationale: The paper describes the MCM as a way to obtain high processor density and short, fast chip-to-chip interconnects in a scalable building block.
data.outcome: The MCM provided an eight-core building block from which larger POWER4 systems could be constructed.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly gives the short-interconnect rationale or simply describes the MCM configuration.

data.title: Balance clock frequency with instructions-per-cycle
data.decision: Design for high frequency but keep the pipeline and microarchitecture balanced so that IPC is not sacrificed solely for frequency.
data.rationale: The paper's design discussion treats frequency as an important lever for performance, but not one to be pursued in isolation from useful work per cycle and system balance.
data.outcome: The resulting POWER4 microarchitecture combined a wide out-of-order core with a high-frequency design target.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly frames this as a trade-off decision rather than simply describing the chosen pipeline and frequency.

data.title: Make RAS features pervasive in the POWER4 system
data.decision: Include error detection, correction, logging, and serviceability mechanisms across caches, buses, memory, and logic.
data.rationale: The paper presents RAS as necessary for enterprise-class availability, fault containment, and field service in POWER4 systems.
data.outcome: POWER4 systems include ECC/parity/redundancy/error-handling features intended to reduce failures and downtime.
data.weakest_point: The exact list of mechanisms and whether the paper uses the term 'pervasive' may be generalized.

data.title: Provide hardware-coherent shared-memory interconnect for scaling
data.decision: Use a coherent shared-memory interconnect so multiple POWER4 chips/MCMs can operate as a single SMP system.
data.rationale: The paper treats hardware coherence and a shared-address-space model as the way to scale processor count while preserving SMP usability.
data.outcome: POWER4 chips/MCMs can be connected into larger cache-coherent shared-memory systems.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper frames this as an explicit design decision or simply describes the coherent interconnect implementation.

assumptions_invoked: Actuarial method: PV of drawdowns = PV of repayments+charges, discounted at monthly periods, then annualized via (1+i_month)^12 - 1

The €100 arrangement fee, paid at conclusion (t=0), is treated as DEDUCTED from the loan proceeds actually made available to the consumer — net amount drawn down used in the equation is €10,000 - €100 = €9,900, while the repayment schedule (24 × €450) remains based on the full €10,000 nominal principal
Repayments of €450 occur at t=1,2,...,24 months (ordinary annuity, first payment one month after drawdown, as stated)
data.iterations: Iter1: i=0.0060 -> annuity factor f(i)=(1-(1+i)^-24)/i = 22.286 (target factor = 9900/450 = 22.000, too high). Iter2: i=0.0070 -> f(i)=22.022 (still slightly high). Iter3: i=0.0072 -> f(i)=21.968 (now too low). Linear interpolation between iter2/iter3 gives i≈0.007082. Convergence check: f(0.007082)=22.001 ≈ 22.000 (residual 0.001, accepted). Converged monthly i≈0.7082%.

assumptions_invoked: Duration of the overdraft assumed to be 3 months, per the case's explicit instruction (note: this is NOT the CCD Annex I default assumption of 1 year for credit without a fixed duration — the case text directed a 3-month assumption, which is followed here rather than the directive's own general default)
Full credit limit (€3,000) treated as drawn down at t=0 and outstanding for the entire 3-month assumed duration, per the directive's additional assumption for undetermined drawdown patterns
12% nominal per annum charged monthly = 1.00% monthly rate, compounding monthly onto the outstanding balance
€25 monthly account fee assumed payable at the end of each month (t=1,2,3 in months), i.e. concurrently with any interest settlement at t=3
Single balloon repayment of principal + compounded interest at t=3 (end of assumed duration), since no interim principal repayment schedule is specified
data.iterations: Iter1: i=0.0100 -> PV=24.7525+24.5074+3024.35=3073.61 (target 3000, too high, PV must fall). Iter2: i=0.0200 -> PV=24.5098+24.0292+2936.66=2985.20 (now too low). Iter3: i=0.0181 -> PV=24.5556+24.1189+2953.58=3002.25 (slightly high). Refine: i=0.0183 -> PV=24.5507+24.1094+2950.85=2999.51 (slightly low). Convergence check: interpolating between iter3(0.0181) and the 0.0183 trial gives i≈0.018264, PV≈3000.0 (residual <0.3, accepted).

assumptions_invoked: Full €1,500 limit drawn immediately (stated in case)

Repayment structure of 12 equal monthly instalments is an assumed simplification for this worked case (source-logic: mirrors the directive's general fallback of assuming a plausible, fully-amortizing repayment schedule when the actual open-end repayment pattern is not otherwise specified) — this is NOT a specific numbered CCD Annex I assumption being cited, but a constructed convention for tractability
18% nominal per annum, monthly compounding = 1.5% monthly rate, applied uniformly to both the amortization schedule and the discounting rate
No fees or charges other than interest, so the equal instalment is exactly the standard amortizing-loan payment at the same rate used for discounting
data.equation: 1500 = A * [1-(1.015)^-12]/0.015, where A is solved as the standard annuity payment: A = 1500*0.015/[1-(1.015)^-12] = 137.52; since drawdown and repayment side are both built from i=0.015 by construction, APRC = (1.015)^12 - 1 directly
data.iterations: No iterative root-finding required: because the instalment amount A was derived directly from the stated 1.5%-monthly rate as a standard amortization formula, the PV equation is satisfied exactly at i=0.015 by construction (closed-form; residual = 0 by definition). Convergence check: substituting i=0.015 back into the PV equation reproduces 1500 exactly (verified algebraically, not iteratively).

assumptions_invoked: Full €5,000 limit drawn down at t=0, assumed because the case specifies an 'unascertainable drawdown timing/pattern,' and the directive's general fallback in such cases is to assume the maximum/full amount is drawn immediately (a conservative, fully-drawn assumption analogous to the overdraft full-drawdown convention)

Rate of 8% nominal per annum applied as simple annual compounding over the single 12-month period (since there is only one compounding interval between drawdown and the single repayment, nominal annual and effective annual coincide here)

The €200 broker fee is FINANCED into the balance: it is added to the outstanding principal (5000+200=5200) at t=0 and therefore itself accrues interest at 8% for the year, but it is NOT part of the amount actually made available to the consumer for their own use — so the 'amount of credit' on the drawdown side of the APRC equation remains €5,000, while the repayment side is based on the grown 5200 balance
data.iterations: No iterative solving required: single drawdown / single repayment pair gives a closed-form solution. (1+X) = 5616/5000 = 1.1232, so X = 0.1232. Convergence check: substituting X=0.1232 back gives 5616/1.1232 = 5000.0 exactly (verified algebraically).

data.financed_vs_cash_fee_note: Contrast for case 4: a financed fee is added to the principal balance and therefore compounds at the credit's own interest rate for the full period before being repaid, inflating the total repayment (5200*1.08=5616) while leaving the discounted drawdown side unchanged at 5000. A t=0 CASH fee instead reduces the net amount actually drawn down (e.g. 5000-200=4800) while the repayment obligation is computed on the original undiminished principal (5000*1.08=5400) — giving a different equation (4800 = 5400*(1+X)^-1, X=0.125=12.5%) and a different APRC (12.5% vs 12.3%) even though the fee amount and nominal rate are identical, because in the financed case the fee itself earns interest for the period whereas in the cash case it does not.

data.weakest_point: The single largest source of potential divergence from the directive's exact prescribed method is the fee-treatment convention chosen in cases 1 and 4 (whether an upfront/financed fee reduces the net drawdown, is added to the repayment stream, or is added to the accruing principal) — the CCD Annex I text is prescriptive about which convention applies to which fee type, and this computation applied a self-consistent but explicitly-chosen convention rather than one confirmed against the annex's literal fee-classification rules. Secondary risk: case 2's fee-timing assumption (fees paid at month-end, interest compounding monthly rather than simple) and its use of a 3-month duration (as instructed, not the directive's own general 1-year default) are both assumptions of convenience rather than verified annex-mandated treatments.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Global route congestion map (overflow histogram) overlaid on layout
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to localize hotspots beyond what density alone shows

first_checks.check: Pin density / pin access map in the same hotspot regions
first_checks.why_first: local pin clustering often drives congestion even when overall density is fine

first_checks.check: Macro/blockage placement and channel widths near hotspots
first_checks.why_first: cheap visual check for pinched routing channels between macros
