first_checks.check: Layer-by-layer routing utilization near hotspot
first_checks.why_first: identifies whether congestion is layer-specific (e.g., one metal layer starved)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run global placement with higher target density / more whitespace only in hotspot region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: congestion drops substantially -> true placement-driven congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: congestion persists -> points to structural (pin/macro) cause, not density

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if hotspot correlates with a specific macro's pin edge or hard IP boundary
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hotspot hugs macro boundary -> macro pin access is root cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hotspot is diffuse across standard-cell area -> not macro-driven

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion map before/after adding routing blockages or halo around macros
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: adding halo relieves congestion -> confirms macro-adjacent routing squeeze
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> macro not the cause

common_root_causes.cause: local pin/cell clustering (e.g., dense mux or bus fanout)
macro placement leaving narrow routing channels
insufficient routing blockage/halo tuning around hard IP
global placement not congestion-aware enough (bad cost function tuning)
over-constrained layer usage (e.g., too many nets forced to lower layers)

data.classic_trap: Assuming overall placement density is the culprit and globally spreading cells, which wastes area/timing without fixing a localized pin-access or macro-channel problem.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, via pillar and multi-patterning restrictions make even moderate congestion much harder to resolve than at 28nm, so hotspots that were fixable by ECO at 28nm may require re-placement at advanced nodes

data.symptom: setup (max-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS (ideal clock) vs post-CTS timing on the same paths
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see how much of the violation is clock-latency-induced vs pre-existing

first_checks.check: Check clock insertion delay and skew on the failing path's launch/capture pins
first_checks.why_first: directly shows if CTS introduced adverse skew

first_checks.check: Check for useful-skew opportunities already consumed or CTS target mismatches
first_checks.why_first: quick check on whether skew scheduling was applied as intended

first_checks.check: Physical location/routing detour of the failing data path post-CTS buffering
first_checks.why_first: CTS buffer insertion can push data-path cells or add routing detours

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-time the path with post-CTS actual clock latencies but zero skew (idealized) applied manually
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation disappears -> skew/latency from CTS is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation remains -> underlying data path is the bottleneck, not CTS

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing endpoints cluster around specific clock-tree branch/leaf regions
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clustering around one branch -> local CTS imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: failures spread randomly across the design -> more likely global data-path or library/timing-derate issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare setup slack at same corner pre- and post-clock-tree optimization (CTS opt) step
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: large slack recovery after CTS-opt indicates skew scheduling not yet converged
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change indicates true logic/interconnect delay problem

common_root_causes.cause: clock skew/latency changes from real (non-ideal) clock tree vs ideal clock used during placement
long/high-fanout data paths with insufficient buffering
routing detours introduced by CTS buffer placement obstructing data nets
overly pessimistic OCV/derate applied uniformly post-CTS
useful skew not yet exploited by the CTS engine

data.classic_trap: Blaming 'CTS made it worse' and re-running clock tree synthesis repeatedly, when the real issue is a marginal data path that was always going to fail once ideal-clock optimism was removed.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, useful-skew based CTS optimization is much more aggressively used to close setup than at 28nm, where designers more often just fix the data path instead

data.symptom: hold (min-delay) violations after CTS

first_checks.check: Check whether violations are widespread (many short paths) vs isolated to specific register clusters
first_checks.why_first: cheap categorization that quickly narrows between global CTS/skew issue vs local path issue

first_checks.check: Clock skew between launch and capture flops on failing paths
first_checks.why_first: hold violations are extremely sensitive to skew, so this is the first physical suspect

first_checks.check: Check if violating paths are between different clock domains or clock-gating boundaries
first_checks.why_first: cheap structural check since domain crossings are classic hold-violation sources

first_checks.check: Review hold-fixing buffer insertion history/logs from the tool
first_checks.why_first: reveals whether hold-fix cells were already attempted and exhausted in that region

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Set clock skew to zero (ideal) for the failing launch/capture pair and re-check hold
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation persists at zero skew -> genuine min-delay/data-path issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation disappears -> skew is the true cause, driven by CTS

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing paths all cross the same clock-gate/ICG cell or same clock-tree branch merge point
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: common branch/ICG confirmed -> local CTS structural imbalance
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no common structure -> distributed root cause, likely data-path or library issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare hold slack at fast (min) corner with and without on-chip variation derating for clock paths
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hold recovers substantially without derate -> excessive clock-path pessimism is inflating the violation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> not a derating artifact

common_root_causes.cause: clock skew between launch/capture flops introduced by real clock tree
short/fast data paths (e.g., adjacent flops with minimal logic)
clock domain crossing or divider/gating boundary mismatch
excessive OCV/derate pessimism on clock paths vs data paths
hold buffers inserted but themselves subject to variation causing residual violations

data.classic_trap: Blindly inserting delay/hold buffers everywhere a violation shows up without checking for a common skew source, causing area/power bloat and sometimes creating new setup risk.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, hold fixing is far more painful because buffer delay is smaller relative to variation, often requiring many more cells and iterations than at 28nm

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Static/dynamic IR-drop map correlated against the failing timing paths' locations
first_checks.why_first: directly connects the two before deeper analysis

first_checks.check: Power grid density (strap/via count) in the failing region vs rest of chip
first_checks.why_first: cheap visual/structural check for thin power mesh areas

first_checks.check: Switching activity / toggle rate of nearby high-activity logic (e.g., clock buffers, high-fanout drivers)
first_checks.why_first: identifies local current demand spikes causing localized drop

first_checks.check: Decap placement density in the hotspot region
first_checks.why_first: cheap check for missing local charge buffering

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run timing signoff with a flat/derated voltage (no location-based IR-drop map) vs with the IR-drop-aware voltage map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violations appear only with IR-aware analysis -> confirms IR-drop is the driver, not pure delay
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations exist even with flat voltage -> underlying timing margin issue independent of IR

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if failing cells sit specifically on weak power-grid nodes identified in the drop map
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: spatial correlation strong -> power grid weakness confirmed as cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: failing cells are on well-strapped nodes -> IR-drop unlikely to be the driver

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Simulate with reduced local switching activity (vector-based dynamic IR) vs vectorless estimate
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: dynamic (vector-based) shows much worse local drop than vectorless -> activity-driven, not static grid weakness
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: similar in both -> static grid design is the bottleneck, not activity pattern

common_root_causes.cause: thin/insufficient power straps or via density in a local region
localized high switching activity (clock buffers, high-fanout nets) not accounted for in static analysis
insufficient decoupling capacitance near hotspot
package/C4 bump placement causing localized supply starvation
vectorless IR analysis assumptions too optimistic vs real vector-based activity

data.classic_trap: Treating it as a pure timing/library issue and adding buffers or upsizing cells, which increases current draw and can worsen the IR drop instead of fixing it.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, IR-drop signoff is far more central to timing closure and often requires co-optimization with power grid design from the start, unlike 28nm where it's often a late-stage check

data.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: CTS log/report for convergence status and target vs achieved insertion delay per sink group
first_checks.why_first: cheapest direct read of what the tool itself reports as unmet

first_checks.check: Physical distribution of the divergent sinks (clustered vs scattered)
first_checks.why_first: quickly separates a local physical obstruction from a global spec/constraint problem

first_checks.check: Check clock tree exception/constraint file for conflicting skew groups or non-default rules
first_checks.why_first: cheap check for constraint authoring errors before blaming the physical design

first_checks.check: Buffer/inverter library availability and drive-strength options used by CTS in the divergent region
first_checks.why_first: confirms whether the tool had adequate cells to hit the target

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax the insertion-delay/skew target for the divergent sinks and re-run CTS locally
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: convergence achieved easily -> original target was too aggressive for that region's physical constraints
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: still fails even relaxed -> real physical obstruction/blockage issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check routing congestion or blockages specifically along the clock-tree route to the divergent sinks
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: heavy blockage/congestion found on the route -> physical obstruction is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: route is clear -> points to constraint/library issue instead

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare divergent sinks against clock-domain or skew-group boundary definitions
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: divergent sinks all sit at a domain/group boundary -> constraint grouping error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: divergent sinks are mid-domain with no boundary nearby -> not a grouping issue

common_root_causes.cause: physical obstruction/blockage forcing long detours to reach certain sinks
overly aggressive or inconsistent skew/insertion-delay targets set in constraints
sinks physically far outlier from the bulk of the clock domain (e.g., isolated flop)
insufficient buffer drive-strength variety in the library for that region
clock-gating cell or clock-domain crossing structure not modeled correctly in CTS exceptions

data.classic_trap: Repeatedly re-running CTS with minor tweaks hoping it converges, without checking whether the divergent sinks are physical outliers that need floorplan-level intervention (e.g., moving the flop).
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, clock-tree routing resources are scarcer and skew targets tighter, so divergence is more often a true physical/resource problem than at 28nm where it's more often a constraint-authoring issue

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: LVS error summary categorization (missing net vs short vs open count)
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to know which sub-type of failure to chase

first_checks.check: Check if the mismatch correlates with a recent ECO or hand-edit in the netlist/layout
first_checks.why_first: most common trigger, so checking recent changes first is cheap and high-yield

first_checks.check: Layer-vs-layer connectivity check at the flagged coordinates in the layout viewer
first_checks.why_first: directly visualizes whether metal is physically present/connected at that location

first_checks.check: Compare extracted netlist connectivity at the flagged node against schematic/RTL-derived netlist
first_checks.why_first: confirms whether the discrepancy originates in layout extraction or in the reference netlist itself

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the same short/open appears in a clean, unmodified reference/golden layout of the same cell instance
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: does not appear in golden version -> introduced by a local edit/ECO
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: appears in golden version too -> pre-existing library/cell issue, not the edit

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Physically inspect the flagged coordinate for overlapping shapes on adjacent nets vs a genuine gap in intended connection
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: overlapping shapes from two different nets found -> true short
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no overlap, shapes just close but not touching -> false-positive from spacing/rule artifact, not a real short

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the missing-net LVS error corresponds to a filler/tie-cell or dummy metal not intended to connect
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: net is a known non-functional (filler/tap) net -> can be waived as expected mismatch
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: net is a real signal/power net -> genuine connectivity bug

common_root_causes.cause: manual ECO or metal edit that broke or created an unintended connection
via/contact enclosure or missing via causing an open
unconnected/floating filler or tap cell flagged incorrectly
layout-vs-schematic naming/binding mismatch (pin swap or renamed net) rather than a real physical defect
extraction tool setup error (wrong layer stack or connectivity rules)

data.classic_trap: Assuming every reported short is a real physical defect and spending hours in the layout, when it's actually a naming/binding mismatch between schematic and extracted netlist.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, multi-patterning and complex via structures make opens/shorts harder to spot visually and more often require the extraction tool's own diagnostic rather than manual inspection, unlike simpler 28nm stacks

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: LVS property/parameter mismatch report (W/L, finger count, multiplier)
first_checks.why_first: cheapest direct listing of exactly which parameter differs

first_checks.check: Check whether the mismatch is isolated to specific cell instances or an entire cell type across the design
first_checks.why_first: quickly separates a single bad instance from a systemic library/PDK issue

first_checks.check: Compare the library/PDK version or corner used in extraction vs the reference schematic's expected model
first_checks.why_first: common source of systematic size mismatches

first_checks.check: Check for recently added/duplicated devices (e.g., double-instantiated decap or tie cells) at the flagged location
first_checks.why_first: extra-device mismatches are often literal duplicates from automated insertion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Extract the same cell in isolation from a clean library reference and compare device parameters
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: clean extraction matches schematic -> problem introduced downstream (during placement/edit), not in the base cell
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: clean extraction already mismatches -> library/PDK definition issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if the mismatched instances all come from one specific automated insertion step (e.g., filler, decap, or ESD insertion tool run)
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: all extra devices trace to one automated step -> tool/flow duplication bug
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: extra devices are scattered with no common origin -> more likely manual/ECO-introduced

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run extraction with a different device recognition ruleset (e.g., alternate parameter extraction rules) on the flagged instance
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: size mismatch disappears with corrected ruleset -> extraction rule/setup error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: mismatch persists across rulesets -> genuine physical layout size discrepancy

common_root_causes.cause: stale or mismatched PDK/library version between schematic reference and extracted layout
duplicate devices from automated filler/decap/tie-cell insertion re-run
manual sizing edit in schematic not propagated to layout (or vice versa)
device recognition/extraction rule misconfiguration (wrong parameter mapping)
multi-finger device finger-count miscount due to layout generator bug

data.classic_trap: Manually resizing devices in the schematic to match the (wrong) layout extraction to silence LVS, instead of finding the actual duplication or version-skew root cause.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, finFET fin-count/finger parameters add another mismatch dimension not present in planar 28nm devices, making size-mismatch triage more complex

data.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Antenna violation report grouped by net and by metal layer
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to see if violations cluster on specific long nets/layers

first_checks.check: Check ratio of accumulated metal area to gate area on the flagged net
first_checks.why_first: directly identifies how far over the allowed ratio the net is, guiding fix magnitude

first_checks.check: Check if the flagged net already has diode insertion or jumper-layer routing applied
first_checks.why_first: quickly shows if a known fix mechanism just wasn't triggered/placed correctly

first_checks.check: Routing history of the net (was it routed early in a long segment on one layer before via-up)
first_checks.why_first: long single-layer runs before the transistor connects are the classic physical cause

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-route the flagged net with a layer hop (jumper) partway along its length and re-check antenna
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: violation clears -> confirms classic long-wire single-layer antenna accumulation
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation persists -> likely a different accumulation source (e.g., via stack antenna, not wire antenna)

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if violation is only at final signoff extraction but not at earlier ECO-stage antenna check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: only appears late -> a late-stage routing/ECO change introduced it
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: present from early check too -> systemic routing pattern, not a late edit

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert an antenna diode on the flagged net and re-run just that net's check
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: adding diode clears violation -> confirms standard gate-oxide antenna charge issue, fixable by diode
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violation remains despite diode -> likely a via-antenna or multi-segment issue needing jumper instead

common_root_causes.cause: long single-layer wire segment routed well before connecting to the gate (classic wire antenna)
late-stage ECO routing/re-route that bypassed the antenna-aware router settings
missing or incorrectly placed antenna diode cells near the flagged pin
via-stack accumulation across many layers on a net not caught by simple wire-length heuristics
incorrect antenna rule setup/version mismatch between router and signoff tool

data.classic_trap: Blanket-inserting diodes everywhere a violation appears without checking whether a simple jumper/layer-hop would fix it more cleanly, bloating area and sometimes still missing via-stack cases.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, tighter gate-oxide margins and more routing layers make antenna violations more frequent and often require jumpers plus diodes together, unlike simpler single-fix cases common at 28nm

data.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Detailed-route DRC violation map overlaid with global-route congestion estimate for the same region
first_checks.why_first: cheap way to see if global route simply underestimated local difficulty

first_checks.check: Specific DRC rule types flagged (spacing, min-area, min-width, via enclosure)
first_checks.why_first: different rule categories point to very different root causes

first_checks.check: Local pin access / cell orientation in the hotspot area
first_checks.why_first: pin-access-limited cells are a common cheap-to-spot cause not visible at global-route resolution

first_checks.check: Track/grid alignment and non-default-rule (NDR) net usage in the hotspot
first_checks.why_first: special routing rules can create local conflicts invisible to global routing

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run detailed routing with increased local routing effort/iterations restricted to the hotspot only
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: hotspot clears with more effort -> genuinely a router-convergence/resource issue, not a hard physical conflict
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: hotspot persists even with max effort -> real physical/pin-access constraint

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Check if all violations in the hotspot involve the same specific cell type or pin shape
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: one cell type dominates -> cell-level pin-access/layout issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: violations involve many different cell types -> more likely a general congestion/resource shortage

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare hotspot DRCs with and without NDR (wide/spaced) nets routed through the region
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: removing NDR nets clears violations -> special-rule net conflict is the cause
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: no change -> NDR nets not the driver

common_root_causes.cause: local pin-access difficulty on specific standard cells or macro pins
global route underestimating true routing difficulty (resolution mismatch)
non-default-rule (wide/spaced) nets conflicting with dense standard-cell routing nearby
insufficient detailed-router effort/iterations allotted for that region in the flow
cell orientation/flip causing pin misalignment with adjacent rows

data.classic_trap: Repeatedly re-spreading placement globally to 'fix' a hotspot that's actually caused by a handful of cells with poor pin access, wasting turnaround time without addressing the real local issue.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, pin-access DRCs dominate far more than at 28nm due to tighter design rules, so this symptom is often a placement/cell-selection issue rather than a pure router capacity issue

first_checks.why_first: cheap visual check for structural floorplan problems causing global overflow

common_root_causes.cause: overall utilization target too aggressive for the design's connectivity complexity
poor macro floorplan (blocked channels, macros too close, pinwheel arrangement)

data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, cell legalization is much more sensitive to local density spikes, so divergence often requires floorplan-level fixes rather than the simple global density reduction that often sufficed at 28nm

data.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budgeting via period split
data.situation: Two blocks (or a block and top-level interconnect) are implemented separately and communicate synchronously across a boundary; each block's SDC needs input_delay/output_delay values before the other side exists in netlist form.
data.derivation: Start from the shared clock period T at the boundary. Subtract an estimated interconnect delay (wire + any boundary buffering) I, estimated early from floorplan wire-load or a placeholder (e.g. 10-15% of T for a typical reasonably-sized block-to-block wire). The remaining budget (T - I) is split between the launching block's internal output path and the receiving block's internal input path, often roughly proportional to each side's logic depth expectation, but a common starting split is 50/50 when no better info exists. So output_delay on the driving block's SDC = I + (share allocated to receive side), and input_delay on the receiving block's SDC reflects the same I plus driver-side share, expressed as 'time already consumed before this pin'. Iterating: as floorplan matures, replace the wire-load estimate with actual RC-extracted or global-route-estimated delay.
data.wrong_way: Giving both blocks the full period T as available budget without subtracting interconnect delay (i.e., forgetting interconnect is shared, not free), or worse, having each block's owner independently assume they get most of the period, causing double-booking. This silently breaks at integration when actual interconnect delay eats into both sides' assumed slack, and violations only appear at chip-level timing, far too late to easily fix.
data.defense: Point to the interconnect delay estimate's source (early floorplan wire-load model or a prior similar block's actual number), show the 50/50 or logic-depth-weighted split explicitly in a spreadsheet, and cross-check that summed input_delay + output_delay assumptions from both block owners equal (T - I), not more.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (budget assumed smaller interconnect delay than reality): chip-level setup violations at the boundary that require late ECOs or spec relaxation. Too loose (budget over-allocated interconnect delay, starving block-internal budget less than needed): blocks close individually with margin to spare, wasting achievable frequency, discovered only when someone asks why the chip is slower than either block's standalone number.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, interconnect delay is a much larger fraction of period than at 28nm, so the naive 50/50 split is less defensible and teams more often insist on an RC-based estimate even at floorplan stage
data._numeric_confidence_notes: assumes interconnect estimate around 10-15% of period as a common starting point (confidence 0.4); assumes 50/50 split as a common default absent better data (confidence 0.45)

data.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision for slow/quasi-static control signals
data.situation: A path exists in the timing graph (e.g., a mode-select, configuration register, or reset synchronizer output feeding combinational logic) but the signal is known to change far less often than every clock cycle, and normal single-cycle timing would be needlessly hard or impossible to meet.
data.derivation: First determine whether the path is truly never required to be sampled correctly on the very next cycle after a change (justifies false_path) versus is allowed extra cycles but must still eventually be captured correctly within N cycles (justifies multicycle_path -setup N). The distinguishing question: does functional correctness ever depend on the receiving logic seeing the new value within a bounded number of cycles? If yes, use multicycle with N derived from the known minimum interval between legal changes of the source signal (e.g., a signal architecturally guaranteed to be stable for at least 4 cycles after any change becomes 'set_multicycle_path 4 -setup' with a corresponding 'set_multicycle_path 3 -hold' to keep the hold check aligned to the cycle before the new setup edge). If the path is fundamentally asynchronous or functionally irrelevant to timing (e.g., a scan/test-only path, or a signal whose value at the sampling edge genuinely never matters), false_path is used instead.
data.wrong_way: Applying false_path to a signal that actually does need to be captured within a bounded time (common shortcut to 'make timing pass'), which silently removes the path from all timing analysis so a real functional timing failure (data changing too close to a legitimate sample point) is never caught by STA and only shows up as an intermittent functional bug in silicon or emulation.
data.defense: Cite the RTL/microarchitectural guarantee (e.g., a documented minimum hold-time-in-cycles for the control signal, enforced by a counter or handshake in the design) as the basis for the multicycle N, and show the corresponding hold multicycle adjustment (N-1) was also applied so hold checking wasn't silently left at the default single-cycle hold window, which would over-constrain hold and cause unnecessary buffer insertion.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (using single-cycle timing or too small an N when the real guarantee is looser): wastes implementation effort meeting an unnecessarily hard constraint, sometimes forcing pipeline stages that aren't functionally needed. Too loose (false_path where multicycle was appropriate, or N larger than the real guarantee): real setup/hold problems on that path are masked and can cause silicon failures that STA never flagged.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled
data._numeric_confidence_notes: the example of 'stable for at least 4 cycles -> multicycle 4/3' is illustrative only (confidence 0.3 that this specific number pattern generalizes; the setup-N/hold-N-1 relationship itself is standard and confidence is higher, ~0.6)

data.pattern_name: Over-constraining (frequency margin) during early implementation
data.situation: Early in physical implementation (initial placement, early CTS), before parasitics and final library corners are accurate, teams often run timing at a tighter clock period than the actual target to build in margin against later degradation.
data.derivation: Take the true target period T_target and apply a margin percentage M (commonly discussed in the range of 5-10% early on, sometimes more at very early floorplan stages) to get the working period used in early optimization: T_work = T_target * (1 - M). As the design matures (post-route, signoff parasitics available, real OCV/derate applied), M is reduced stage by stage until T_work converges to T_target (or slightly above it, since some residual margin is normal even at final signoff).
data.wrong_way: Keeping the same large early-stage margin all the way through to signoff without relaxing it, which silently wastes area/power (cells oversized, extra buffering) chasing a target no longer necessary, or conversely relaxing the margin too early (before parasitics are trustworthy) so the design looks like it's closing timing when in fact later corners will blow through the true target once real interconnect delay is added.
data.defense: Show the margin-reduction schedule tied to specific implementation milestones (e.g., 'margin relaxed only after post-route parasitics extracted, not before'), and present trend data of slack at each stage to justify that the margin was earning real protection against known sources of change (OCV widening, layer assignment, clock tree insertion) rather than being an arbitrary number.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (margin never relaxed): area/power penalty and possibly missed schedule chasing an artificially hard target. Too loose (margin removed too early or too small from the start): signoff timing violations appear late when the real corners and parasitics are in, often surfacing after the design was believed closed, forcing late ECOs under schedule pressure.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, the gap between early-stage and signoff-stage estimates is typically larger due to increased variation and multi-corner/multi-mode complexity, so margin schedules tend to be more conservative and staged more finely than at 28nm
data._numeric_confidence_notes: assumes 5-10% early margin as a commonly recalled starting range (confidence 0.4)

data.pattern_name: Virtual clock definition for primary I/O timing
data.situation: A block's inputs or outputs are timed relative to an external device or another chip whose internal clock structure is not part of this block's netlist (e.g., a chip-level I/O interface), so there's no physical clock object in this block to reference for input_delay/output_delay.
data.derivation: Define a virtual clock (create_clock with no -add to any real pin, just a name) with the same period and, critically, the same relationship (edge alignment/phase) as the external device's clock is specified to have relative to this chip's I/O clock. input_delay and output_delay values are then set relative to this virtual clock, using the external device's specified setup/hold or valid-delay windows (from its datasheet or interface spec) translated into the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic: for an input, input_delay = external device's clock-to-out max delay + board/trace delay; for an output, output_delay = external receiving device's required setup time + board/trace delay.
data.wrong_way: Reusing the block's internal core clock object directly as if it were the interface clock without checking whether the actual I/O clock has different phase alignment or period (e.g., due to PLL phase shift or a different divide ratio), which silently mis-times every I/O path relative to the real external timing relationship and is often only caught in board bring-up, not simulation or STA.
data.defense: Reference the interface specification document's timing diagram directly (datasheet setup/hold or valid-delay numbers) as the source of the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic, and show that the virtual clock's period/edges match the documented external clock relationship, not an assumption.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (input_delay/output_delay assumed worse external timing than actual): wastes internal timing budget, potentially forcing unnecessary pipeline stages on I/O paths. Too loose (assumed better external timing than actual, e.g., ignoring board trace delay): real interface timing failures only appear at board bring-up since STA showed the path passing.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled
data._numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numbers asserted beyond the general arithmetic shape

data.pattern_name: Generated/divided clock constraint derivation
data.situation: A clock is produced inside the design by dividing or gating a root clock (e.g., a simple toggle flip-flop divider or clock-gating cell producing a slower derived clock domain) and STA needs a correct create_generated_clock rather than an independent create_clock that could desynchronize from the source.
data.derivation: Use create_generated_clock referencing the source clock pin and the actual divide/multiply relationship implemented in the divider logic (e.g., -divide_by 2 for a simple toggle divider), applied at the output pin of the generating register/cell, so the tool derives the generated clock's period, waveform, and phase alignment automatically from the source clock rather than being independently specified. Verify the generated clock's edges align with the expected functional behavior of the divider (e.g., confirming which edge of the source clock the divided clock toggles on) by checking the divider's actual logic, not assuming a textbook 50% duty cycle divider.
data.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as an independent create_clock with a manually computed period, which loses the phase/edge relationship to the source clock entirely; this silently makes the tool treat the two clock domains as unrelated (effectively asynchronous) for timing purposes, so crossing paths between the root clock and the derived clock get analyzed with incorrect (often overly pessimistic or, if false-pathed, dangerously optimistic) skew assumptions instead of the true, tool-derivable relationship.
data.defense: Show the divider RTL/schematic and confirm the create_generated_clock's -divide_by (or -multiply_by) and -edges settings match the actual logic implementation, and demonstrate in the generated clock's reported waveform (from the tool) that it matches the expected functional divided waveform.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight/wrong relationship (e.g., wrong edge assumed): paths between root and divided domain may show false violations that get incorrectly 'fixed' by adding unnecessary margin or exceptions, or conversely real violations get masked because the tool thinks the domains are unrelated. Too loose (treating as fully asynchronous when it's not): crossing paths lose the benefit of the known, analyzable relationship and either get over-margined (wasting timing) or under-constrained if someone false-paths them assuming asynchrony that doesn't actually exist.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous clock-domain-crossing (CDC) constraint via false_path plus synchronizer awareness
data.situation: A signal crosses from one clock domain to a genuinely unrelated (asynchronous) clock domain through a synchronizer (e.g., a 2-flop synchronizer chain), and the path between the two domains needs an SDC exception since no valid static timing relationship exists between the clocks.
data.derivation: Apply set_false_path (or set_clock_groups -asynchronous for the whole domain pair, if broader) specifically from the synchronizer's first-stage input to its capturing flop, so STA does not attempt to compute a meaningless setup/hold check across unrelated clocks. Critically, the false_path (or async group) is scoped as narrowly as possible -- typically just the crossing point itself -- so that all other timing within each domain (including from the synchronizer's output onward) remains fully and normally checked; the exception must not accidentally blanket-cover logic that is not actually part of the crossing.
data.wrong_way: Applying a broad set_clock_groups -asynchronous between the two entire clock domains (rather than scoping to just the crossing flops) when there are actually other legitimate, related paths between those domains elsewhere in the design (e.g., a shared reset tree or a second, intentionally synchronous path), which silently removes real timing checks on paths that do need them, masking genuine violations elsewhere in the two domains' interaction.
data.defense: Point to the synchronizer's schematic/RTL showing it is a proper multi-flop synchronizer (not a single flop, which would be a metastability/CDC design bug independent of SDC), and show the false_path/async-group scoping is limited to exactly the crossing pins, verified by checking the SDC exception report for unintended path coverage.
data.signoff_risk: Too broad an exception (covers more than the true crossing): real synchronous paths elsewhere between the domains lose timing coverage, and violations there go undetected until functional failure. Missing or too narrow an exception (crossing not excepted at all): STA reports a spurious, unfixable 'violation' on an inherently asynchronous path, which teams sometimes 'fix' by adding meaningless buffering that does nothing for actual metastability risk (which is a separate CDC/MTBF concern, not a static timing one).
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Interconnect budgeting between two not-yet-implemented blocks using a placeholder wire-load/RC estimate
data.situation: At RTL/early floorplan stage, two blocks that will eventually be connected through top-level routing need boundary timing constraints (input_delay/output_delay) before either block or the top-level interconnect has real layout.
data.derivation: Estimate interconnect delay using a rough distance-based or wire-load-model-based number derived from the expected floorplan (e.g., block A and B are expected to be roughly adjacent vs across the die), producing a placeholder delay value I_est. This I_est is subtracted from the shared period the same way as boundary budgeting (see the period-split pattern), but flagged explicitly as provisional pending floorplan. A tracking mechanism (e.g., a budget spreadsheet or comment in the SDC) records the assumption so it can be revisited once floorplan or global-route estimates are available.
data.wrong_way: Treating the early placeholder I_est as final and never revisiting it once real floorplan/placement data exists, so if the actual distance between the blocks turns out much larger than assumed (e.g., a late floorplan change moves one block across the die), the boundary timing silently becomes wrong and isn't caught until block-level or chip-level signoff, by which point both blocks may have already been 'closed' to the wrong budget.
data.defense: Show the placeholder estimate is explicitly labeled provisional and tied to a specific floorplan assumption (e.g., 'assumes blocks share an edge'), with a defined checkpoint (e.g., 'to be revisited at floorplan freeze') rather than presented as a firm number.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (I_est assumed larger than reality): blocks over-budget for interconnect, individually closing with unnecessary margin, wasted effort. Too loose (I_est assumed smaller than the eventual real distance): chip-level integration reveals a boundary timing violation that neither block owner expected, often discovered late and expensive to fix since both blocks were independently signed off against the wrong assumption.
data.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, placeholder interconnect estimates are far riskier because wire delay is proportionally larger and less linear with distance, so teams more often insist on at least a rough global-route-based estimate rather than a pure wire-load-model guess even at early stages
data._numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numeric margin asserted; pattern is about process/tracking discipline rather than a specific arithmetic constant

data.title: Clock frequency vs. chip design philosophy
data.decision: POWER4 was designed with high clock frequency as a primary goal, achieved through deep pipelining and circuit/custom design rather than relying solely on architectural features.
data.rationale: The paper argues frequency alone doesn't determine performance, but that combining frequency with a balanced, well-architected system (memory bandwidth, multiple cores) yields greater overall system throughput than chasing frequency in isolation.
data.outcome: POWER4 achieved multi-GHz frequencies while maintaining a balanced system design intended to avoid bottlenecks elsewhere.
data.weakest_point: I recall the general theme (frequency is not the only goal, balance matters) but cannot confirm exact framing or that it's called out this way structurally.

data.title: Single-chip module vs. multi-chip module (MCM) packaging
data.decision: The paper describes packaging four POWER4 chips (eight cores total) together on a multi-chip module to form a larger SMP building block.
data.rationale: Packaging multiple chips together allowed fast, low-latency chip-to-chip communication for building larger symmetric multiprocessor systems without going through slower off-module paths.
data.outcome: The MCM approach enabled systems scaling from a single chip up to 32-way (four MCMs) configurations reportedly discussed in the paper.
data.weakest_point: Exact numbers (four chips per MCM, resulting core/way counts) may be slightly misremembered; this is somewhat general POWER4 knowledge blended with paper-specific recall.

data.title: On-chip dual-core design with shared L2
data.where_in_paper: Chip overview / core and cache hierarchy section
data.decision: POWER4 placed two processor cores on a single chip sharing an on-chip L2 cache.
data.rationale: Sharing L2 between two cores was intended to improve efficiency of cache usage and inter-core communication compared to giving each core a private, non-shared L2.
data.outcome: This became a defining architectural feature of POWER4, described as enabling efficient chip-level multiprocessing.
data.weakest_point: I am fairly confident of the dual-core-shared-L2 fact from general knowledge, but less sure how the paper frames it as a 'decision with rationale' versus a plain description.

data.title: RAS (Reliability, Availability, Serviceability) design approach
data.decision: The paper describes building RAS features (such as error checking/correction, dynamic deallocation of faulty resources) directly into the POWER4 microarchitecture rather than treating reliability as an afterthought.
data.rationale: Enterprise/server customers require high availability; the designers state RAS must be designed in from the start rather than added later, since retrofitting reliability into a design is less effective.
data.outcome: POWER4 included various RAS mechanisms integrated into the chip and system design.
data.weakest_point: I recall this theme exists in POWER4-related IBM literature broadly but am not fully certain of its specific placement or exact wording in this particular paper.

assumptions_invoked: €100 arrangement fee paid at t=0 is treated as a charge at t=0, reducing the net amount made available to the consumer: net drawdown = €10,000 - €100 = €9,900 at t=0
24 equal monthly repayments of €450 commence one month after drawdown: times t = k/12 years for k = 1..24
Periods expressed in years; one month = 1/12 year (Annex I remark (c), 30.41666 days/month, so 1 month = 1/12 exactly)
Result rounded to one decimal place per Annex I remark (d) (round half up)
Annex I Part II assumption (d): for overdrafts the total amount is deemed to be drawn in full for the whole duration of the contract
Duration not determinable => assumed 3 months (directive's fallback of 3 months / one quarter = 0.25 years) per Annex I Part II assumption (c)
12% nominal per annum charged monthly => monthly rate = 12%/12 = 1%; interest on €3,000 for 3 months = €3,000*((1.01)^3 - 1) = €90.90
€25 monthly account fee for 3 months = €75.00; total repaid at 3 months = €3,000 + €90.90 + €75.00 = €3,165.90
All charges (interest + fees) paid as a single repayment at t = 3/12 years; one month = 1/12 year; result to one decimal place
Annex I Part II assumption (a): where the consumer has freedom of drawdown (open-end credit), the total credit is deemed to be drawn immediately and in full => €1,500 at t=0
Repayment in 12 equal monthly instalments (source-logic: assumption of equal amortisation over the assumed 12-month horizon, one month = 1/12 year)
18% nominal per annum, monthly compounding => monthly rate i = 0.18/12 = 1.5%; payment p = 1500 / sum_{k=1..12}(1.015)^(-k) = €137.52
No other fees; result to one decimal place
Unascertainable drawdown => Annex I Part II assumption (a): total credit deemed drawn immediately and in full at t=0, so €5,000 drawn at t=0
€200 broker fee financed into the balance at t=0 => added to the amount drawn/borrowed, giving drawdown = €5,000 + €200 = €5,200 at t=0 (this is why it differs from a t=0 cash fee: see below)
Single repayment at 12 months; 8% nominal per annum => repayment = €5,200 * 1.08 = €5,616 at t = 1 year
One month = 1/12 year; result to one decimal place
data.financed_fee_note: A t=0 cash fee reduces the net amount made available to the consumer (net drawdown = principal - fee), leaving the repayment stream unchanged - it raises the APRC because the consumer receives less up front. A fee financed into the balance instead increases the drawn amount (drawdown rises from €5,000 to €5,200) while the repayment is calculated on that larger balance; here the repayment is 8% of €5,200, so the APRC remains exactly 8% - the fee is silently amortised into the loan rather than paid out of pocket.

data.weakest_point: Case 2 is the most assumption-heavy and therefore most likely to diverge from the directive's exact method: the treatment of the €25 monthly fee and monthly interest (single lump repayment at 3 months vs. deducted/charged each month), the 3-month duration fallback, and whether the fee reduces the net drawdown or is a separate charge all affect the PV equation. Case 1's treatment of the arrangement fee as a t=0 charge (reducing net drawdown to €9,900 rather than a separate outflow) is the next-most-likely divergence point. The monthly-to-year conversion uses exactly 1/12 throughout, consistent with the Annex convention.

data.reasoning: "more than 2 percent" is strict inequality (>2%), so only values strictly greater than 2% trigger.
"more than 36 months" is strict (>36), so only durations strictly exceeding 36 months trigger.
"1.5 or more percentage points" is inclusive (>=1.5), so spreads at or above 1.5 trigger.
"does not exceed ... by 2.25 or more" negates an inclusive condition, making the effective pass boundary strict (<2.25).
"less than" is strict (<), so both revenue and income must be strictly below thresholds to pass; only the pair with both below passes.
"equal to or greater than 16%" is inclusive (>=16%), so ETRs at or above 16% pass.
"at least equal to 50%" is inclusive (>=50%), so ratios at or above 50% pass.
"equal to or greater than" the minimum is inclusive (>=), so values at or above threshold pass.

data.weakest_point: Rule 5 (GloBE de-minimis): I am least certain I have the exact verbatim phrasing of the OECD GloBE rules regarding the de-minimis exclusion, as the consolidated commentary may use slightly different formulations like 'is less than' versus 'does not exceed'.

data.symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals whether placement blocked pin access channels

first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — misdirected high-fanout nets create artificial congestion

discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global routing capacity or layer-assignment issue

Datapath too long (placement too spread out)
Missing or wrong clock-tree exceptions on gating cells
OCV / AOCV / POCV on-clock-path variation at advanced nodes

data.symptom: IR-drop-induced timing failure

first_checks.check: Overlay dynamic IR-drop map with failing-path physical locations
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — spatial correlation confirms voltage drop causing delay

first_checks.check: Check decap placement density and power-grid stripe spacing
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals grid weakness before re-simulation

first_checks.check: Inspect switching-activity vectors for peak coincident toggle windows
first_checks.why_first: rules out vector-driven worst-case vs real workload

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Rerun timing with IR-drop annotation (voltage-aware timing); if slack matches signoff failure, IR drop is confirmed causal
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: IR drop causing cell slowdown
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: pure timing or constraint issue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If failures cluster in one power domain or grid window vs scattered globally, it is local grid weakness; if global, it is system-level power delivery
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: local grid or decap insufficiency
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: package or board-level power delivery

common_root_causes.cause: Insufficient power-grid stripe density or width
High simultaneous switching on clock or data paths
Inadequate decap placement in high-activity regions
Package or board-level PDN resonance

data.classic_trap: Blaming cell delay or process variation when the path is actually slowing down due to local voltage drop
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: IR drop is drastically worse due to lower operating voltage and thinner metals, making voltage-aware timing signoff mandatory

data.symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Check CTS exceptions: float pins, exclude pins, sink types on gating/mux cells
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — wrong exceptions cause the majority of divergence

first_checks.check: Verify placement of divergent sinks relative to clock root
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals physical distance driving imbalance

first_checks.check: Inspect clock-cell sizing uniformity (no mix of drive strengths on same branch)
first_checks.why_first: rules out tool auto-sizing creating imbalance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all divergent sinks sit behind one clock-gating cell, fix exception on that cell; if spread across branches, re-balance tree topology
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: exception or gating-cell misconfiguration
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global tree-topology imbalance

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Force all sinks to same insertion delay target with relaxed transition; if convergence achieved, original target was physically unroutable
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: target physically impossible given placement
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: tool configuration or exception error

common_root_causes.cause: Missing or wrong CTS exceptions on clock-gating cells
Asymmetric placement of sink clusters
Mixed buffer drive strengths creating unbalanced branches
Clock-mux structure not properly balanced

data.classic_trap: Re-running CTS with more effort instead of auditing exceptions on gating/mux cells
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: useful skew methodology is more accepted, so some divergence is intentional; 28nm expected near-zero skew

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Check ECO connectivity changes vs original netlist
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — ECO disconnects cause majority of missing/shorted nets

first_checks.check: Verify power/ground pin connectivity and strap-to-pin connections
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — PG opens/shorts are common and easy to spot

first_checks.check: Inspect routing shorts in congested macro-corner regions
first_checks.why_first: rules out physical routing error before schematic blame

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS with ECO netlist only (no layout changes); if mismatch persists, it is netlist-side ECO error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: netlist/schematic mismatch from ECO
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: layout routing error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If all shorts are between two specific nets across many locations, it is a routing DRC or via-stack error; if single location, it is local short
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: systematic routing or via-definition error
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: isolated manufacturing or extraction glitch

common_root_causes.cause: ECO introduced disconnected or wrongly connected net
Routing short in high-congestion region near macros
Power-grid strap shorting to signal routing
Extraction setup error (wrong layer mapping)

data.classic_trap: Assuming routing tool bug when the netlist ECO disconnected a pin
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: multi-patterning decomposition errors can create opens/shorts not visible in standard extraction, requiring color-aware LVS

data.symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Check filler-cell and end-cap insertion — these appear as extra devices in layout
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — filler cells are the #1 false-extra-device report

first_checks.check: Verify tap/well-connect cell placement and recognition
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — well-tap cells often misidentified as extra transistors

first_checks.check: Compare netlist device count vs GDS device count per module
first_checks.why_first: rules out systematic sizing mismatch before spot-checking

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS excluding filler and tap cells; if mismatch resolves, it is cell-recognition issue not real device error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: filler/tap cells misinterpreted as functional devices
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: real device sizing or insertion error

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If extra devices are all minimum-size transistors in unused channel regions, they are fillers; if clustered in one functional block, it is ECO or synthesis error
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: filler or well-tap artifact
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: functional netlist error

common_root_causes.cause: Filler cells reported as extra devices
Tap/well-connect cells misidentified
ECO inserted wrong-drive-strength cell
Synthesis vs layout library cell-mapping mismatch

data.classic_trap: Debugging a 'device size mismatch' that is actually filler cells being swept into the device count
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: well-isolation and tap structures are more complex, generating more false-extra-device reports from LVS

data.symptom: antenna (process-antenna-effect) violations at signoff

first_checks.check: Check metal-layer assignment on longest violating nets
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — upper-layer long routes are the dominant antenna source

first_checks.check: Verify antenna jumper / diode insertion was enabled in routing
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — reveals if fix was never attempted

first_checks.check: Inspect gate-area ratios on violating pins
first_checks.why_first: rules out small-gate devices being disproportionately exposed

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert jumpers on top 10 violating nets and re-extract; if violations clear, it is pure metal-area accumulation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: metal-area to gate-area ratio exceeded
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: diode or layer-rule misconfiguration

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If violations are all on one metal layer, it is layer-specific rule or routing preference; if across layers, it is global antenna ratio issue
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: layer-specific routing directive problem
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global antenna-rule or design-wide issue

common_root_causes.cause: Long uninterrupted metal routes on upper layers
Missing or disabled antenna-fix insertion during routing
Small-gate devices with large fanout
Multi-patterning decomposition creating antenna exposure on split masks

data.classic_trap: Adding jumpers everywhere instead of re-routing high-violation nets to lower layers or inserting diodes at gates
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: multi-patterning creates cumulative antenna across masks, making antenna violations much more frequent and complex

data.symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Check DRC rule deck version vs design rules used in global route
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — version mismatch causes false hotspots

first_checks.check: Inspect via-doubling and via-enclosure rules at hotspot locations
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — via rules are the most common detailed-route-only constraint

first_checks.check: Verify cell-boundary spacing and DFM rules near standard cells
first_checks.why_first: rules out cell-edge DFM constraints

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Relax via-doubling rules in test run; if hotspots vanish, it is via-rule conflict not wire congestion
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: via-rule or enclosure constraint
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: wire-spacing or track congestion

discriminating_experiments.experiment: If hotspots are all at cell boundaries vs track interiors, it is cell-level DFM; if in track interiors, it is global-route capacity overestimation
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: cell-boundary DFM or spacing rule
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: global router capacity model error

common_root_causes.cause: Via-doubling or enclosure rules not modeled in global router
DFM spacing rules at cell boundaries
Global router overestimated track availability (double-patterning or coloring conflict)
Wire-spacing rules tighter than global-route grid resolution

data.classic_trap: Blaming detailed router and re-running with more effort when global router capacity model was wrong
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: DRC rule count explodes (order of 10,000+ rules), and global router almost never models all DFM rules, making hotspots routine

data.symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check overall utilization and local utilization hot spots
first_checks.why_first: rules out the most — high utilization is the primary cause

first_checks.check: Inspect macro placement and channel width between macros
first_checks.why_first: cheapest — macros blocking routing channels causes overflow even at low utilisation

first_checks.check: Verify pin-density map vs routing-track capacity
first_checks.why_first: rules out pin-congestion driving overflow

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Remove all macros and re-place; if overflow resolves, it is macro-placement blocking channels
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: macro placement blocking routing resources
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: std-cell density or netlist complexity

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reduce utilization by 10% and re-place; if overflow resolves, it is pure capacity; if not, it is pin-density or macro-channel
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: utilization too high for available routing layers
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: structural blockage (macro or pin density)

common_root_causes.cause: Overall placement utilization too high for routing layer count
Macro placement creating unroutable channels
High pin density on specific nets exceeding track capacity
Netlist with excessive connectivity (high fanin/fanout) not partitioned

data.classic_trap: Pushing placement utilisation higher when the overflow is actually caused by macro placement blocking routing channels
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more routing layers available but pin dimensions smaller and double-patterning reduces effective track count, so sweet spot utilisation is lower

data.pattern_name: Hierarchical block input-delay budget from unimplemented launch block
data.situation: Two blocks A and B in same clock domain; B has input port driven by A; A not yet implemented; need set_input_delay on B's input so B's implementation leaves enough margin for A to be built later.
data.derivation: Assume clock period T = 10ns (confidence 0.2 — example only). Budget split: launch logic (A internal) = 0.50  T = 5ns (confidence 0.4 on 50% split), interconnect/wire delay = 0.10  T = 1ns (confidence 0.4 on 10% interconnect), capture internal (B input-to-flop) = 0.40  T = 4ns (confidence 0.4 on 40% capture). set_input_delay -clock clk [get_ports IN] value = launch + interconnect = 0.60  T = 6ns. Remaining time for B's internal logic = T - input_delay - T_setup = 4ns - T_setup. If A later requires more than 5ns, B's budget is already consumed and integration fails.
data.wrong_way: Setting input_delay = T (period) leaves 0ns for B internal logic — always fails STA. Setting input_delay = 0 leaves full period for B but A can never meet its launch delay in integration. Silently breaks: over-constrained B wastes area/power; under-constrained B passes STA but system fails at integration.
data.defense: Engineer presents the budget spreadsheet showing the 50/10/40 split justified by pipeline stage count and wire-load estimates from similar blocks; claims this is conservative for A's complexity.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: B over-optimized, wasted power/area, possible failure to close timing. Too loose: A cannot meet launch delay at integration, system timing failure on silicon.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: OCV/POCV requires extra 10-15% margin in budget split (confidence 0.6), reducing the capture-side allocation

data.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle on slow control/configuration registers
data.situation: Configuration or reset signal that changes only at boot or infrequently; crosses flops in same clock domain but data is not required to be valid next cycle.
data.derivation: If signal only needs to propagate in N cycles (e.g., N=2 for a two-cycle config write), set_multicycle_path N -from [src_regs] -to [dest_regs]. For same-clock slow control, set_multicycle_path 2. Hold check defaults to same edge; add set_multicycle_path 1 -hold to keep hold check at launch edge. Arithmetic: setup check moves to cycle N, so required time = N*T - T_setup. If truly async and never timed (e.g., test reset), set_false_path -from [src] -to [dest].
data.wrong_way: Setting set_false_path on a signal that actually changes at operational speed — silently breaks: chip works at low speed or in simulation but fails intermittently at target frequency because data arrives late relative to capture edge.
data.defense: Engineer shows waveform or protocol spec proving signal only toggles once per N cycles; points to RTL state machine guaranteeing N-cycle separation.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight (no exception): wasted effort fixing unneeded paths, area/power penalty. Too loose (false path when multicycle needed): data corruption if signal changes faster than assumed; intermittent system failure.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Early-implementation over-constraint margin
data.situation: Block synthesis or pre-CTS, before final clock tree and routing; want margin so later stages don't invalidate timing closure.
data.derivation: Target clock period = T. Set constraint to 0.80  T (i.e., 20% margin) (confidence 0.5 on 20% being typical; some teams use 10-15%). Alternatively, set_clock_uncertainty additional 0.05  T (confidence 0.5 on 5% extra). Arithmetic: if T=5ns, constrain to 4ns. Relax to T after CTS or route. Over-constraint removed in final signoff constraint set.
data.wrong_way: Over-constraining by 50% (0.5*T) — tool cannot close timing, wasted iterations, team blames flow. Or forgetting to relax before tapeout — chip ships over-margined, wasted power/area, no benefit.
data.defense: Engineer cites historical data from prior tapeouts showing post-CTS insertion delay consumed 15-20% of period (confidence 0.5); margin chosen to absorb this.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: area/power penalty, possible failure to close timing, schedule slip. Too loose (no margin): post-P&R timing fails, late ECO required, tapeout delay.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: over-constrain by less (e.g., 10%) because tool has harder time closing on aggressive targets due to wire delay dominance (confidence 0.55)

data.pattern_name: Virtual clock for external-device input timing
data.situation: Chip receives data from external device with known t_co, board trace delay; need to constrain input port relative to external clock.
data.derivation: Create virtual clock: create_clock -name vclk -period T. set_input_delay -clock vclk -max t_co_ext + t_board_delay [get_ports IN]. Assume T=10ns (confidence 0.2), t_co_ext=2ns (confidence 0.3), t_board=1ns (confidence 0.3). Input delay = 3ns. Required internal arrival = T - input_delay - T_setup = 10 - 3 - 0.1 = 6.9ns for internal logic.
data.wrong_way: Using real internal clock with offset instead of virtual clock — creates false clock relationship, breaks timing analysis. Ignoring board delay — silently breaks: STA passes but system fails at board level because trace delay was not accounted.
data.defense: Engineer presents external device datasheet t_co max, board stack-up trace delay estimate, and system-level timing budget showing the arithmetic.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: STA fails unnecessarily, over-design of input buffer. Too loose: system integration failure, external device setup not met at board level.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Generated clock from divider for low-power domain
data.situation: Internal divided clock from PLL or RTL divider for a slower domain; need to constrain paths through divided clock and crossings back to fast domain.
data.derivation: create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [master_pin] -divide_by 2 [divider_output]. Period of clk_div2 = 2*T. For paths from fast to slow domain: launch period = T, capture period = 2T. Default setup check at first slow-clock edge (T) may be too tight; often set_multicycle_path 2 -to [slow_domain_regs] to allow full 2T. Arithmetic: if T=5ns, fast-to-slow default setup check at 5ns; with multicycle 2, check at 10ns.
data.wrong_way: Using create_clock instead of create_generated_clock — breaks clock relationship, timing engine treats as async, no cross-domain paths analyzed. Silently breaks: paths between domains either falsely pass (no check) or are over-constrained.
data.defense: Engineer shows clock tree schematic, divider ratio, and cross-domain path report proving correct clock relationship and multicycle exception.
data.signoff_risk: Wrong command or missing multicycle: complete loss of valid timing checks or false violations; silicon failure if critical path escapes.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.pattern_name: Asynchronous CDC handshake max-delay constraint for MTBF
data.situation: Two async clock domains with handshake; clocks unrelated; need to bound metastability probability with max-delay on synchronizer flops.
data.derivation: set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clkA} -group {clkB}. For synchronizer flops, set_max_delay 0.5 * T_fast (confidence 0.4 on 0.5 factor; typical range 0.3-0.7). If T_fast=2ns, max_delay=1ns. This bounds the time for signal to propagate through first sync flop, reducing metastability window. Arithmetic: MTBF ∝ exp(delay/metastability_time_constant); tighter max_delay improves MTBF.
data.wrong_way: No constraint at all — no MTBF check, potential for rare metastability failures in field. Silently breaks: chip passes STA but fails intermittently in system due to unresolved CDC.
data.defense: Engineer presents MTBF calculation spreadsheet showing max_delay value achieves target MTBF (e.g., >1 year mean time between failures) given process metastability parameters.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: routing congestion, wasted resources on short paths. Too loose: metastability not bounded, system fails intermittently; field returns.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: smaller nodes have smaller metastability window, so max_delay needs to be tighter (e.g., 0.3*T_fast, confidence 0.6); POCV also affects MTBF calculation

data.pattern_name: Clock uncertainty budgeting for PLL jitter and variation
data.situation: Setting clock_uncertainty for setup/hold to account for PLL jitter, AOCV/POCV, and clock-tree variation at various implementation stages.
data.derivation: Uncertainty = PLL_jitter + variation_margin. Assume PLL_jitter = 0.05  T (confidence 0.5 on 5%), AOCV_margin = 0.02  T (confidence 0.5 on 2%). Total = 0.07  T. For T=5ns, uncertainty = 0.35ns. Applied via set_clock_uncertainty 0.35 [get_clocks clk]. Pre-CTS: add estimated clock skew (e.g., 0.10T, confidence 0.4). Post-CTS: remove skew, keep jitter + variation.
data.wrong_way: Setting uncertainty = 0 — no margin for jitter; silicon fails at speed. Setting too high (e.g., 0.3*T) — cannot close timing, wasted area/power. Silently breaks: wrong uncertainty hides real timing problems or creates false failures.
data.defense: Engineer presents PLL datasheet jitter spec, process variation model (AOCV/POCV derate tables), and clock-tree insertion-delay estimate to justify the split.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: fails STA, over-design. Too loose: silicon timing failure, chip doesn't meet frequency rating.
data.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: POCV adds significant uncertainty, typically 2-3x 28nm (confidence 0.6), requiring higher budget or statistical timing

data.pattern_name: Output delay budget to external device
data.situation: Chip outputs data to external device with known t_su and board trace delay; need set_output_delay to constrain internal logic.
data.derivation: Create virtual clock vclk with period T. set_output_delay -clock vclk -max T - t_su_ext - t_board_delay [get_ports OUT]. Assume T=10ns (confidence 0.2), t_su_ext=1ns (confidence 0.3), t_board=0.5ns (confidence 0.3). Output_delay = 10 - 1 - 0.5 = 8.5ns. Internal logic must produce data 8.5ns after clock edge. Slack = T - output_delay - T_internal_delay - T_skew.
data.wrong_way: Setting output_delay = 0 — internal logic gets full period but external device misses data because t_su not accounted. Silently breaks: STA passes, board-level system fails.
data.defense: Engineer presents external device t_su spec, board trace delay calculation, and system timing budget showing the subtraction arithmetic.
data.signoff_risk: Too tight: internal logic over-optimized, power/area wasted. Too loose: external device setup violation at system level, board failure.
data.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

data.title: Dual-core chip-multiprocessor (two cores on one die)
data.decision: Implement two full processor cores on a single die sharing a centralized on-chip L2 cache, presenting as a symmetric multiprocessor (SMP).
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Single-core scaling to a wider/larger core; separate L2 caches per core.
data.rationale: To deliver SMP capability on a single chip, improve aggregate throughput, and simplify multi-chip SMP system design while managing wire delay and complexity at 0.18-micron technology.
data.outcome: POWER4 shipped as a dual-core processor; two cores shared the on-chip L2 and competed for L3 and memory bandwidth through a shared memory controller.
data.weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly frames separate-L2 as a rejected alternative versus simply describing the chosen shared-L2 design.

data.title: Off-chip L3 cache as a backing store rather than larger on-chip L2
data.decision: Use a moderate-sized on-chip shared L2 cache backed by a large off-chip L3 cache rather than integrating a very large L2 on-chip.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Integrating a much larger L2 on-chip; relying solely on off-chip memory without L3.
data.rationale: On-chip area and wire-delay constraints limited practical L2 size; an off-chip L3 provided high-bandwidth, high-capacity backing store without consuming die area needed for dual cores and logic.
data.outcome: POWER4 system included an on-chip L2 and an off-chip L3 controlled by on-chip L3 controllers, improving effective memory latency.
data.weakest_point: The paper may present this as a natural hierarchy rather than an explicit weighed decision with named alternatives.

data.title: System interconnect: shared-bus fabric for multi-chip SMP
data.decision: Use a high-frequency shared-bus interconnect (the processor bus) to link multiple POWER4 chips and the memory controller rather than a switch-based interconnect.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Crossbar or packet-switched interconnect between chips.
data.rationale: A shared bus with snooping provided a proven, lower-complexity coherence mechanism for the target 1–4 socket systems; switch complexity was not justified for the targeted system scale.
data.outcome: Multi-chip POWER4 systems used the shared processor bus with snooping; the design met bandwidth goals for commercial workloads.
data.weakest_point: The paper may describe the bus without explicitly weighing it against a crossbar alternative; this may be general knowledge dressed as paper content.

data.title: RAS: checkstop and recovery philosophy
data.decision: Implement extensive error detection with checkstop on unrecoverable errors and selective recovery/retry for correctable errors, including ECC on caches and buffers.
data.alternatives_or_rejected: Lockstep redundant cores or full fault-tolerance (rejected as too costly for commercial microprocessor).
data.rationale: Mainframe-class RAS was a design objective for enterprise systems, but full redundancy was area- and power-prohibitive; detection-plus-checkstop provided a practical middle ground.
data.outcome: POWER4 included pervasive ECC, parity, and checkstop logic; the paper reports this met enterprise RAS expectations.
data.weakest_point: Whether lockstep redundancy is explicitly named as a rejected alternative in the paper or is general background knowledge.
